titleStmt.title: Historia naturalis; or, The Natural History, part II: On the Properties of Animals

sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise auto-generee (IA, non relue par un latiniste) a partir du texte latin du corpus zoomathia sous zoo63/1l (Iohannes Egidius Zamorensis [Juan Gil de Zamora], Historia naturalis, partie II "De proprietatibus animalium"). Le texte latin source est issu de la base de donnees Sourcencyme (IRHT, dir. Francois Bougard, 2023) -- une source academique reputee, non issue d'un pipeline d'encodage automatique par IA. La structure du texte latin source (oeuvre : livre "De proprietatibus animalium" > partie 1 "in generali" [25 traites generaux, prologue] et partie 2 "in speciali" [11 traites par animal, organises alphabetiquement, certains subdivises en chapitres] ; 391 citations organisees en <cit> avec <bibl> d'attribution et <quote>) est integralement preservee ci-dessous, div par div. Le texte latin source s'interrompt lui-meme, dans son etat actuel au sein du corpus, au milieu de l'entree "De aranea" (l'araignee), n'ayant traite que les animaux dont le nom latin commence par la lettre A -- ceci reflete fidelement l'etendue du texte tel qu'il existe dans le corpus zoomathia (zoo63/1l), et non une troncature introduite lors de cette traduction. Les citations sans attribution bibliographique explicite dans le texte source ont ete laissees sans <bibl>. Traduction fournie a titre de meilleur effort ; a verifier par un latiniste avant toute citation savante. Correspond au texte latin deja present dans le corpus sous zoo63/1l.

div.head: <DE PROPRIETATIBUS ANIMALIUM>
<MEDITACIO PROHEMIALIS>

bibl.author: Iohannes Egidius Zamorensis, Historia naturalis Iohannis Egidii Zamorensis
Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Here begins the introductory meditation on the treatise on the properties of animals in general and in particular — beasts, that is, livestock, draught animals, snakes, worms, and serpents — which brother Juan Gil, of the Order of Friars Minor, compiled from the sayings of Aristotle, Avicenna, Galen, Constantine, Pliny, Jorath, and from the sayings of other philosophers and saints, whose opinions were and are approved, without prejudice to a better opinion, always presupposing in all sayings and writings the foundation of the orthodox faith.

Since I ardently desired to investigate and know the natures, powers, and workings of all the animals that have generally come to men's notice — beasts, that is, draught animals, livestock, creeping things, worms, and serpents — so that I might make from them a ladder by which I might rise to a clearer knowledge and delight in the Creator, that word suddenly fell upon my mind which is contained in the first chapter of Genesis, namely, that the Most High and eternal God brought forth from the earth three kinds of animal: draught animals, that is, creeping things and beasts. Draught animals as helps for work or food; creeping things and beasts, however, for the exercise of man destined to sin.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: So that I might, as far as is possible for a man, arrive more easily and better at knowledge of all these animals, I went through the opinions of Aristotle and Avicenna and Pliny and Jorath and Isidore and other philosophers and saints on animals, and, without prejudice to their opinions, I arranged the general and particular matters — disputed from Solomon, from the elephant down to the little worm — for grasping the natures of animals, according to the order noted below.

Let all my rivals know, then, who know nothing else but to bark against studious men, that up to this day nothing more complete or more perfect has been handed down to them concerning the natures and properties of animals, great and small alike, than what will be treated in this work, with God Most High as guide, without prejudice, according to the order set out below. Here ends the prologue.

div.head: <DE NATURIS ET PROPRIETATIBUS ANIMALIUM IN GENERALI>

cit.quote: Here begin the titles concerning the natures and properties of animals in general and also in particular. The first treatise will be on the primary production of animals and their primary naming, and their manifold difference and distinction. The second treatise will be on the difference and distinction of creeping things, serpents, and worms in general, since particulars will be given each in its own place. The third treatise will be on the necessary condition of the members and senses in general, and their proper ordering — smell also, and breath, voice, waking, and sleeping. The fourth treatise will be on the nourishment of animals, that is, eating and drinking. The fifth treatise will be on the boldness, greed, and generation, or begetting of offspring, of animals. The sixth treatise will be on the lengthening and shortening of animals' lives. The seventh treatise will be on the complexion of animals' flesh and its proper ordering for human consumption. The eighth treatise will be on the artificial preparation of animals' flesh. The ninth treatise will be on the proper ordering of animals' manifold usefulness to men, medicinal usefulness included. The tenth treatise will be on the nature of milk. The eleventh, on the nature of whey. The twelfth treatise, on the nature of butter. The thirteenth, on the nature of cheese. The fourteenth, on the nature of rennet. The fifteenth, on the nature of wool. The sixteenth, on the nature of blood. The seventeenth, on the nature of dung. The eighteenth, on the nature of urine. The nineteenth treatise will be on seed. The twentieth treatise will be on the menses. The twenty-first, on tears. The twenty-second, on saliva. The twenty-third, on sweat. The twenty-fourth, on sleeping and waking. The twenty-fifth, on the death and life of animals. The twenty-sixth, on the particular natural condition of each animal, according to alphabetical order, beginning with animals — that is, livestock, beasts, and draught animals, snakes, serpents, and worms — beginning from the letter A, then from B, then from C, until Z is reached, which is the last letter in alphabetical order. The twenty-seventh will be on the perfection of plants, animals, and men — that is, the vegetative, sensitive, and rational soul. Here end the titles. Here it truly begins.

div.head: TRACTATUS PRIMUS, DE PRIMARIA ORIGINACIONE ANIMALIUM ET EORUM MULTIPLICI DIFFERENCIA ET DISTINCCIONE ET NOMINUM PRIMARIA IMPOSICIONE

cit.quote: The Most High God, truthful and eternal, having adorned all the upper parts of the world — that is, the heaven, the air, and the water — at last on the sixth day adorned the lowest part of the world, namely the earth. For God brought forth from the earth three kinds of animal, that is, draught animals, creeping things, and beasts. For the Most High and eternal God, foreseeing that man was to fall through sin into the penalty of labor, or was to perish miserably, gave him draught animals as helps for his own work and food, and creeping things and beasts for his exercise.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis, Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Adam first gave names according to Isidore, in the fifteenth book of the Etymologies. But the peoples afterward gave a word to each of the animals from their own language. For Adam did not impose those names according to the Latin tongue, or the Greek, or that of any barbarous peoples, but according to that language which before the Flood was the one tongue of all, which is called Hebrew, according to Isidore. In Latin, moreover, animals or living things are so called because they are animated by life and moved by spirit. Quadrupeds are so called because they walk on four feet. These, though they resemble livestock, are nonetheless not under human care, as stags, fallow deer, wild asses, and the like. But neither are they beasts, like lions; nor draught animals, in that they can help in the use of men. We call 'pecus' [livestock] everything that lacks human speech and shape. Properly, however, the name 'pecora' is usually applied to those animals that are fit to be eaten, like sheep and swine, or suited to man's use, like horses and oxen. There is a difference, however, between 'pecora' and 'pecudes,' for the ancients commonly used 'pecora' to signify all animals. 'Pecudes,' however, are only those animals that are eaten, as though 'pacudes' [from 'pascere,' to feed]. Generally, however, every grazing animal is called 'pecus' from grazing ['pascendo']. 'Iumenta' [draught animals], however, took their name from the fact that they help ['iuvent'] our labor or burden by carrying or plowing. For the ox draws carts and turns over the hardest clods of earth. The horse and the ass carry burdens and ease men's labor in walking. Hence 'iumenta' are so called from helping men, for they are animals of great strength. Indeed, they are also called 'armenta,' either because we plow ['aramus'] with them, or because we use them in arms; others, however, understand 'armenta' to mean only oxen, from plowing, as though 'aramenta,' or because they are armed with horns. Similarly there is a difference between 'armenta' and 'greges' [flocks], for 'armenta' belong to horses and oxen, while 'greges' belong to goats and sheep. Thus far Isidore, in the Etymologies.

It should be noted that in the body of an animal there are three modes of composition. The first is the mixture of the elements in like members; the second is the mixture of like parts into functional organs; the third is of organs from unlike parts, as the hand is composed of sinews and bones. And the sense of this is prior in all like members; the operations, however, are in the organic members, that is, through the power of sense, motion, and appetite of animals. Each animal has bodily instruments suited to its own power; for the lion, since it is of bold and irascible disposition, has a strong and heavy body, claws on its feet, and the sharpest teeth in its mouth; the hare, however, since it is most timid, has limbs most suited by their excessive lightness to flight. He made man ruddy, as befitted the creation of his blood. He made the breasts and testicles white, for the making of milk and seed. In this way he made all the members suited to their proper actions. There are three kinds of actions, however: animal, spiritual, and natural, to which the bodily instruments correspond. In some animals horns were created for strength and help; some, however, have weak horns, suited neither for strength nor for fighting; some have none at all, since nature gave them another kind of strength and help, such as speed to horses, bodily size to elephants and camels, and prominent tusks to pigs. In some it placed strength in the hooves, and so deprived their heads of horns, unless perhaps they have a single horn, as the Indian ass does; but the multitude of branching in a stag's horns is closer to being a hindrance than a help, and so another help was given to it, namely speed of running. The wild cow, too, has horns curving inward toward each other, and for this reason nature gave it another help, namely the casting of its dung far off, so that the hunter is held back by it. The elephant, however, has a long and strong nose, which it uses in place of a hand for taking food and drink and in everything it needs, even for uprooting trees. An animal with many toes on its feet uses the front ones, as a man uses his hands, since it fights with them and drives harm from itself. An animal with hooves, however, does this with its hind feet, since the front ones are not suited to this. In these ways animals differ from one another: they differ also in intelligence, voice, food, sleep, mating and generation, friendship and discord, origin of place or dwelling.

Some animals are of the air and flying, like birds; some swimming, like fish; some walking, like wild land creatures. The first have their proper dwelling in the air, the second in the waters, the third on land. Moses makes clear in the first chapter of Genesis that there are three kinds of living creature, saying that God made draught animals, and beasts, and creeping things.

bibl.author: Basilius Cesariensis, Homilie in Hexameron Basilii Cesariensis

cit.quote: Speaking of these, Basil says thus in the book of the Hexaemeron, that is, the Book of the Six Days: draught animals are animals given over to the use and help of man. Some are appointed to labor, like horses, oxen, and camels; some for wool-making, like sheep and the like; some for eating, like swine and pigs.

Creeping things, however, are those that move and are driven forward by the contraction and extension of their body, like worms, snakes, and serpents. There are three kinds: those that draw themselves by the mouth, like little worms, which drag themselves by the mouth; those that crawl, like snakes, which propel themselves by the force of their ribs; and those that creep on feet, like lizards and toads and the like. Beasts, moreover, are so called as though 'vastie' [devastating], since they have a native ferocity; for they strike now with claw, now with horn, now with tooth, like boars, lions, tigers, and wolves. Commonly, 'beasts' is used for untamed animals that are naturally fiercer than draught animals, but gentler than the most savage beasts, like stags and the like.

In all animals there is a motive and sensitive power, but in greater or lesser degree. For, according to the purity and fineness of their blood, some are of livelier sense and stronger judgment and greater cunning. Hence the ox is sluggish and steady, the ass foolish, the horse ardent in lust, the wolf untamed, the lion bold, the fox cunning and deceitful, the dog affectionate and mindful of friendship, and so of the rest. Whence the goodness or malice of character in animals follows the goodness or malice of their complexion, as Basil says.

Aristotle likewise affirms this in the book On Animals. For he says that animals differ according to character. Some are of great gentleness, like the cow and the sheep; some of untamed ferocity, like the tiger and the wild boar; some of great boldness and magnanimity, like the lion; and some of great strength, cunning, and evil deeds, like the wolf, the fox, and the like. And this diversity comes from the diverse working of the active power, differently in different creatures. For, as the same author says in the second book, some animals have blood and some do not, like bees and every wrinkled-bodied animal; but they sometimes have a fluid in place of blood. Those with blood, however, are of greater body and strength. Hence some animals love company and travel in flocks, like stags, wild asses, and camels; and some avoid company and cannot dwell together socially, like hook-taloned birds and beasts that live by plunder.
To this Avicenna says, in the first book: some animals are urban and some rustic. And among all animals, man alone cannot live alone. Cranes, bees, and ants share in this with man.

Animals differ greatly in their nourishment, as the same says. For some feed only on flesh, like the lion and tiger and the like; some feed indiscriminately on everything, like the domestic dog and the like; some are nourished on grasses and crops, like horses, stags, and the like. And, as Aristotle says in the first book, some animals have their own particular taste, like bees, whose taste is honey and a few other sweet things; as the spider's taste is the fly, for it lives by hunting flies; and some are animals that hunt other animals, like the lion, the wolf, and the like; and some gather up their nourishment, like the hedgehog and the ant.

The reason why every animal needs nourishment, as Avicenna says, is the moisture of its substance and the heat that dissolves the moisture, and the surrounding hot air. Hence, since a continuous loss occurs through the heat consuming the moisture, restoration by the benefit of nourishment is necessary.
And some seek their living by night, like light-fleeing birds, and some by day.

Aristotle also says, as does Avicenna, that some animals are wild at every season, and some are domestic, like man, the mule, and the goat, and some are quickly domesticated, like the elephant. In every kind of domestic animal, wild ones are also found, as the wild man, the wild horse, the wild dog, the wild pig.

Some animals are of great impetuosity and combativeness, especially at the time of mating and love. For in all living creatures there is an appetite for affection, and then the males are jealous and fight for the females. And some animals harden themselves, so that at that time their bodies become tough, like wild boars, which, rubbing themselves against trees, enter the mud and dry it on themselves, and then they fight.
...the dog, the camel, and the ass, and some are of weak memory, like the ostrich and the dove.

There is, he says, a certain admirable prudence in brute beasts, in which, though there is, properly speaking, no knowledge, a certain likeness of knowledge is nonetheless found in them. For they have evident skill in the rearing of their young, in the building of dens and dwelling, in the seeking out of nourishment, in the treatment of wounds, in fleeing from harmful things, in the foreknowledge of coming changes of season, in the recognition and love of their own young. For the stag loves the hind, and the lion the lioness, and the bear the she-bear, and so of the rest.

Aristotle also says that in every animal there is a fundamental member, which is the source of all its natural, spiritual, and animal powers. And this is the heart, or something in its place. From this root, as Avicenna says, the creation, formation, and shaping of the animal begins. Once the brute animal has been formed and perfected, it has its face turned back toward its material and original source, namely, toward the earth itself. For upright stature alone has been reserved by the principle of nature for man, in whom man's nature has been ennobled and marvelously exalted above all living things. Hence the Poet says: 'he gave man a face turned upward, and bade him behold the sky,' and so on.

For which reason Basil says: if a man is defiled by bodily pleasure, obeying the lust of the belly, he is compared to draught animals in likeness, and is like them. Basil also says: nearly all the living creatures of the earth are moved, spurred by the heat of their generative organ, to the propagation of their kind and the succession of offspring. And this occurs especially in the spring season, when the power of the heavenly heat begins in some way to dominate in the bodies of living creatures.

Aristotle says something similar, and Avicenna too: every animal having seed, he says, generates an animal like itself. And therefore, to an animal unable to preserve its species by itself, nature gave one member to expel the seed and another to receive it, as in the female is the womb. And this is general in all animals in which there is distinction of sex, since the male is disposed after the manner of form and the female after the manner of matter. And therefore every female animal has a womb, or something in place of a womb, in which it receives its offspring. But this happens differently in different animals, for it is one way in egg-laying creatures and another way in other animals that conceive their young fully formed inside, as Avicenna exemplifies with many cases. Avicenna and Aristotle [compare] all blooded animals to bloodless ones. And he says that the former are simply greater and nobler in quantity and power, except for a few aquatic and sea monsters. And he adds that every noble blooded animal moves by four instruments, whether by four feet, as in brute beasts, or by two hands and two feet, as is plain in men, and likewise by two wings and two feet, as is plain in birds and feathered creatures.

Many living things are nonetheless found having more feet, as is plain in crabs and in caterpillars and others. Likewise also more wings, as is plain in butterflies, bees, and locusts; but in these, blood, which is the treasure of nature, thrives less. For this reason the four organs in the first group work more and more effectively than the many organs in the second. And likewise many animals are more agile and effective in working with their front parts than with their hind parts, since they share more in the heat of the heart's blood and are nearer to it.

Avicenna touches on the general properties of animals, saying thus: some animals share common members, as man and horse share flesh and sinew. They differ from one another, however, in the quality and disposition of their members, both simple and composite, as the tortoise has a shell and the hedgehog spines, and man does not; and the horse has a tail, and man does not. Likewise they differ in quantity, as the eye-opening of the owl is large, and the eye-opening of the eagle small. Likewise they differ in number, since some are two-footed and some four-footed and some many-footed, as is plain in spiders, of which some have eight feet and some ten. Likewise in quality, that is, in color and shape, or in softness and hardness, as the ox's foot is very hard, but man's foot is very soft. Likewise they differ in position, as is plain in the teats of the mare and the elephant. For the elephant's teats are placed beneath the chest, and the mare's beneath the groin. Likewise they differ in function, as is plain in the elephant's ears, with which it fights, and its trunk, with which it fights. Likewise they differ in susceptibility, as is plain in the eyes of the bat, which are very weak, while those of the swallow, on the contrary, are very strong, as Avicenna says.

For some are of strong appetite for mating and some weak, like the elephant and the turtledove. And some desire mating with every species and some only with their own, and some are always continent, like bees. Likewise some are of great greed and voracity in eating. And so some hunt by night, like wolves, which are called nocturnal animals, and some by day, like the hawk and the eagle; and some at both times, that is, day and night, like cats.

div.head: DE REPTILIUM ET SERPENTUM ET VERMIUM DISTINCCIONE, SECUNDUS TRACTATUS

cit.quote: There are three kinds of creeping things, as has been said: those that drag themselves, like worms, which pull themselves along by the mouth; those that crawl, like snakes, which propel themselves by the force of their ribs; and those that creep on feet, like lizards and toads. There are many kinds of worms; for worms belong to the earth, or the water, or the air, or flesh, or foliage, or wood, or garments. There are as many venoms among serpents as there are kinds, as many destructions as species, as many pains as colors. All serpents, however, are by nature cold, and do not strike except when they are warmed; for when they are cold, they touch nothing. Hence their venoms harm more by day than by night, for they grow sluggish in the chill of night. And rightly so, since they are chilled by the night dew. Some serpents inject venom by biting, some by stinging, or by mere breath, or even by a certain hidden power, as by spirit, voice, or gaze, just as happens with certain other animals and with men who cast spells. Some are venomous by nature, some by contagion. And some bring sudden death, some suffering, and some only danger. It should also be known that differences of place, season, and food make for variety in bites; for in winter, when they enter their den or immediately after, their bites grow weak and are nearly harmless; but in mountainous and rough places, dry and hotter, all are fiercer, since they are stronger there; in a moister region, however, they are soft and languid; for this reason too they are most savage around mating time, and their fury and strength can be increased by whatever food they eat. Creeping things, however, are not harmful to all animals; for both pigs and stags eat serpents, and some are devoured harmlessly by others. Many other things are found harmful to some and wholesome to others. Creeping things kill not only by biting but also by breath, causing harm through weapons, wood, or stones in between. Such too is the power of their bite, that if they bite the root of a tree, the whole tree sheds its leaves. Of all the smallest animals, which are usually born either from carcasses or from humors, there are six kinds: some come into being from exhalations, like gnats from wine, butterflies from water; some from the corruption of humors, like worms in cisterns; some from carcasses, like bees from draught animals, beetles and hornets from horses; some from the corruption of wood, like wood-worms; some from the corruption of bile, like moths from bones; some from the corruption of fruit, like weevils from beans. Of these, then, it is said that those born without corruption are those made from exhalations in that first condition of animals; those born from corruption, however, arose after sin, from corrupted things. And indeed all animals were then created gentle and harmless; but after sin some became harmful to man, that is, for punishment, correction, and instruction.

A serpent ['serpens'] is so called because it crawls ['serpit'] by hidden approaches, not by open steps, but creeps by the tiniest efforts of its scales. Those creatures, however, that use four feet, like lizards and newts, are called not serpents but creeping things. Serpents, however, are also creeping things, since they crawl on belly and chest. Of these there are as many venoms as kinds, as many destructions as species, as many pains as colors. Aristotle also says, in the book On Animals: serpents hide themselves and lurk in the earth. They are, however, midway between blooded land animals and water creatures; for most remain on land, and few in water. There are indeed various kinds of serpents in the sea, and they do not stay in the depths, but near the shore.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: What happens to swallow chicks also happens to serpents, namely, that if someone pierces and blinds their eye, their sight returns again. The tails of serpents, too, as has been said, grow back after they are cut off. Pliny also, in the eighth book: for some animals, food is provided in winter, for others sleep serves in place of food. Of serpents, the viper alone is said to bury itself in the earth; the rest, however, endure the year's hunger in the hollows of trees or rocks, once their chill alone is taken away. But all of them sleep at the season of withdrawal, drained of venom.

bibl.author: Liber de natura rerum Thome Cantimpratensis

cit.quote: Also in the eleventh book: the hiss of serpents is long; and even in serpents, the most savage kind of animal, there are signs of feeling. Also from the Book of the Nature of Things: serpents hide in winter in rocks or hollow trees and endure without food; in springtime they come forth. They are hot by nature; hence, once they have grown cold, they do little or no harm. So they harm less by night than by day, since they are chilled by the night dew. In winter's cold they curl into knots, but in summer they loosen. Ambrose also: a lion's surpassing beauty is set off by the maned tufts of its neck, when, chest raised, it lifts its face like a snake.
...since this will be said sufficiently under the letter S.

A worm is an animal generally born from flesh, or wood, or any earthly matter, without any earthly mating, although sometimes they are also born from eggs, as the scorpion is. A worm, however, does not crawl like a serpent, by open steps or by the effort of its scales, since it has no stiffness of spine, nor is it snake-like; but it carries out its motion by extending, degree by degree, the contracted parts of its little body forward and contracting the extended ones, and so, thus driven, it glides along. Aristotle also: the crawling of worms is on the belly.

Some animals generate worms, and some of these move at the very hour of their generation, some not until days later. Certain flies generate worms, and from the mating of little bees come worms resembling eggs. Further, those generated from worm-like animals are not complete when generated; then they grow; and what has the shape of a worm becomes large as it grows, and its shape becomes like an egg, since the outer covering — that is, the containing skin — hardens. At that time they are mobile. This is shown in worms generated from wasps and bees, and in those generated from animals; at first they feed, then they take no more food, but remain motionless, like the little bees, which are of a golden color.

Also, the black Indian worm is said to be first compared in appearance to a caterpillar; afterward, more resembling a chrysalis, and afterward it seems to take on wings with finer, more delicate threads. From these threads are made those soft fabrics with which those who dwell in the houses of kings are clothed.

bibl.author: Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris, Plinius maior

cit.quote: Pliny also, in the ninth book: in the Ganges, Statius Sebosus affirms there are worms with two arms, sixty cubits long, called 'blue-faced,' of which indeed something has already been said above among the sea monsters, and will be said further below. Also in the twenty-ninth book: crushed earthworms applied are good against scorpion stings. Many other remedies are also made from these, taken in honey. Of these more will be said below, under the letter V.

div.head: DE MEMBRORUM ANIMALIUM ET SENSUUM NECCESSARIA CONDICIONE IN GENERALI ET DEBITA SENSUUM ORDINACIONE, OLFATU QUOQUE ET HANELITU, VOCE ET VIGILIA ET DORMICIONE, TERCIUS TRACTATUS

cit.quote: All animals need various members that serve one another because of the diversity of their functions. Hence bones too are needed, that they may support the whole body. Cartilage is needed to protect the flesh from injury by the bones. Sinews too are needed for the joining of members and the conveying of sense and motion through the members. And they are hard, resisting cutting, and flexible for bending. Flesh was needed to fill what would otherwise be empty and to preserve the vital heat. The heart is needed as the source of life and the generation of the vital spirits. The lung, for the necessity of breathing and drawing in cold air to temper the heart's heat. The stomach, for the first digestion of food. The substance of the liver is also needed for the generation of blood. The veins are needed to carry blood through the members. The kidneys and genitals, for the preservation of the species. The intestines were needed for carrying off and expelling waste. The gall bladder is needed to aid digestion. The spleen, for gathering the melancholic humor. The head, with its contents, was needed for giving sense and government to the whole body. The neck was needed for joining head and body, forming the voice, and conveying food and drink to the stomach. The chest is needed to protect the heart and the vital organs. The arms and hands, for working. The sides and ribs, for the completion of the vital organs. The legs and feet, for supporting the body and for its voluntary movement from place to place. The skin is needed to guard all the inner parts from outside harm. And hairs are needed to protect the skin. Claws were needed to guard the extremities and, in many animals, also for defense. For nature has contrived that in each living creature there be some protection against harm. And so stags have horns, boars their tusks, and lions use their claws as blades. And so it is plain that in animals nothing is superfluous, nothing lacking. Smaller animals, lacking sharp teeth, claws, and horns, are instead protected by the agility of their members for flight, as is plain in hares, does, and the like. Likewise every animal that generates another animal has eyes, except the mole, which has its eyes covered by a membrane. This membrane is given to it because of its weak sight. And every animal with ears moves them, except man. And every animal breathes. But some by open passages, that is, through mouth and nostrils, and some by hidden passages, that is, through their eyes and pores, like bees and flies and animals of ringed body. And every four-footed animal with blood has marrow. And man especially has much marrow in proportion to his body. And this was necessary because of his many activities. And every horned animal has cloven hooves, except the Indian ass, which has one horn on its forehead and a single hoof on its foot, like the horse. And every horned animal has a hollow horn, except the stag and the unicorn. And every horned animal is a quadruped, having horns naturally, except a certain serpent in Egypt, which is found horned and is called by many the 'cerastes.' And I speak of animals having horns that are of the nature of bone. For tortoises have certain soft, sticky projections; these, however, are not horns but rather a kind of addition, with which tortoises, being weak of sight, feel out their way. And if something hard comes against them, they immediately withdraw these projections and hide within their little shells. For they use their shells as homes and as fortresses. Some animals also have teeth in both jaws, and some only below, and some only above. And those that lack teeth in the upper jaw are horned, since that matter passes over into horns. No animal has both curved teeth, or tusks, like the boar's, and horns, since that matter passes into tusks instead. For tusks and horns do not occur together. And animals appointed to prey have divided, sharp teeth, so as better to seize prey and tear off a piece, like wolves and lions. Domestic animals, however, like the cow, or semi-domestic ones, like the elephant or camel, have teeth that are even and paired, as though a single ridge, so that they may chew grass better and cut it more evenly close to the ground.

No animal has more than two rows of teeth in its mouth, except fish, which, besides the larger teeth, saw-edged and spaced apart in the jaws, have, further within, teeth of a sort limited in number, with which, as Aristotle says, they gather in their food, so that it is not too quickly dissolved away by the wetness of the water, as is plain in water-wolves, that is, pikes, and in many others.

In India, however, there is said to be a monstrous animal, like a bear in body and mane, but with a man's face, and it has a head red as vermilion and a huge, dreadful mouth, and in each jaw three rows of teeth set apart from one another. Its extremities are like a lion's, and its tail is like the tail of a wild scorpion having an eye, and it strikes with its bristles as a wild boar does with its quills. It has the voice of a trumpet, is swift of foot, and eats men. Indeed, among all the beasts of the earth, none is found more cruel nor more monstrous, as Avicenna says. This beast is called in Greek 'baricus,' as the same author says.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Pliny also, in the eighth book, chapter twenty-two: among the Indians, he says, as Ctesias writes, there is a most dangerous beast which he calls the 'manticore,' having a triple row of teeth meeting one another like a comb. It resembles a man in ears and face. It has grey-green eyes and a blood-red color, and is like a lion in its tail. And like a scorpion it darts and drives in its spines. And it has a voice resembling a man's voice, so much so that, if mixed with the sound of a man's voice, it seems to blend like the pipe and the trumpet in harmony. Hence it is the same animal Avicenna speaks of and Pliny too.

Likewise every animal that generates another animal has two kidneys and a bladder. But egg-laying animals have neither kidneys nor bladder. For in birds the excess of moisture passes instead into their claws and feathers. In swimming creatures, however, it passes into their shells and scales, and so they do not need a member to receive the surplus moisture.

Likewise every horned animal lacking upper teeth ruminates and has several stomachs, one very large, and another smaller and long, and another broad. And the reason it has many stomachs is multiple digestion, since its food is dry and not well chewed at first because of its eagerness to eat, and so it must be chewed again. For from the larger stomach the food is drawn back up to the mouth, to be chewed again, and, once so chewed, it is passed on to the second, to be digested there. And this second chewing is called rumination, as Avicenna says.

The same author also says, in the second book, first chapter: I say that every animal having suet has a fatty brain, and one that lacks suet lacks oily marrow. And everything that breathes has a lung, or something else in its place, as fish have gills, through which water is drawn in with air and then expelled. And every animal with blood has a heart. Those lacking blood, however, lack a heart. They have, nonetheless, something in its place, in which the seat of life resides. Likewise all generating animals have gall, but some hidden, like the horse and the mule, and some visible. The dolphin alone lacks gall, though it generates young and breathes. Egg-laying animals, however, have gall either large or small, like fish and serpents.

The same author also says that every animal with blood has seed. And every blooded animal that generates another animal has five senses, like a certain kind of mouse, whose eyes are covered and which has a pupil beneath its skin. But the passages of the senses in some are hidden, as the ears and nostrils in fish, which hear, as is plain since they flee from noise, and which smell — otherwise they would not come to the net for the sake of milk and roasted meats, for the sake of which crabs enter fishermen's baskets. And so Aristotle says, as does Avicenna, that dolphins and one other kind of fish, at thunder and other loud motion and sudden noise, fall to the bottom, as though they had epilepsy. And then they are caught as though drunk. And they flee from the place where another killed fish has been washed and flee from another fish's blood. And they flee dirty nets and unclean baskets and gladly enter new ones. Ring-bodied animals have keen senses though hidden, like bees and ants. Hence they hear from a distance and smell, and delight in certain odors and are killed by others, as by the smell of sulphur and burnt hide and burnt stag's horn. Hence bees do not stay in a place of foul odor, but rest in a fragrant place and where there is sweetness, as the same author says. Likewise, as the same says, animals differ in their manner of crying out, since some have a strong, sharp voice, some a weak and faint one, and some a very small voice or none at all. Only those animals having a windpipe and lung, and that breathe, give voice; but those that do not breathe make some other sound or a hiss. And voice-making animals produce tones. And those animals that cry out and chatter most at the time of mating and love recognize each other by their own voices and invite each other to embrace.
A blooded animal walks, wakes, and sleeps. And every animal with eyelids closes them when it sleeps. And every egg-laying animal sleeps lightly.

div.head: DE ANIMALIUM NUTRIMENTO, VIDELICET CIBACIONE ET POTACIONE, QUARTUS TRACTATUS

cit.quote: An animal needs nourishment suited to it and matching its complexion. And this is necessary either for the sustenance of the individual, or for its growth, or for the restoration of what is lost through natural heat. But there is a great difference in the manner of taking food. Likewise also in taking drink; for walking animals, which have a complete and even lip, drink by sucking, like man, the horse, the cow, the mule, and so on; other animals, however, which have an uneven lip, in which the lower lip does not match the upper evenly but is shorter, drink by lapping, like the dog, the cat, and the like. Hence, according to the disposition of the lips, by evenness or unevenness, some suck and some lap. And so nature has contrived that the dog, and so on. Lapping animals have a thinner, longer, and more flexible tongue, the better suited for gathering up water and carrying it to the mouth.

There are, however, many animals, even four-footed ones, that scarcely drink at all, like hares and rabbits and the like; because the food of such animals is very moist, and its moisture takes the place of drink for them and suffices for carrying the food through their members and for tempering their natural heat. Other living creatures, however, which are of much heat, of much heat and dryness by complexion or by accident, and use dry or hot food, need drink for the reasons mentioned. This is why doves and other birds that are not birds of prey drink, since they eat grain and the like. And their food is coarse, hot, and dry. The aforesaid birds, however, actually use moist food and so drink only rarely. And when they do drink, it is a sign of sickness and that there is an excess of heat in them, as Aristotle says, and Avicenna too.

div.head: DE ANIMALIUM AUDACIA, AVIDITATE ET GENERACIONE SEU FETUUM PROCREACIONE, QUINTUS TRACTATUS

cit.quote: Avicenna says that small-bodied animals are more ingenious than large-bodied ones, as is plain in spiders and bees and ants, whose works are so fine that human perception cannot achieve the like. For nature supplies in them, in sense and cunning, what seems lacking to them in strength and power, as the same author says.

bibl.author: Solinus Caius Iulius, Collectanea rerum memorabilium

cit.quote: The philosopher Solinus also says, in the book On the Wonders of the World, near the end, that every animal with serrated teeth is gluttonous and combative, as is plain in the dog, the panther, the bear, and the lion. And the females of such animals bear their young incomplete, as the dog bears them blind, and the she-bear bears shapeless lumps of flesh with no distinct outline, which she broods beneath her armpits, as a hen broods over eggs, and, by licking, shapes them until they gradually take on their proper shape and form. The panther and the lioness likewise bring forth young, but not perfectly formed or complete. Likewise, every animal that bears many young loves the firstborn most and counts it most truly its own; and so some animals devour their young except the first, as certain sows are accustomed to do, as the same author says. Likewise the same author: in all animals that bear incomplete young, the cause of that incompleteness is gluttony; for if nature waited until they were complete, they would kill their mother by suckling, through the excess of their appetite. And so nature is quick in such creatures, so that they are born quickly and die quickly, lest those giving birth be too greatly burdened.

Since such animals, so generated, are combative and, on account of food, as Avicenna says, hostile to one another, nature has contrived a remedy for the preservation of the species, namely, that many young be born together, so that, if perhaps many perish in strife, at least the species may be preserved and saved in the few; and so the she-wolf bears many young, as does the bitch. Likewise the viper, it is said, bears nine young at once, as the same author says; and so, since the viper's many young live together at once in the womb, out of greed for nourishment they suck and draw much fluid. Hence the mother, unable to nourish them all, fails and dies before she can fully give birth to all her young.

Aristotle and Avicenna also say that animals having teeth joined together like an axe-blade have few young; those, however, having divided and sharp teeth have many young and much seed. And small-bodied animals are of greater fecundity than large-bodied ones. And animals of lesser fecundity have fewer teats, differing also in their placement; and so the bitch has many teats, and likewise the sow, since they are animals with many young.

div.head: DE VITE ANIMALIUM PROLONGACIONE ET ABREVIACIONE, SEXTUS TRACTATUS

cit.quote: Animals of excessive and continual mating are of shorter life than those that mate rarely and moderately. And for this reason eunuchs live longer, since the sinew through which the seed descends is cut in them. Galen says the same in the book On Seed. Constantine says likewise.

Avicenna assigns the reason for this in the book On Animals, where he says that seed is made from good blood, fully digested, which is already capable of being converted into nourishment for the members; and so, when a man expels that nourishment or that seminal fluid, the body is much more discolored and weakened than if forty times as much blood left the body; for seed is a thing already fitted to pass into the members, and so, when it leaves, the natural nourishment of the members is taken away, and there is a great loss of the vital spirits and powers in the animal's body. Hence frequent and immoderate mating is the reason the body is broken down, and life is consequently shortened. And so the elephant lives longest of all, since it loves chastity and rarely gives itself to lust, as the same author says. Thus far Aristotle and Avicenna and Solinus.

div.head: DE CARNIUM ANIMALIUM COMPLEXIONE ET IPSARUM AD ESUM HOMINUM ORDINACIONE, SEPTIMUS TRACTATUS

bibl.author: Isaac Iudeus, De dietis universalibus et particularibus Isaac Israeli

cit.quote: Some animals suit the human complexion well, as Isaac says in the Universal Diets — kids, lambs, sheep, and pigs among the domestic animals, and stags and roe-deer among the wild ones — while some are entirely opposed to it. This is either because of excessive heat, as in serpents and snakes, or excessive cold, as in spiders and scorpions. Some, however, are unlike man's nature, but not entirely repugnant or deadly, such as hedgehogs, hares, and foxes, and other animals whose flesh has a heavy odor. Such animals provide the worst nourishment for the human body. Wild animals, however, are hotter, drier, and leaner than domestic ones, both because of their continual movement and the heat of the air they inhabit, and also because of the dryness of their food. And so their flesh is tougher and less digestible. This is plain, since their flesh, once killed, does not decay as quickly as domestic flesh does.

Hence all wild animals are less tasty and less nourishing than domestic ones, except wild roe-deer, which are tastier, more praiseworthy, and more nourishing than the rest. For their bodies are rarefied by movement and their humors refined, and their pores opened, and the humors that cause heaviness of odor are dissolved; and so they become tastier by accident, through the reason of movement and exertion. For by this their natural coldness is tempered. And so in wild animals of much exercise and much movement, the heaviness of flavor and odor is cut away, and the flesh becomes more tender, its pores open and its humors resolved, so that its flesh is digested more easily and quickly and incorporated into the members, and, by reason of its natural dryness, dissolves more slowly from the members.

Among these animals, some are raised in moist and watery places, and their flesh is very nourishing and quickly digested, but is also quickly dissolved from the members; some, however, graze in dry and mountainous places, and so their flesh is more praiseworthy and more suited to preserving and maintaining health, and more effective in strengthening and enduring in the members; but animals that are domesticated and pastured in houses have flesh that is more viscous and coarser, because of frequent feeding and the corruption of their food, and so are of tougher nourishment and slower to digest in the stomach and liver. For, as Hippocrates says, to know the goodness of animals' nature as regards bodily nourishment, it helps to know the places and pastures where they are fed, the moist or dry air in which they are kept, and the amount of their movement and rest — whether, that is, they are disposed to exercise or idleness, naturally or by circumstance.

Animals that are naturally domestic, however, are of less heat and greater moisture than wild ones, and so their flesh is softer and easier to digest. For from much rest the pores close, and, through the enclosed heat, coarse humors are dissolved. Hence their flesh softens and thins. And, because they eat and drink too much, the excess of humors increases and their fat multiplies, and so the bodies of such animals are very nourishing and tasty and easily penetrate through the pores and veins. From the great quantity of moisture and stickiness, however, they are close to corruption and putrefaction and generate excess humor. And, although they naturally nourish greatly, nonetheless, because of the excess of moisture and stickiness, they dissolve quickly from the members. And so, by accident, they provide the body with less nourishment than wild animals do; for wild animals, though they nourish little by nature, are nonetheless, since they are tough and slow to dissolve, longer-lasting in the members to which they become assimilated. And so the ancients asserted that, by accident, they nourish greatly. Also, in every kind of animal, the males are hotter than the females and of less moisture, and so the flesh of males is finer and more praiseworthy for nourishment than that of females, except in goats, where the female's flesh is naturally more praiseworthy than the male's; for in the female her moisture tempers her dryness of complexion, but in the male his heat increases his natural dryness. And therefore the female flesh in this species is more praiseworthy than the male's, since it is more tempered and further removed from an excess of dryness — this whether it is still suckling or older, and especially because it is still close to milk, since then its natural dryness is tempered, and the goodness of milk is the goodness of the female nature.

Castrated animals, however, are intermediate in complexion between male and female; for the flesh of the castrated warms males less, females more; it is digested more slowly by males and more quickly by females. And so it is of less nourishment, and worse, for males, and greater for females. And it is Aristotle's rule: among animals naturally moist, the males are better than the females, and better in mature age than in immature; among those naturally dry, however, the females are better than the males, and this more in immature age than mature, as the same author says. Likewise the goodness of animals varies with the diversity of ages; for animals very close to milk are of great moisture and stickiness and slipperiness, and so their flesh generates phlegmatic excesses, unless they are naturally dry, like the flesh of oxen and goats. The flesh of such animals at that age is more praiseworthy, especially if they have been nourished on good milk. Better, however, is the flesh of animals weaned from milk, since it is of less moisture and stickiness and of tempered firmness. In young adulthood, however, when animals are in their prime, their flesh is then tougher and drier, and especially if the animals are of dry complexion. And so their flesh is tougher to digest. In strengthening the members, however, it is praiseworthy, and more so in durability than in producing health, as the same author says. In the fourth age, however, that is, in decrepitude, their flesh is for the most part useless for eating, for two reasons: because it is close to the extinguishing of natural heat and the consuming of substantial moisture, and so their flesh is very tough and entirely indigestible, especially if they are of dry complexion. And so it is general among all animals, both flying and walking, that, while they are growing, they are more praiseworthy for nourishment than when, after their decline, they are more advanced in old age, as the same author says.

There is also diversity as regards food. For those that graze on mountains have thinner and sharper blood, because of the scarcity of food; those, however, that are fed in marshy places have coarser blood, greater fatness, less heat, and more blockage. Animals that graze on taller grasses, like oxen, are leaner in winter than in spring or summer, since their nourishment fails in winter, and so after mid-spring in the year their flesh fattens and increases and becomes tastier and more praiseworthy, because of the abundance of suitable food; animals that graze on small grasses, however, from the beginning of spring to mid-summer, are fatter and more tender and more praiseworthy in the goodness of their flesh, since then they find more suitable food. There are also other animals that graze on the tips of branches and shoots, and these are good from the beginning of summer until winter, since then the branches are more tender and moist. Hence animals that feed on small, dry grasses are better than those nourished on moist grasses. And those that eat tender branches or foliage are better than those fed at home on fruits. And those that eat and drink little are better than those that eat and drink much. For both mountain and plain animals are better than those raised at home, because of the frequency of their exercise and movement; for finer and drier air is drawn by such animals by reason of their running about, whence the excesses of humors are diminished and dried up, and so their complexions are tempered. On the contrary, however, those raised at home, from the scarcity of pure air, the lack of movement, and the abundance of food and drink, are found less praiseworthy in their complexion. Animals also differ according to fatness, leanness, and a middle state. For those that are very fat are worst for eating; for they harm digestion, since they float on top of the food and bloat it, and soften the villi of the stomach and draw in and induce slipperiness and stickiness in the stomach. And so excessive fatness dissolves a moist stomach, its retentive, strengthening, and expulsive power failing. A stomach that is too hot, however, it inflames, just as fire is usually kindled more from without by fat. And so the ancients prescribed that of the fattest animals only the red flesh, stripped of fat, should generally be eaten. The leanest animals, however, are sinewy, having little blood, little moisture, and so provide little or scant nourishment to the human body. But animals that are between leanness and fatness are more temperate and praiseworthy, since they have neither so much fat as to inflame heat and make the villi of the stomach slippery, nor so much leanness as to chill the nature and impoverish or deprive it of blood.

bibl.author: De proprietatibus elementorum Pseudo Aristotelis, Aristoteles

cit.quote: Diversity is also found in animals according to the change of seasons; for some animals in one season are depleted of marrow and blood, which in the opposite season are found full. And this appears perceptibly in sea shellfish and in the brain of man, and perhaps of every animal, as Aristotle expressly says in the book On the Properties of the Elements. And so many are ill in one part of the month or year, who in the opposite season are safe from every attack of illness, as is plain in lunatics, the insane, and epileptics. Inquire of this further below, in the chapter On the Moon, and also in the treatise On Astrology.

Avicenna says of the ape that, according to the change of seasons, and especially according to the course of the moon, they grow joyful or sad. So too certain animals grow lean in one season, however abundant their food then is, and the same, in the opposite season, grow fat even while sleeping, as Avicenna says: dormice, he says, do not move in the winter season, but lie as though dead, and, eating nothing, grow fat; but they crawl about in summertime and move about in summer against the sun's heat.

...swallows and certain other birds, which are found as though dead in the hollows of trees in wintertime, and which afterward regain their strength and, made stronger by sleeping, show themselves agile in summertime. So too the she-bear, according to Avicenna and Aristotle, after conceiving hides herself for a long time in hidden places, and at that time, it is said, takes no food at all. Inquire further below, in the chapter On the Bear.

So too fish fatten in one season or month and immediately grow lean in the following one. And some fatten with the north wind, like long fish, and some with the south wind, like broad fish, and some in rainy weather, as Aristotle says in the same place: rainwater, he says, suits all shelled and dry-skinned creatures, except the fish called 'rocoarus,' which, if it tastes rainwater, dies that same day. And rain harms some, since it blinds them, if it is heavy.
...the crab its shells, and the stag its horns, and the hawk its feathers.

As Isaac also says: the flesh of animals in which dryness and heat dominate, like camel's flesh, is unpraiseworthy in summer, but suitable in winter. And the flesh of animals that are hot and moist, like that of the stag, is good in spring and suitable in autumn; cold and dry flesh, however, like goat's flesh, is unpraiseworthy; cold and moist, like pork, is best from midsummer to its end and worst in winter, but is moderate in spring and autumn, as Hippocrates says: pork, he says, is good in summer, less good in spring and autumn, but most to be avoided in winter. Goat's flesh is good in summer, sheep's in spring, beef is most praiseworthy at the end of spring and the beginning of summer. On this matter, consult further in the treatise On Flesh, under the letter C.

div.head: DE CARNIUM ANIMALIUM ARTIFICIALI PREPARACIONE, OCTAVUS TRACTATUS

bibl.author: Isaac Iudeus, De dietis universalibus et particularibus Isaac Israeli

cit.quote: The flesh of animals, too, insofar as it is ordered for human consumption, varies according to its different preparation. For, as Isaac says, the flesh of animals is sometimes roasted, sometimes also fried, sometimes boiled with salt and water. Roasted and fried flesh is, for nourishment, coarser and drier and harder to digest; since, its moisture consumed by the fire, it takes on dryness. Nor should very fatty flesh be eaten except roasted, so that its unwholesome moisture is drawn out of its substance. Boiled flesh, however, is moister and easier to digest, since the water tempers and moistens it. Sometimes, however, it is boiled in water to which spices are added, making various seasonings that preserve the flesh in its nature and goodness and render it better both in smell and in taste, and more effective in driving off various illnesses. It is fitting, however, for the flesh of dry and lean animals to be boiled, that of moist animals to be roasted, and that of animals in between to be prepared with various seasonings. This manifold preparation exists because some flesh is found wholesome and suitable roasted, but unpraiseworthy boiled. For goat's and beef's flesh is better boiled than roasted, and pork better roasted than boiled. For by boiling, dry flesh is moistened, and by roasting, moist flesh is dried; and so it is good to roast pork, because of its moisture, and to boil goat's or beef's flesh, because of its excess dryness. The flesh of these same animals also varies according to these circumstances; for pork improves through roasting and becomes worse through boiling; goat's flesh, however, is better boiled and worse when roasted. And judgment should be made likewise for the rest. Thus far Isaac, in the Diets.

div.head: DE ANIMALIUM DEBITA ORDINACIONE AD MULTIPLICEM HOMINIS UTILITATEM ECIAM MEDICINALEM, NONUS TRACTATUS

cit.quote: Animals are also ordered, not only for the nourishment of the body, but also for the remedy of illnesses and manifold medicine. For all kinds of animals, whether draught animals, creeping things, or beasts, were created for the best use of man, as Pliny says, and John Damascene. But of these, some are for eating, like livestock, stags, and the like; some for man's service, like horses, donkeys, oxen, and camels; others for man's delight, like apes, blackbirds, and peacocks; others still were created for man's exercise, so that man might recognize his own weakness and unworthiness and God's power. And so fleas and lice were created, as were lions, tigers, and bears, so that man might, in the first place, come to recognize his own weakness, and, terrified by serpents, that is, creeping things, and by wild beasts, might have recourse to calling on the name of God.

Moreover, animals were created to relieve the manifold necessity of human illness, as the flesh of the viper for treacle, and the gall of the bull and of other animals and birds for treating clouding of the eyes. Serpent skin, boiled in oil, wonderfully eases earache, as Dioscorides says. In the book of Aesculapius, On the Hidden Powers of the Members, it is said that a patient suffering from hemorrhoids, if he sits on a lion's skin, will be rid of them. And whoever anoints his body with a lion's kidney-fat, or who is anointed with its dung, wolves flee from him. Also in the same place, the same author says: if someone hangs a live wolf's tail at a cattle stall, no wolf will approach it.

...a bear's, plucked out and bound on a man's right arm, ease his quartan fever. Likewise: a wolf's canine teeth, at the outset, cure those who suffer from lunacy, as the same author says. Pythagoras and Pliny say the same, and say that if domestic quadrupeds see a wolf's plucked-out eye, they flee it and are afraid.
Also in the book of the Viaticum, Constantine says: the hairs of a white dog having no black spot on it, if hung around the neck of a patient, help an epileptic and prevent his falling fit.

Pythagoras says something similar in the Book of the Romans: let a ring be made from the hoof of a black-free donkey, and let the epileptic wear it: it helps and prevents his falling fit. And he says that bull's gall, anointed below the navel, loosens the bowels. The same author also says: a serpent's tooth, extracted while it still lives, hung on a quartan-fever sufferer, cures his quartan fever. And if you fumigate a house with a donkey's lung, it clears it of every creeping thing and serpent.

Pliny says that these and many other admirable powers lie hidden in the members of animals, as will be said and has been said in the natures of particular animals afterward. For there is nothing in an animal's body that lacks either manifest or hidden medicinal power; for the hide, hair, claw, flesh, and blood of the stag are not without remedy, nor even its dung. But let these things, said generally here, suffice for the present.

div.head: DE NATURA LACTIS, DECIMUS TRACTATUS

cit.quote: The tenth treatise on animals is on the nature of milk. Milk is a sweet, white liquid, generated in the teats from blood by the action of heat. Or, as Aristotle says in the eighteenth book, milk is blood, cooked, digested, but not corrupted. For when the young cannot, because of its size, be nourished through the navel any longer, milk is prepared for it beforehand from the blood, drawn off and diverted to the teats, where it is digested and cooked, and, through the whiteness of the glands of the teats, is transformed into the appearance of whiteness.

Constantine also says, in the nineteenth book, first part: the nature of blood and of milk is the same mixture, and so nature created milk for the food of the newborn, by which it is fed once outside the womb. Milk, therefore, should not exist before the time of birth, nor long after, unless some error against nature occurs. For at that time the digestion of milk is completed in animals that have a single fixed term for giving birth; but in women it varies. And for this reason milk must necessarily be good after seven months. And milk is sweet when it is well digested. And it was necessary for the food of the young animal, which is sweet; for the food of all animals is nothing but something sweet and highly digestible, as the same author says in the same place, that is, the eighteenth book.

Aristotle also says, in the third book: egg-laying animals have neither milk nor teats. And in milk there is a thin, watery part, and a thick part, which is called cheese. And the thicker the milk, the hotter it is. And the milk of toothless animals curdles from cold; but the milk of an animal with teeth, and a wide jaw, does not, nor does its suet, and the milk of such an animal is thin and sweet, like camel's milk, and mare's milk, and after that, ass's milk. He also says, in the same place: in certain regions people do not wait for goats to become pregnant, but take nettle and rub the udder with it, and afterward blood comes out, then pus, and afterward good milk, no worse than the milk of pregnant animals. And there is generally much milk in the teats of female dogs, though it sometimes seems to happen otherwise. Certain plants have a milky sap, like spurge. And there is a certain tree, the fig, whose sap, as Aristotle says, curdles the milk of animals. And dogs' milk is thicker than the milk of all animals except hares and pigs. It is thickest, however, at birth, but afterward thins, as Aristotle says at the end of the sixth book. The cow has no milk before giving birth, but has good milk after; but when it first curdles it becomes like suet. And this happens when it is mixed with water, as the same author says in the same place. Also in the ninth book: when a little water is put into warm milk, the child's teeth come in more quickly; and after birth and purification, a woman's milk increases. Some women have milk only in the tip of their teats and some in other parts of them. And when it is not well digested, it curdles and the teats harden, since the whole teat is otherwise very soft. And if a hair happens to grow there, a great sickness follows, called 'hairiness,' and the pain will not cease until the hair comes out with the milk, or until it putrefies and comes out. And while the milk is flowing, generally no menstrual blood is found; some nursing women, however, diminish their milk when their moist blood becomes menstrual. And when children are nursed on thick, abundant milk, they suffer spasms, and become thin-bodied while nursing, and then an excess of milk is harmful to them. And a dark-skinned woman has better and more nourishing milk than a fair one, as the same author says.

bibl.author: Isaac Iudeus, De dietis universalibus et particularibus Isaac Israeli

cit.quote: Milk, he says, is generally divided in three ways: it is either sweet, freshly come from the teats, or it is sour or sharp, having already been milked a long time, or it is moderate, between the two. Sweet milk, however, is more flavorful, close to blood and friendly to it, easily converted into it; and so its nourishment is praiseworthy. It is composed, however, of three substances, differing and diverse in power and effect: one is thinning and cleansing, another is thick and obstructing, the third is softening and expanding. For the watery, serous part is sharp and thinning; the thick, serous part is sharp too; and the cheesy part is cold, formed, thick, and thus entirely obstructing; the buttery part, however, is potent and softening. Hence milk, with its watery, sharp substance, cuts and thins coarse humors, loosens the internal organs, irritates the intestines, loosens the bowels and readily expels waste, cleanses corrupted humors both within and without the body, penetrates the veins, opens blockages of the spleen and liver — especially if it comes from hot-complexioned animals, like camels. Such milk, he says, is helpful for the dropsical. And he continues: milk that is praiseworthy is so in all three of its substances: tempered, by its wateriness it cleanses the members; by its butteriness it resists poisons and moistens the members; by its heat it presses food from the mouth of the stomach down to its base — for, if taken in moderation and at the proper time, the body first having been cleansed, it nourishes the body praiseworthily and its substance resembles blood; but if taken when the body is unclean and at an unsuitable time, it is converted into the bad humors it finds there and increases them, resolving into hot, bilious vapors; and so it will be a cure for headache. And if they find matter for fever, it will inflame the feverish heat; or, if they find the natural heat weak, it easily curdles and turns sour in the stomach. For when there is excess moisture and little heat, sourness or phlegmatic putrefaction is generated, and so milk should not be taken often, unless the body is in a tempered state and the stomach empty; for if the body is free and purged of putrid and bilious humors, if the milk is well digested, it will provide the body with much good nourishment, will generate praiseworthy blood, increase the flesh, moisten the body, and make the outer skin tender and beautiful, as the same author says.

The same author, Rufus, further says: it is fitting that those who drink milk do so fasting, and that it be warm, as it is fresh from the udder, and that nothing be eaten until the substance of the milk is digested. One must also avoid exertion and excessive movement until it descends to the place of digestion and is digested, since, from disordered movement and sudden excessive heat, its oiliness would resolve into a harmful vapor, and, its coarser part remaining undigested, manifold corruption would be generated, as the same author says. Choice milk, as the same author says in the same place, should have four qualities: smell, color, consistency, and taste. Its color should be the whitest and clearest, entirely free from yellowness, redness, and lividness; its smell pleasant, free from any hint of rankness or heaviness; its consistency midway between thin and thick, the sign of which moderation is that a drop placed on the fingernail remains gathered and does not run, this drop being broad below and pointed above; its taste is acceptable when mixed with neither bitterness, nor saltiness, nor sourness.

Among these differences of milk, however, woman's milk is eaten as more tempered, since every milk naturally imitates the nature and complexion of the animal to which it belongs. Woman's milk is the most tempered, for which reason it is the most nourishing, moistening, and notably soothing to the roughness at the corners of the eye. And whatever has been said of the goodness of milk applies entirely to this milk too.

On camel's milk. Camel's milk, from the animal's hot complexion, is hotter than the rest, and thinner, and least oily, and least nourishing, diuretic, and opening to blockages; and so it is most helpful to the dropsical arising from blockage. For the camel is of the hottest nature, and for this reason the dominant heat of its blood draws off the oiliness, and so the blood remains without oiliness. Since, then, milk is nothing other than blood cooked a second time, the taste of camel's blood is salty and sharp; and so the humor is cutting, thinning, and reducing thickness. Consult above, in the treatise on animals, under the camel. Cow's milk is the opposite of camel's milk; for the cow does not have so much heat as to draw off the oiliness of its blood, and so its milk becomes most nourishing and very oily; for cow's milk nourishes more than pig's milk, although sheep's milk is hotter than cow's. The reason for this, as the same author says, is that, since cow's milk does not have as much heat as sheep's, a small amount of oiliness suffices for it, and that all remains in the milk and exceeds the cheesy part; and so it nourishes more, since the substance of oiliness is more nourishing than the cheesy part, being hotter, moister, closer to the heat of blood, and easier to convert into blood. And, as the ancients say, those things nourish better and more quickly that are more quickly and easily converted into blood, as is said in the same place. Fatty milk, however, nourishes more than the fat itself, since it is hotter; for the substance of milk has a liquid wateriness that thins and penetrates the inner parts of the body, but fat alone floats on the surface by its airiness and, because of the coarseness of its substantial moisture, quickly congeals and hardens. And so cow's milk, by its wateriness, penetrates to the interior, by its oiliness strengthens the natural heat, and by the smallness of its cheesy part does not greatly burden nature, but rather helps and sustains it, as the same author says. Milk, then, is to be used one way for nourishment, since then all three of its substances are to be used equally; another way for cleansing and calming heat, since then the watery serum is to be separated from the buttery part; another way for warming and moistening, and then the oiliness of the butter is to be used. The use of milk, then, is considered according to its thinness, thickness, and moderateness, as the same author says. Thinness, however, is noted both in substance and in effect. In substance, that which is closer to the human complexion is better, as woman's milk, which is more useful the closer it is to the teat, more effective against poisons, against kidney and bladder ailments, against lung wounds, so long as it does not touch the air and its quality is not altered by the air's own quality. Thinness in effect, however, occurs when its buttery part has become cheesy, is separated, and its wateriness with sharpness then increases, as is plain in camel's milk, which nourishes less, but by its heat and thin liquid helps and comes to the aid of the dropsical.

Cow's milk, however, is the thickest, less liquid and watery than the rest, less sharp and more buttery. Hence it nourishes well, suits the stomach, strengthens the members, cools the heat of the stomach and liver, fattens and increases the body, and heals wounds of the intestines and of the womb. It will be even better and more wholesome if, with heated river stones quenched inside it, most of its wateriness is consumed. On goat's milk. Goat's milk holds a middle place among the aforesaid kinds, since, after woman's milk, it is believed to be, in its three substances, the most tempered, and so, with sugar, it is of great benefit against lung wounds and kidney and bladder ailments. Its whey, separated from cheese and butter, is especially purifying, cleansing, and bile-suppressing. Goat's milk alone, however, drunk in quantity, readily curdles in the stomach, and so, lest it cause harm, it is tempered with a little honey and rock salt, and it will never curdle. And if it begins to curdle, it dissolves in the stomach. And, since goats graze on dry things and the tips of branches, their milk is less watery and more astringent and suited to the stomach. For milk varies according to pasture; for those fed on tender, fresh grasses produce watery, thin milk, which is harmful to the stomach; those fed on purgative grasses, however, produce milk that is irritating and stinging to the sinews, and is harmful, though laxative.

Sheep's milk is hotter and drier than cow's, having less butteriness and more cheesiness, and so nourishes less and does not suit the body as well. This is shown by the heaviness of its smell. For, as Galen says, sheep's milk is heavier in smell than cow's, and so more phlegmatic. It nourishes more than goat's milk, however, but less than cow's; yet it is less tempered than goat's.

Ass's milk is tempered, nourishing, and restorative, though it loosens the bowels, softens the sinews, moistens members hardened by dryness and heat, aids the chest, eases difficult breathing, and heals wounds of the kidneys and bladder.

On mare's milk. Mare's milk is close to camel's milk in thinness, and, being sharp and hot, is helpful and opening for abscesses of the womb, and provokes menstrual flow, if the cause of the menses is hot and dry — a property that milk has apart from all other milk, as Isaac says. On pig's milk. Pig's milk, according to Isaac, is thin and watery, since, from its coldness, it remains uncooked and undigested, and so, if taken medicinally, it provides little or no benefit; but if boiled with barley juice, it generates good nourishment, as the same author says.

Milk very close to the time of birth is thin and watery, since watery humors gather in animals at the time of birth, since the mouth of the womb closes and the milk is mixed with watery humors, and so at that time it is harmful, provoking vomiting and disgust, softening roughness, making the villi of the stomach slippery, loosening the bowels, hard to digest, astringent, curdling in the stomach, generative of the worst illnesses, driving back the vapor rising to the brain, curative of headache, and inducing bad breath and foul teeth. Hence milk, if it is corrupted, or taken in excess of what is fitting, or in another manner or at another time than is proper, generates many illnesses, nourishes bad and slippery humors, corrupts good humors, gathers gravel in the bladder and kidneys and turns it to stone, weakens natural heat and inflames unnatural and feverish heat, infects the gums and teeth, cures the worst pustules and scabies in infants, excites rumbling and flatulence, causes blockage of the kidneys, spleen, and liver, burdens the stomach and, by its slipperiness, expels food before digestion, thus inducing dysentery. The corruption of milk induces these and many other conditions.

...in cow's milk the buttery part multiplies; the milk of camels near to giving birth has too much butteriness and cheesiness and is very thin; and the milk of she-asses, having less butteriness, is thin; and goats' milk is tempered; and sheep's milk is thick and fatty; and cow's milk is fattier and thicker; and mares' milk is like that of camels near to giving birth, thin and watery.

The milk that is best for men is woman's milk. And the best milk is that which is drunk sucked from the breast, or as it is freshly milked. And the best of it is that of vivid whiteness, uniform substance, which, dropped on the fingernail, holds firm and does not run, and whose animal's pasture is good grass, and which has no foreign taste inclining toward sourness or bitterness or acridness, nor any foreign, unpleasant smell. And it should be administered as soon as it is milked, before it changes. And the milk of any animal whose gestation is longer than a woman's is bad; wherefore that which is closest in kind to it, like cow's milk, is most proportionate. Its wateriness is warm, and its butteriness tends toward wateriness, though it inclines toward heat away from equality. And sour milk is cold and dry; its wateriness is thinning and there is no irritation in it. Milk is nourishing, equalizes the humors, strengthens the body, and cleanses. And when drunk with honey, it cleanses internal ulcers of coarse humors and ripens them, and is of good humor, and makes the blood abundant, and increases growth in the brain, and properly so woman's milk. Milk, indeed, is close to being already digested. And how could it not be, since it is generated from blood that is at the height of digestion, upon which some further digestion supervenes, even though it comes from a member inclined to cold? For the body is not nourished by it until it is put into the condition of food, which requires much preparation and clarification. After clarification — indeed, when good heat governs it — it swiftly restores it to the nature of well-balanced blood.

What Rufus said of it is good.
