And, unless it is contradicted, and because of its slight inclination toward cold, it harms phlegmatic people when their heat does not convert it into blood as it should, and the body makes use of it before its conversion, precisely because it is so close to blood already. And for this reason it benefits those with a hot, dry blockage, when there is no bile in their stomach.

Further: milk has certain correspondences with bodies whose causes are not understood. He who drinks milk should rest afterward, so that it is not corrupted and does not turn sour; but he should not sleep upon it, nor take any other food upon it until it has descended. And it suits the mature more than the young, who have a hot complexion, for in them it turns to bile; and it also benefits the old, since it moistens and removes the itching that is proper to them. But it should be fittingly digested with honey. And often milk begins by loosening and drawing out the excesses that are in the parts of the intestines; then it begins to nourish and settle into the body and retain its nature, and it is inflammatory until it begins to ferment. It is composed of a dissolving part, which is its wateriness, and a constringing part, which is its cheesiness. And colostrum is slow to digest, of coarse humor, and slow to descend. Honey, however, corrects it and the body draws more nourishment from it, and sour milk is of raw humor, and that which is cooked, and properly that which is thicker, is more constringent. All milk, indeed, causes blockages, and properly in the liver, except the milk of newly-calved camels and the like, because of the smallness of its cheesy part and the cleansing quality of its wateriness. And it helps against matters that flow toward the inner members and harm them by their sharpness and irritation; for it weakens them, since it washes them beyond mere washing with water, by virtue of the cleansing property in its wateriness, which is not present in plain water, and by the equalizing of their quality because of its correspondence with the member, since that which separates is similar to the member; then it glues them together, between the member and the bad humor. So the humor does not meet it bare. And it harms those with a flux of blood. Milk, moreover, is not good for the internal organs. Goats' milk is less harmful to the internal organs than the rest; for most of what it grazes on is constringent. Sheep's milk, on the contrary, is sour and is not praiseworthy, and there is inflammation in it. Milk, in its substance, converts quickly, and properly toward heat. And nothing is more harmful to the body than bad milk. Ass's milk is watery. Sow's milk is watery, unripe. And spring milk is watery compared to summer milk. And likewise the milk of an animal whose pasture is a riverbank or muddy ground, since spring plants are watery compared to summer plants. And the more summer advances toward autumn, the thicker the milk becomes. And the best is that of midsummer. It is feared, however, that heat will convert it after it is drunk; this is not feared in spring. Cow's milk, moreover, has the most butter, and sheep's milk has the most cheesiness and butteriness; but cheesiness in camel's milk is little, then in mare's milk, then in ass's. And for this reason it rarely or never curdles in the stomach and upper belly more than other milk. And in camel's milk there is saltiness, since camels love sour things. And this milk is better. And, when it is said that it is exceedingly slow in the stomach and upper belly, know that milk varies according to the species of animal and according to age, whether young, old, or middling; and according to form, whether the animal is of light or tough flesh, fat or lean; white or another color. And the weakest milk, it is said, is that of the 'aralib,' and it is the fastest to descend. Much use of milk generates lice, as some have supposed, and they do not depart. Yet it clears foul scars from the skin when applied, and gives a very good complexion when drunk. But it often causes filth to break out, except the milk of newly-calved camels, which is rarely feared for this. And when drunk with sugar, it gives a very good complexion, even to women. And it fattens, so much so that even whey-water fattens those of hot, dry complexion, when it is resolved by drinking it for its own reason, and it fattens them only because it moistens and draws out bad humor, thereby correcting their nourishment. And 'aralib' milk with dregs fattens them quickly. Whey-water removes blemishes and scars when applied. And it sometimes helps them when drunk. Often those afflicted with bad abscesses and carbuncles and eczema and scabies and itching are healed by drinking milk, when their complexion is not such as to corrupt it and turn it to bile. Milk is harmful to those with internal hot abscesses. Milk heals internal ulcers because it washes and binds and cleanses. And, when nothing in the complexion corrupts it or turns it to bile, it benefits those with ulcers. And whey-water with myrobalans is suitable for scabies. Milk is bad for the sinews and for those with sinew ailments, especially cold and phlegmatic ones. Goats' milk helps catarrh and holds it back and improves its sharpness, and helps ulcers of the palate. And milk is a cause of dry forgetfulness, sadness, and confusion. Milk indeed harms the teeth and corrodes them, hollows them out, and consumes them, especially when a tooth is of cold complexion, and it makes the gum loose. Rather, one should rinse the mouth afterward with honey, or wine and honey, or oxymel. Ass's milk, it is said, when the mouth is rinsed with it, strengthens the teeth and gums, and is not suitable for those with heartburn, dizziness, and ringing in the ears, and sleeping after it generally harms those with weak heads. Milk causes dimness and clouding of sight; nonetheless, when applied in the eye, it helps ophthalmia and the harm of hot matter flowing to the eye, and roughness. And likewise it is first mixed with egg white and raw rose oil and placed on the eye. And its instillation helps a stye. Ass's and goat's milk are good for cough and wasting and the spitting of blood, according to what its place signifies. And sheep's milk helps in the spitting of blood. And milk is also among the medicines for lung ulcers and wasting, and helps when the mouth is rinsed with it, and as a gargle for suffocation and quinsy and abscesses of the uvula and tonsils. It is harmful, however, to those with moist heart-tremor, whether from blood or phlegm. And the milk of newly-calved camels helps asthma and shortness of breath. And milk is more suited to the chest than to the head and stomach. Milk causes blockages in the mesenteric vessels. And whey-water helps jaundice. And goat's milk and the milk of walking, newly-calved camels, and ass's milk help dropsy, and all three help hardness of the spleen. The milk of newly-calved camels with oil is suitable for internal hardnesses, but causes bloating and stomach pain, especially colostrum. Both provoke hiccups and smoky belching, especially milk, and it harms those with spleen and liver trouble and those on a thinning regimen, except the milk of camels near giving birth; for that helps many illnesses of spleen and liver and renews the liver. The milk of newly-calved camels helps dropsy greatly, especially when drunk with the urine of newly-calved Arabian camels, and it excites the appetite for food and causes coughing. Sour milk is very slow to digest and of raw humor; but a naturally or accidentally hot stomach digests it and is helped by it and does not belch smokily, because the butter has been removed from it. Whey-water, by loosening, draws out burnt bile, and with epithyme dissolves burnt melancholy. And milk causes stones to form. And milk boiled until its wateriness is consumed constringes the bowels and checks the flow of blood downward. And the milk of newly-calved camels provokes menstruation. And that from which butter has been extracted is good for biliousness, and an enema is made from freshly milked milk for ulcers of the intestines and the womb. Goat's milk is good for bladder ulcers. And milk relieves the harm of intercourse and gives vigor for it, and causes swelling in ulcers. All thick milk excites bile and generates stones, and colostrum especially. Milk indeed excites desire for mating, even sour milk, and it dwells in bodies of hot complexion. It does this because it moistens and swells the spleen and often loosens the bowels, especially mare's, camel's, and ass's milk, then cow's milk, then goat's milk. And the more its wateriness is reduced, the more, at times, an excess of it loosens the bowels, since it is not digested. And salt helps loosen it and loosen the water of the milk. Boiled milk, however, in which coals have been quenched, and which has been heated with fired stones and iron plates, undoubtedly constringes the bowels. And milk helps abrasion of the intestines. And sour milk checks bilious and bloody flux. And the milk of newly-calved camels helps hemorrhoids. Mare's milk is applied to abscesses of the anus and their ulcers, abscesses of the thigh and their ulcers; it helps and calms the pain occurring in these members. Goat's milk and ass's milk are good for consumption, according to how it settles in its place. And sour milk often expels consumptive fevers, when its butter is brought to it, and makes it well digested. Fresh, very thick milk often causes fevers to occur, and it should not be given at all to one already suffering fever. Milk is good to drink for sea-hare poisoning, wild rue gum, henbane, and 'benet,' and especially for one who has drunk blister-beetles, sea-hare, wild rue gum, hellebore, and the poison called 'adib,' leopard's-bane, and all corrosive, putrefying medicines; and the cure for one who has drunk 'benet' is this, for it restores his reason.

div.head: DE NATURA ET PROPRIETATE SERI, UNDECIMUS TRACTATUS

cit.quote: Whey is the watery part of milk, separated from that part of the milk by rennet; for rennet joins the buttery and cheesy parts together and divides and separates them from what is liquid and watery. Its effects have been recounted above. It has a power to wash away putrefaction; for it washes the intestines and cleanses ulcers of the intestines of pus, purifies the chest, quenches thirst, calms the sharpness of red bile, purges scabies and impetigo, and opens blockages of spleen and liver. Consult above, at the beginning, according to Isaac.

div.head: DE BUTIRO, DUODECIMUS TRACTATUS

cit.quote: Butter, according to Huguccio, is named from 'buendo,' that is, 'soaking through'; for by its oiliness and moisture it soaks into the body it touches. For butter is the flower of milk, having much heat and moisture along with a dominance of airiness, by reason of which it has much oiliness. For it is a buttery substance, naturally hot and moist, sticky and oily to the human complexion, as Isaac said. Hence, often eaten, it moistens the stomach and loosens the bowels, especially if it is fresh. And so the ancients, as the same author says, compared butter to oil mixed with fat, saying that, if someone takes it, it helps abscesses of the chest and lung, especially if there is an abscess, since it is properly ripening and dissolving of humors and cleansing of the surplus of the chest, especially if eaten with honey or sugar; but then it is too ripening and too helpful for lancing, as the same author adds in the same place. Butter resists poisons, moistens the members, softens and clears the roughness of the eyes when washed with it, dissolves and ripens abscesses, wonderfully cleanses wounds of the lung, throat, and chest, calms bites of the kidneys and intestines, softens and loosens sinews that are inflamed, contracted, and in spasm, as the same author says.

Avicenna also says that it is a singular remedy against poisons taken internally, if the poisoned man drinks butter dissolved in warm milk in a great quantity; for by its oiliness it blocks the passages, so that the force of the poison does not suddenly rise to the heart. Moreover, it draws all the flatulence to itself and, enveloping it, expels and drives it from the body by vomiting, as the same author says.

The flower of milk, or the fat floating on top, is gathered thus: in a clean vessel, with a certain broad, round, perforated piece of wood, it is struck for a very long time with force and motion; from this motion the natural heat of the milk's substance is roused and strengthened, and gathers all the oiliness together, which, by its lightness, seeks the surface; the serous wateriness, together with the cheesy parts, however, descends below and lies beneath the butter, yielding, as the less noble part, to the bottom, and that buttery part that floats on the surface is gathered and kept in a very clean vessel for various necessary uses. The fresher this is, the tastier and more delightful to the palate it is found. It is soft and liquid at first, but, as the natural heat gradually prevails over the moist parts and consumes them, it hardens moderately. Hence it nourishes and refreshes well and cleanly, and seasons dishes well in place of blood or oil. It is somewhat salted, so as to keep better, and so that its potential moisture is tempered by the dryness of the salt, and also so that its flavorfulness is increased. For it is more pleasing to the taste when moderately salted. But when it becomes too old, its flavor diminishes along with its smell, and it changes into a heavy odor and a taste horrible to the palate. And then it is no longer good for seasoning food; it is, however, good for various medicines and ointments, since it often happens that what does not suit the palate is nonetheless suited to some medicine.

Butter, according to Avicenna, in the second treatise of the second book, is hot and moist in the first degree, and its degree in moisture is higher. It is ripening, dissolving, softening, and its dissolving action occurs in bodies that are medium, not hard, and in tender bodies it occurs easily. And its vapor is drying. It constringes easily and calms the pains of matter flowing to the members. The body and belly are anointed with it, and it nourishes and fattens. It helps wounds of the sinews and fills and cleanses ulcers. Medicines for eruptions of the membranes of the brain and abscesses at the root of the ears and nostrils and mouth and abscesses of the gums, and for bile, are drunk with it. And the gums of infants are anointed with it, so that the emergence of teeth is easy. It helps cold, dry cough, especially with almonds and sugar. And likewise in pleurisy and pneumonia.

And it makes coughing up easy, and ripens. And likewise with almond oil its ripening effect is greatest; its cleansing action alone, however, is less than its ripening. And with sugar it is the opposite. And it prevents the spitting of blood and helps vomiting of blood and pus, and with it one takes a lick of about a dram and a half with honey. It is softening. And its extensive use is dissolving. An enema is made from it for hot abscesses of the intestines and womb and testicles. And it is put into medicines for wounds of the bladder opening. It resists poisons, and especially a viper's bite is anointed with it.

div.head: DE CASEO, DECIMUS TERCIUS TRACTATUS

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis, Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Cheese, according to Isidore, in the twentieth book, is named from 'lacking' ['carendo'], since it is left in the vessel until it lacks whey and is separated from the watery substance of the milk. Hence it is called 'caseus' as though 'carens' [lacking], since, when it is dry, it lacks moisture or liquid, as the same author says. According to Huguccio, however, cheese is named from 'falling' ['cadendo'], since it easily falls and slips away. For it falls and slips between the fingers of the one making it. Cheese, moreover, is the dregs of milk.

For, as Isaac says, the cheesy substance of milk is cold and thick, tough to digest, slow also to leave the stomach, and belongs more to constriction than to loosening, and is heavy on the stomach and liver, kidneys and spleen, especially if those organs are already disposed to blockage, and generates kidney stones. And so, because of these bad effects, Constantine says that all cheese universally is bad. Cheese close to the milk in freshness, however, is less harmful.

bibl.author: Isaac Iudeus, De dietis universalibus et particularibus Isaac Israeli

cit.quote: Hence Isaac distinguishes among fresh, old, and moderate cheese. Fresh cheese, being still fresh, does not generate bad humors, since it still retains some of the sweetness and wateriness of the milk itself, and so is easier to digest, more praiseworthy for nourishment, and more loosening to the bowels — especially if it is not so salted that the saltiness takes away its sweetness and flavor. For too salted cheese is too drying and harmful to the stomach; entirely without salt, however, it is more nourishing and moistening to the body and more increasing of flesh; it is, however, harmful to the stomach, easily resolving into vapors, and if the stomach is cold, easily turning sour. Moderately salted, then, it digests better and is less harmful to the stomach; without salt it easily turns sour; too salted it becomes irritating to the stomach and inflames the blood. Old cheese, however, is sharp and very dry, coarse for nourishment, and too hard to leave the stomach, since its watery part of the milk has been taken from it. The sharpness and dryness of the rennet dominates it, so that it loses its thinness and undergoes inflammation, and so the body's excess is not thinned by it as by other thinning things. Hence it harms the body in two ways: first, because its corruption and coarseness thickens and corrupts the excess of nourishment; second, it harms because, through the sharpness of the rennet, it opposes everything else that would otherwise help, and those helpful things are converted into worse nourishment. Hence, if it finds coarse humors in the body, it forms stones in the kidneys and bladder; for it gathers and compacts coarse, hot, inflamed humors together. Such old cheese is therefore to be avoided; for it provides no benefit nor nourishment, nor does it obey digestion, nor generate good blood, nor moisten the bowels, nor provoke urine, but instead constringes and dries out whatever moisture it finds. All old cheese, then, hard, spongy, dry, and porous, easily broken because of its dryness, having no oiliness or moisture, is harmful to the body. Less bad, however, is cheese that is joined and compact than one that is riddled with holes and porous; for the latter is a sign of oiliness and moisture, whereas porous cheese is less bad when fresh than when very old; for, as Elias says, old cheese constringes the bowels, especially when boiled, or if, drawn from water, it is then roasted, and especially if taken before a meal; for by its coarseness it blocks the passage of the stomach and does not let food descend to the intestines; taken after a meal, however, it compresses the food like a press and forces it to descend to the place of exit. Cheese midway between old and new is very nourishing because of its flavor and thickness, and because it hardens quickly by natural heat; for the more natural heat is denied to it, the more strongly it clings together. Thus far Isaac, in the Diets.

According to Dioscorides, however, and Aristotle in the third book, the more cheese there is in milk, the more nourishing it will be. Cheese, moreover, according to Dioscorides, is opposed to poison; for by its thickness and butteriness it blocks the passages of the veins and does not let the force of the poison rise to the heart. Fresh cheese, applied hot, also draws poison out from venomous bites. And the sign of this is that, applied to the bite of a rabid dog or a serpent, the whole whiteness of the cheese turns to a livid color. It is good against anthrax and other venomous abscesses, whether applied externally or eaten. It is also suited to many other medicines, as the same author says.

Cheese, according to Avicenna, in the second treatise of the second book, is sometimes made from milk, sometimes from whey, and that kind is called 'recocta' [twice-cooked]. Fresh cheese is cold and moist in the third degree, and old, salted cheese is hot and dry in it. In cheese-water, however, since there is in it a nitrous quality acquired first from the blood, and a bilious part, there is a certain heat. The one midway between the kind that stretches like sinew and the crumbly kind is better. And both extremes are bad. And that which is lacking in flavor, inclined toward sweetness and pleasantness, moderate in salt, which does not remain long in the organs, and crumbled in vinegar, is better than these. And the thinning ingredients increase its harmfulness, since they make it penetrate and drive it further in.

And cheese from goats fed on thinning plants is better than the cheese of goats fed on nothing in particular, and coarse fodder. In it there is a cleansing property; and fresh cheese is thinning, nourishing, fattening, cleansing; and honey is eaten after it. And old cheese is hot, cleansing, purifying; and eaten, it produces bilious humor. Salted cheese, however, is intermediate between the two. Cheese-water fattens dogs greatly and nourishes them. And in 'recocta' is the summit of cheeses: it has a dissolving power. Drinking cheese-water with medicines that cleanse melancholy helps tinea. And fresh cheese, boiled with as much wine as there is in the rind of a pomegranate, until it thickens, prevents facial spasm. Old, salted cheese thins the body; fresh, unsalted cheese prevents wounds from becoming abscessed. Old cheese is good for bad ulcers and wounds, and fresh cheese for mild, fresh wounds; fresh cheese is stronger in this and prevents their turning into abscesses, especially with laurel and wild sorrel leaves. And whey-water should be drunk for scabies.

It is ground with oil, or with the water of salted pig's feet, and a plaster is made from it for hardness of the joints, and it draws out matter from them as plaster of Paris does, without difficulty, and is of great benefit. Both unsalted and salted, a plaster is made for ophthalmia and a struck eyelid edge. When cheese is boiled in water and given to nursing women to drink, it increases their milk.

Salted cheese is bad for the stomach, and likewise unsalted. In salted cheese, however, there is some expulsive quality. And Dioscorides indeed said that fresh cheese is good for the stomach. And this is one of the points of disagreement among authorities. Salted but not old cheese is intermediate between them and is quicker to digest than old cheese and descends more quickly. 'Recocta,' however, is less harmful to the stomach than old cheese. It generates stones in the kidneys and bladder, especially moist ones, especially when eaten with seeds that promote penetration; unsalted cheese, however, loosens the bowels. Certain worms feed on what is in themselves and expel the excess of the food, like the young of wasps and bees; some feed from outside, like the worms of vegetables and others of that kind. The beginning of a worm's growth is from the upper part, and its food from the lower.

div.head: DE COAGULO, DECIMUS QUARTUS TRACTATUS

cit.quote: Rennet is milk thickened in the stomachs of certain animals, by whose power the milk of other animals is curdled. In it the buttery part, curdled by itself, is gathered together and separated from the serous, watery part. Aristotle says, in the third book of the Physics: the thicker milk is, the more suited it is to become cheese and to curdle. But the milk of an animal lacking upper teeth curdles; the milk of one having teeth in both jaws does not, nor does its suet. He also says, in the same place: milk curdles from rennet, and also with fig-milk, when the fig-milk is gathered onto wool; then that wool is washed with a little milk, and that milk quickly curdles what remains, and so the whole thing curdles. Also in the same place: rennet is found only in the stomach of ruminating animals still suckling; in those that have teeth in both jaws it is not found, except in the hare. The more esteemed the rennet, however, the better it is, and it is good against flux of the bowels, especially that of the young hare, and only the young one, as the same Aristotle says. The same Aristotle also says, in the sixteenth book: it happens to milk that it curdles by rennet; since rennet is milk in which there is a spiritual heat, and so it helps and sustains the milk, just as the male sustains the material blood of the female in the womb. For the nature of milk, blood, and menstrual fluid is the same, as the same author says in the same place.

Rennet, he says, curdles by the power of its own sharpness and heat, and by the dryness that dominates it, by which its moisture is brought to an end. And, although rennet is present in every cheese, it is felt less in fresh cheese, because of the abundance of its moisture.

Rennet, then, is found in the stomach of a suckling, ruminating animal, mixed with what it has drunk, and so it is dried and hardened over the fire, and a small portion of it, dissolved with a little warm milk and mixed with the rest of the milk, curdles and thickens the whole of what is curdleable. Hence it is plain that a power similar to that present in the substance of male seed lies hidden in the substance of rennet, as Aristotle, Avicenna, Isaac, and others say. Let what has been said of liquids now suffice.
...of the hare

In the category of rennet, according to Avicenna in the second treatise of the second book, all are hot, dry, and fiery. It dissolves every congealed mass of blood, curdled milk, and coarse humor, and curdles everything liquid and everything cutting, and checks every flow and flux of women's blood, and is entirely thinning. And there is no doubt of this, since along with this it is also drying.

Galen says: what is sharp among rennets should not be administered where constriction is needed. All rennets help epilepsy when drunk, and especially camel's rennet: it dissolves congealed blood in the lung, dissolves curdled milk in the stomach when drunk with wine, and dissolves congealed blood in the stomach, but is bad for the stomach. Given as a suppository after menstrual purgation, it helps toward conception and helps suffocation of the womb, and especially camel's rennet; and it helps ulcers of the intestines, and especially the rennet of a foal. All are a bezoar and help against black henbane. And more helpful for that are the rennets of the kid, the fawn, the calf, and the lamb. And they heal from all poisons and bites, three drams of them, and their draught, is five carats, with a linctus. And kid's rennet is the bezoar for spurge poisoning.

div.head: DE LANA, DECIMUS QUINTUS TRACTATUS

cit.quote: There are various kinds and colors of wool, of which more will be said in the particular treatise on each animal. Burnt wool, according to Avicenna in the second treatise of the second book of the Canon, is helpful for ulcers and for added flesh. Wool with the natural grease still in it, according to Dioscorides, is good, soft, and useful, from the neck and thighs alike. It is applied as necessary to wounds, fractures, or bruises. Steeped in vinegar and oil or wine, it is more emollient, relieves headaches, restores the stomach to health, and drives off various illnesses. Burnt, however, it has a warming, scarring, astringent, and softening power; it removes proud flesh from wounds and induces scarring.

It is burned thus: put clean, carded wool into a clean pot, with fire beneath. Tow and purple wool may also be burned this way. Many burn it anointed with honey; others put oil and a fragment of pottery beneath it, with small splinters of pine-torch placed there. And so they set it alight. And the burning of wool, mixed with the smell of pine-torch, is gathered up. What has been gathered is stored with that pine-torch fat. Burnt wool is washed in a basin. And whatever settles is mixed with the collected substance. The greasy wool has a hot, softening power, easing wounds. It is useful for hysterical complaints. Applied as a suppository with honey and butter, it retains the menses, causes miscarriage, expels the afterbirth. With goose fat added, it cures earache and stomach pain, removes itching of the eyes, soothes roughness and scabies of the eyelids, checks falling hair. The grease itself is rendered thus: pour the aforementioned grease into a new pottery vessel and set it over a slow fire, until the fat itself is fully rendered. The powder of this burning is mixed with the collected substance. Taken with a small drink, that is, with wine, it counters venomous bites, heals coeliac and dysenteric complaints, checks the flow of blood, dissolves congealed blood, cleanses wounds of the chest. Applied after purgation as a pessary, mixed with butter, and inserted into the womb, it prevents conception. And if a little is drunk, it makes a woman fertile. 'Isopus,' moreover, is the name for that grease gathered from wool still greasy. This softens and soothes. It is mixed into salves for inflammation and into pessaries. It is made thus: soft, raw wool is taken and washed in hot water under a strong sun, and all the filth is squeezed out; this is put into a basket and stirred vigorously with water until it foams abundantly; afterward the foam is gathered; sea water is sprinkled on it, and, once it has settled, the fat floating on top is gathered into another earthen vessel, and sea water is poured on again with constant stirring, until it stops foaming; then that fat is gathered and worked by hand, so that, if any impurities are mixed in, they are separated out. Then, the first water poured off and another poured on, with continued stirring, it is worked by hand until it appears white and fatty, and so it is stored in an earthen vessel.

div.head: DE SANGUINE, DECIMUS SEXTUS TRACTATUS

cit.quote: Human blood and pig's blood, according to Avicenna in the second treatise of the second book of the Canon, are alike in every respect. And the flesh of both is very close in every respect, so much so that there was a certain man who sold human flesh as though it were pig's flesh. And this was hidden until human fingers were found in it. And some have said that whoever wishes to test something regarding human blood tests it on pig's blood; for, though it is of weaker power than human blood, it is nonetheless similar to it. And we shall now write down what has been said of blood; but most of it is of no medical concern, and there are some things that are of concern.

...horse's blood is burning and putrefying and altogether of weak digestion, especially when thick. Hare's blood, warm, applied to vitiligo and tinea, helps them. Bat's blood, it is said, prevents the growth of hair; this is not true. The blood of green frogs and of 'alhenlem' is even more preventive. And bat's blood, it is said, keeps the breast in its natural condition; but this is not verified.

Hare's blood ripens hot abscesses quickly, as does goat's blood, and it is administered after congealing. And menstrual blood, it is said, is applied to erysipelas, and warm bull's blood to hard abscesses, and warm hare's blood to soft abscesses. It is said that warm menstrual blood is dropped onto gout and helps it. The blood of the dove, the 'gauriscem,' and the turtledove, dropped in warm, onto a constricted and painful excoriation, prevents the forming of an abscess from a fall, when mixed with lukewarm rose oil. Galen said: this is because of the warmth of its quality, not for any other reason. And if it is set aside and warm rose oil is administered in its place, it achieves the same effect. And likewise for what is said of hen's blood. Ass's blood, applied as a nasal plug, stops nosebleed. And the blood of a wild tortoise cures epilepsy with wine. And likewise lamb's blood. And it is said that camel's blood helps epilepsy; but this is not true. Galen said that it is not of strong cutting power; I, however, say that, if this is verified by experience, it should not be measured against its apparent power alone but against a hidden property in it. The blood of the 'guatis' and of the lizard strengthens sight. The blood of the 'alharbe' prevents the growth of eyelashes. And likewise the blood of green frogs, it is said; but experience has not verified this. The blood of the dove, the 'alguarescem,' and turtledoves, and especially the blood of the wing-veins, is dropped onto a stye. And likewise the blood of the other 'albeit' bird. And likewise if the roots of feathers dipped in the blood of these birds are applied to it. And Galen said: apart from this there is no excuse for not trying it.

The owl's blood is a great help for asthma, and likewise its broth and its flesh. And some have said that bat's blood keeps the breast firm and standing; but there is no basis for this. From the fresh blood of a kid, before it congeals, if one dram is taken and mixed with vinegar and drunk, warmed, over three days, some have testified that it also helps this condition. Menstrual blood, applied as a suppository, prevents pregnancy, according to what some have supposed. The blood of the he-goat, the she-goat, and the camel, dried and fried, checks flux. And goat's blood, drunk with honey, helps dysentery. And dried he-goat's blood breaks kidney stones. The fried blood of he-goat, camel, and hare helps the harm of an Armenian arrow-wound, when drunk with wine. And likewise dog's blood, and even the blood of a rabid dog, it is commonly said, helps against a rabid dog's bite — this on Dioscorides's own authority. Pig's blood, according to Dioscorides, cures earache and ear wounds. This heals all wounds. Goose, swan, and duck's blood is mixed into antidotes. Fresh blood of kid, turtledove, wood-pigeon, and partridge prevents bruises from swelling, and most wholesomely cures moles and bleeding from head wounds. The warm blood of he-goat, she-goat, stag, and hare, anointed on, checks spiders and unhealthy wounds. Dog's blood, drunk, cures a rabid dog's bite, and is a healthful remedy for those who have drunk poison. The blood of the river 'guleus,' drunk, is said to benefit epileptics; the sea one, however, drunk with wine and hare's rennet and cumin, is a healthful remedy for venomous bites and for those who have swallowed tiny frogs.

Bull's blood is diaphoretic and softening, dissolving hardness when applied with barley meal as a plaster. The blood of stallions, that is, of horses, is mixed into caustic medicines. Snake's blood, anointed on, removes hair, especially eyelashes. Green frog's blood can do this even better. Menstrual flow, anointed onto the bodies of other women, prevents their conceiving, and especially where it has been poured, if a woman crosses over it, she does not conceive. Anointed on, it eases gouty pains and brings shingles to healing.

div.head: DE STERCORE, DECIMUS SEPTIMUS TRACTATUS

cit.quote: There are many kinds of dung or manure, according to Avicenna in the second treatise of the second book of the Canon. All dung, according to him, is warming, dissolving, and drying. 'Adab' dung helps large freckles and tinea by its cleansing power. And camel dung cleanses and destroys warts, even large ones. 'Adab' dung helps dandruff by its cleansing power, and camel dung stops nosebleed, and, drunk with medicines, helps epilepsy. 'Adab' dung clears white spots on the eye. Camel dung dissolves 'bothoret' sores. And likewise sheep dung applied over honey ointment.

Goat dung strongly dissolves scrofula. And likewise camel dung. And sheep dung is good for erysipelas. Camel dung calms pains of the joints and their swellings. Dry goat dung with wool prevents flooding of the womb. Goat dung is refined by boiling a dram of it in five 'astanets' of dark wine, and used fresh. A plaster is also made from it for the thirst-causing bite of a viper. And burnt sheep dung, especially prepared with vinegar, is applied to the bite of a rabid dog.

Also according to the same author, in another chapter of the same book: dungs vary according to the diversity of the species of animal; indeed, they sometimes vary even according to the diversity of individuals of a single species, and especially of men. Duck dung is not administered, on account of the excess of its heat. And the dung of the hawk, the kestrel, the 'dasich,' and the other birds of prey is rarely administered, since it is very excessive. None of the dungs is cooling or moistening. Dove dung is the hottest of the dungs that are administered, and that of doves kept in houses is milder than that of those that forage outside.

Goat dung, and especially that of mountain goats, is administered for every flow of blood. Donkey dung, burnt or unburnt, for every course of blood. Dove dung is among the reddening agents, and, with barley flour, dissolving. Burnt goat dung becomes finer but not hotter. Sheep dung with vinegar is suitable for ant-like warts, which are like nails and mulberries. And locust dung helps tinea and vitiligo. And likewise the dung of thrushes that eat rice, and likewise the dung of the lizard and the 'stellio,' which also gives a pleasant smell. Goat dung, especially mountain goat's, burnt, is suitable for alopecia. And likewise mole dung is of great benefit. Dove dung, too, is among the medicines that improve complexion. Lizard dung has been tested to remove tinea. Cow dung with vinegar, applied over hot boils, calms them. Goat and sheep dung with vinegar is suitable applied over fire-burns, with wax and rose oil. Dove dung with honey and linseed is useful in summer for fire-burns and scorching. Goat dung is good for excoriation. Dove and bustard dung for impetigo. And likewise that of thrushes that eat rice. Bone-fed dog dung with honey helps old ulcers. From cow dung a plaster is made for sciatica. Goat dung, especially mountain goat's, with pig fat, applied over gout, is suitable for sciatica. Dried pig dung with vinegar is drunk for weakness of the limbs, and with wax ointment is applied to nerve corrosion and to every kind of hardness.

Dove dung is suitable for pain of the joints. Goat dung is among the things tested for hardness of the joints and their abscesses, especially mixed with vinegar, and it is tested — Galen. And likewise with barley flour. And it is more suitable for one whose flesh is tougher and thicker. Ass dung is smelled for a strong nosebleed, or its moisture is squeezed into the nostril. And it is held that dove dung helps 'saaterac.' Galen says: when the dung of house-kept doves is administered with heath seed, it is useful for the heartburn called 'gallea.' Cow dung is suitable for abscesses behind the ears.

...the dung of the 'stellio,' the lizard, and the crocodile is good for white spots on the eye. Swallow dung is remarkable in this, and I have already tested it myself. Pig dung with water and wine helps spitting of blood and pain in the side. Bone-eating dog's dung, applied with a finger to the palate, treats quinsy, as does an infant's dung, so that it sometimes spares one from bloodletting; but the infant should be fed bread with lupin beans, so that the stench is lessened. Cow dung is among those given for the lung in consumption and similar conditions. Goat dung, especially mountain goat's, is drunk for jaundice with certain spices, such as cumin and the like, and this is tested, and it helps dropsy applied like a plaster and drunk; but the plaster and poultice from it should be made in the sun. Fumigation of the womb's protrusion is made from bull dung. Goat dung, especially mountain goat's, is drunk with certain spices, such as pepper and cinnamon, and it provokes menstruation and causes miscarriage and dissolves hardness of the spleen; and the dry kind is ground and applied to flow of blood from the womb, especially with frankincense; and this is tested.

Hen dung is good for colic. And 'adhib' dung is also suitable for colic that is not from an abscess, drunk in water or decocted, or in a decoction of spices such as pepper and cumin and the rest taken from thorny plants, or applied as a plaster, lifted from the ground, white, containing bones, so that it is hung in salted 'adhib' skin, or in a woolen cloth made from an 'adhib' sheep's escaped wool, or in camel hide, or, as Galen did, placed in a silver vessel. And its top should be hung upward. And it helps colic. And when drunk and administered during its quiet periods, it prevents it, as Galen testified. It always, or by degrees, brings order, gently checking it. 'Aramachamati' dung causes miscarriage by fumigation. Mouse dung with frankincense, drunk, breaks a stone, and applied and loosens the bowels of infants. And dove dung helps colic pain when administered in an enema. And the dung of a bone-eating dog helps in loosening and in ulcers of the intestines, given as an enema or drunk in boiled milk with iron, or applied with stones. Elephant dung, it is said, prevents conception. Goat dung, especially mountain goat's, boiled with vinegar and drunk, helps the sting of venomous worms; indeed, on Galen's testimony, it helps a viper's bite.

And dry dung of a grazing donkey, with wine, is very good for a scorpion's sting. Hen dung has been tested as an antidote for choking mushrooms, and makes one spit up a thick, viscous humor. And in goat dung there is a drawing power; for it draws out wasp venom. Bull dung especially drives away venomous worms and bedbugs, when used as fumigation. And it should be noted that Avicenna, in the second treatise of the second book, devotes three chapters to dung.

Sheep dung or manure, according to Dioscorides, applied with vinegar as a poultice, removes black spots, takes away corns as they form on the body, cures erysipelas when applied, and, mixed with oil, heals burns. Boar's dung, dried, pounded, and drunk with wine or water, is a singular remedy for those spitting up blood: it cures pains of the side, chronic and old, with vinegar; it sets bruises and broken bones; it helps dislocations, especially mixed with rose oil and wax. Ass's and horse's dung, raw and burnt, restrains flowing blood from wounds, vinegar being added. Ass dung from those fed on vine-shoots: dry or dried, given to drink with wine, helps scorpion stings.

Wood-pigeon dung, hot and caustic, ground with vinegar and applied, cures scrofula, bursts carbuncles; mixed with honey, linseed, and oil, applied like a poultice, treats burns. It usefully cures all conditions and especially colic sufferers, if drunk. Mixed into a drink, it is a remedy for those who have eaten poisonous mushrooms. It works better if drunk with wine and vinegar. The dung of the 'palargia' bird, which the Latins call the stork, given in water to drink, cures epileptics. Vulture dung, its fumigation exposes hidden things; ground with vinegar it clears up epilepsy; pounded with rosemary and drunk with wine it expels stones; ground and applied it opens the bowels. Dog dung gathered in the dog days and dried, drunk with wine, restrains the bowels; the white dung of the same treats the curved-spine illness. Human dung, if applied to wounds, prevents swelling and promotes healing; dried, with honey, it cures quinsy. Land-crocodile dung, gathered and dried, works like natural saltpeter when applied; it gives a pleasant, snow-white complexion, especially if it is white and smooth like starch, and, put in water, dissolves quickly. Many, however, adulterate it thus: they grind barley and shape it like the real dung. Others mix chalk and starch with seed and color it, then shape it on boards like little worms, and so sell it. Fresh dung of a grazing buffalo, applied, removes swelling of wounds and is suitable for sciatica; apply this dung wrapped in leaves and warmed with coals to the aforesaid wounds. Applied similarly with vinegar it helps sciatica. Applied as a poultice it purges hardness and scrofula, resolves pustules. Fumigation with the dung of a male ox is of greatest benefit for prolapse of the womb in women. This same dung drives away and destroys gnats. Wild goat dung, drunk with wine, one cupful, over three days, cures the jaundiced; drunk with spikenard leaf and spike, it provokes menstruation; dried, ground with frankincense and bound in linen and applied as a suppository, it regulates menstruation; applied with vinegar it checks other flows of blood; burnt and ground with vinegar or oxymel it corrects alopecia; mixed with lard it heals gout; boiled with wine or vinegar it counters venomous bites; it helps ulcers, which the Greeks call herpes, and swollen glands; it is a singular remedy for sciatica, if dry dung is applied like a cautery, which you should treat thus: make a cautery from that same dung, and, if the right side aches, place the cautery on the right side; if the left, on the left; and leave the cautery on the shoulder as long as the effect is felt in the hips, while it acts through the shoulder. This burning is called 'atanica.' Goat dung is sharp and diaphoretic in power; it is therefore useful for those with sclerosis, such as hardness like stone, and swelling, and it works more on other members than on hardness of the spleen. I myself have used this dung with barley flour, and afterward as a poultice, on a long-standing swelling of someone's knee, and I marveled at how swiftly it was healed. For it is so sharp that it should not be applied to women, children, and men with soft, fair flesh, or to eunuchs. Goat dung is fine in texture and mostly thinning in effect, once its sharpness is removed. And so it is used for alopecia and for all remedies that are cast off, such as those for leprosy, impetigo, scabies, and the like, which purge by being cast off. Hen dung, given to drink with vinegar and wine, has an effect on bilious people, whether from eating troublesome mushrooms. White camel dung, ground with honey and applied, represses swellings and cleanses wounds thoroughly. Cattle dung has a drying power and, tested, removes proud flesh; anointed, it helps the stings of bees, hornets, and wasps; anointed on a dropsical person, if left lying long in the sun, it dries them out.

div.head: DE URINA, DECIMUS OCTAVUS TRACTATUS

cit.quote: True urine is most of all camel's urine, according to Avicenna in the second treatise of the second book of the Canon. And human urine is weaker than other urines. Weaker still than that is the urine of castrated domestic pigs. And among these, older urine is stronger. And the urine of a castrated animal of any kind is weaker. And of all urines, human urine is the most cleansing: it is hot and dry. All urine cleanses.

And human urine is applied with vine ash over a site of bleeding and stops it. Camel's urine helps dandruff, washed with it. And likewise bull's urine cleanses vitiligo. Ass's urine helps creeping and moist ulcers. Human urine too, especially aged, helps excoriation, itching, and leprosy, especially with saltpeter and vinegar-water. And the sediment of urine is applied to erysipelas and helps. And it helps, applied, scabies, favus, worm-infested ulcers, and ulcers of the feet. There are cases where it is urinated upon and left until healed. It helps nerve pains, especially the urine of domestic and mountain goats, and especially spasm and stretching. And likewise a head-purge is made for stretching. In bull's urine, when myrrh is dissolved and dropped finely into the ear, it calms its pain. And likewise goat's urine alone and with myrrh. And aged human urine prevents the discharge of putrid matter from the ear. And camel's urine greatly helps foul-smelling nostrils and forcefully opens blockages of the filtering organs. Let it congeal in a bronze vessel, and then it helps white spots and scabies, especially the urine of children; and likewise boiled with leeks. The urine of nursing infants helps the widening of the breath. A certain man with a diseased spleen dreamed he was told in his sleep to drink his own urine three times a day, and he would be healed; he tried this and found it marvelous. And indeed human urine and camel's urine help dropsy. And it is anointed on the spleen, especially with milk, that is, camel's milk. And goat's urine is good for anasarca, especially that of mountain goats, and especially with fragrant spikenard. And likewise aged sheep's urine for such things, with strong wine. Pig's urine breaks a stone in the kidneys and bladder, and, by provoking urination, draws it out of both. And ass's urine helps kidney pain. And human urine boiled with leeks helps pains of the womb, when women sit in it, once every five days. Human urine helps a viper's bite, drunk and poured over it, especially against the 'petrose' viper; and with saltpeter, over the bite of a rabid dog; and it is good for every bite and sting. And aged urine helps against all poisons and against sea-hare poisoning.

Urine, or one's own water, according to Dioscorides, whoever drinks it, heals one struck by a viper, benefits those who have drunk poison, cures the dropsical in its early stage, and likewise cures the stings of the sea-urchin, the scorpion, and the sea-dragon. Dog's urine, with saltpeter added and made into a remedy, removes leprosy and itching. Old human urine, applied medicinally, cures dandruff, sores, scabies, and spreading wounds, expels and cures putrefaction of the belly and pustules of the ears, and drives out and cures ear-worms with pomegranate rind, if it is decocted. The urine of an unweaned boy cures joint pain. Boiled in a bronze vessel with honey and applied, it checks gum wounds, removes clouding of the eyes. Poured and boiled in a copper vessel, it causes coagulation. What settles in a vessel from urine checks an active fire.

Bull's urine, with myrrh added, eases earache. Goat's urine does all these same things; drunk, it breaks and expels stones. Hare's urine, drunk with spikenard and two cups of water, cures the dropsical, provokes urine in infants, softens the bowels, eases earache. Lynx urine, which many call 'ligurium,' as soon as it is passed becomes a stone, which many call 'electorius': it eases stomach pains, checks rheumatism of the bowels. Ass's urine, drunk, cures kidney ailments. Goat's urine, boiled in a vessel and applied with wool as a pessary, cures hysterical pains, removes eye wounds, checks itching of the eyelids.

div.head: DE SPERMATE, DECIMUS NONUS TRACTATUS

cit.quote: The ancients said, according to Aristotle, that seed is that which comes forth from the whole body. They proved this also by the fact that pleasure is greatest in that same act, and that perfect produces perfect. Likewise, conversely, offspring resemble their parents, not only in their natural formation but also in accidental features. And many offspring have marks resembling their parents, and in the same places. We, however, say that seed is that which has the nature of being suited to the whole and does not come from the whole. They said that seed is a dissolution of the body. We, however, say that it is a surplus that is needed, and it is better that it be the last such surplus. For that it comes about by way of surplus, and not by way of dissolution, is shown by the fact that large-bodied animals are of little fecundity; for it is necessary that in them much is dissolved and little surplus remains, for the reason given above. Moreover, everything that is dissolved from the body is corrupted and changes its nature. Furthermore, what is dissolved has no natural place in the body, but wanders randomly. Likewise, dissolution always weakens; but the emission of seed relieves, and it is not the living seed alone that comes forth, but seed together with the surplus matter within it, which is weak. For this reason many men do not generate offspring.

There is, however, no seed in the young, because of growth; for seed passes instead into the body's growth; nor is there seed in the old, because of poor digestion, since nature can no longer digest well; nor in the sick, because of weakness. Some, however, are of much seed, some of little, some of none at all, not because of weakness, but for the opposite reason; for when there is much flesh and much fat, they produce little seed and desire mating only rarely. The same happens to women. For the surplus that is in fat bodies is digested and turns into fat. This same thing happens too in fertile vines, because of the abundance of nourishment, whose fruit is thereby diminished and spoiled. And so, since he-goats, when overly fattened, mate only rarely, wise shepherds make them lean before mating. Farmers do the same for barren vines. It is clear, then, that seed is the surplus food that is needed from the last, bloody food, which is scattered through the members and gives them great vigor. And so seed weakens the body. When it is digested and cooked, it comes out changed and altered, that is, white, not the color of blood, unless it comes out undigested. When a man is too eager to mate, bloody seed comes out. Sons rightly resemble their fathers and forebears, since what comes out from the members is like what remains. And so seed, although no distinction of members appears in it, is nonetheless potentially like each member. Seed multiplies in a body whose complexion is hot and moist. Every animal of much fat has little seed. Man, among other animals, in proportion to his body, is of much seed. Both natural and accidental moisture are suited to the generation of seed. The heat of the sun, then, and animal heat, are both present in seed.

div.head: DE MENSTRUO, VIGESSIMUS TRACTATUS

cit.quote: The menstrual fluid in females is like seed in males, and is nothing other than undigested seed. But it is not suited to generation, since, if it were seed, it would not be menstrual fluid, and vice versa. A sign of this is that the nature of females is weak and of lesser heat, and their bodies are softer and lighter and have less hair than male bodies. They are also smaller in every kind of animal that generates a live animal. And the discharge of menstrual fluid occurs only in these kinds. But the generation of seed and of menstrual fluid does not occur by the same process. Nor does offspring arise from the mixture of two seeds, since a woman is often impregnated without pleasure at the time of mating, and sometimes both man and woman produce seed and yet nothing is generated from them, unless there is in the womb a tempered moisture from the residue of menstrual fluid. For this reason a female that does not menstruate does not give birth at all. Egg-laying animals do not menstruate, because of the dryness of their bodies; animals, however, that bear live young expel this moisture, except in those that arise from crossbreeding in generation, like the kind of mules. The flow of blood, however, does not appear in the females of other animals as it does in women; for internally a woman has more blood than the females of other animals, and for this reason menstruation occurs in her. For this reason too she is less often ill than the male. Nursing women do not menstruate at all, or only slightly. Those, however, who lack menstruation are, for the most part, barren.

div.head: DE LACRIMA, VIGESSIMUS PRIMUS TRACTATUS

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis, Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: A tear, as Isidore says, some think named from 'laceration of the mind,' since it usually proceeds from grief of mind and, as it were, offends the mind itself, torn as it is by the feeling of grief; but this only in man, endowed with a rational mind. Some, nonetheless, of the other animals too are found to have wept from a similar feeling. It is a drop or droplet, liquid, bright, and salty, flowing from the eyes. It comes forth sometimes from anger and indignation, sometimes from anguish or grief of heart or body, sometimes from pity or compassion, and sometimes from desire, joy, or love. Isidore also says, in the book of the Etymologies: the horse alone, besides man, is said to weep and to feel grief. When their masters are killed or dying, then, they shed many tears.

div.head: DE SALIVA, VIGESSIMUS SECUNDUS TRACTATUS

cit.quote: Saliva, according to Gregory, flows down into the mouth or from the head; from the mouth it is carried to the stomach when swallowed.

Avicenna also, in the fourth book of the Canon: saliva varies according to each particular complexion. Its power is entirely ripening and dissolving. It cleanses tinea, freckles, and dead blood. It also resists poisons, and the spittle of a fasting man kills scorpions. Likewise, impetigo is rubbed with the saliva of a fasting man and with camphor. This same saliva, when dropped into an ear afflicted by worms, kills them and immediately expels them.

div.head: DE SUDORE, VIGESSIMUS TERCIUS TRACTATUS

cit.quote: The sweat of beasts arises from the moist surplus of the small veins, and only occurs when the body is heated and the openings of the veins are opened. Now, bloody sweat happens to some men because of a fault of complexion, since their body is very porous and disposed to flux, and their blood very moist and watery, from weakness of heat and small veins. For when blood is digested it thickens; heat cannot digest it because of the abundance of food. Avicenna also, in the second treatise of the second book of the Canon: sweat is the watery part of blood, to which bile was previously mixed. And it is more fully digested than urine; for it is the surplus of oiliness and moisture after the final digestion. Urine, however, is the surplus of the second digestion. Sweat varies, however, according to the animal. In it there is no small dissolving power. Athletes' sweat helps abscesses of the groin and dissolves them. The dry sweat of nursing women, with henna oil, dissolves abscesses of the breast; with rose oil, however, it is applied to congealed milk in the breast. Moreover, the grime of nursing women, which gathers on their bodies when they are anointed with oil and mixes with the powder that gathers on patients from their vapors and sweats, is dissolving and evenly ripening, draws out thorns and splinters, and is useful for sciatica and also helps hardness of the womb. The same author, in the second treatise of the second book of the Canon: the sweat of venomous beasts is itself venomous, and its surface becomes green and abscessed, and a foul-smelling sweat issues from the body and from the armpits. Its cure is vomiting with warm water and treacle made from sealed earth.

div.head: DE SOMPNO ET VIGILIA, VIGESSIMUS QUARTUS TRACTATUS

bibl.author: Aristoteles, De vegetabilibus et plantis Nicolai Damasceni
Aristoteles, De somno et vigilia Aristotelis

cit.quote: Sleep, according to Aristotle, occurs in animals having a brain, since it cools the food coming to it by the course of the blood. Heat, however, along with the blood, flees downward, and, when it gathers in the lower place, sleep results. And so the heads of quadrupeds too grow heavy before the time of sleep. Sleep seems to be a middle state between being alive and not being alive. And so, if the body of a sleeping man is pricked, as much blood will not come out as if he were awake, since then there is manifestly little or much blood within. Fish, too, rest in sleep and nothing moves except the tail, and that only a little. The same author, in the book On Plants: waking is an effect of sense, while sleeping is the weakening of that same sense. And when an animal is awake, vapor rises to the head, and it sleeps; but when that same vapor is consumed, it wakes. In some animals this vapor is abundant, and yet they sleep little. And sleep is a compression of motion. Compression is the rest of a thing in motion. The same author, in the book On Sleep and Waking: waking and sleep are proper to animals; and if to be awake is nothing other than to have sensation, it is clear that in whatever they have sensation, in that same thing they are also awake. We say, then, that sleep is a certain condition of the sensitive part, like a bond upon the senses, and a certain immobility, a loosening or a slackening — for waking is...

Also: sleep is the disabling of the primary organ of sensation, so that it cannot act. And this does not occur in plants because, without sensation, there is neither sleep nor waking. In whatever has sensation, there is also grief and joy; and in whatever has these, there is also desire. In plants, however, none of these is present. Touch, then, being a passive faculty, sleep and waking belong to all animals, since touch alone belongs to all of them. And when the organ of touch is disabled, the organs of all the other senses must necessarily also be deficient. Rest or sleep, however, exists as though for the health of animals. For rest is unnecessary and useless for anything born to move, if it could move always and continually with pleasure; for the nutritive faculty performs its work in the body more during sleep than during waking, as though needing nothing from the senses for this. To move, moreover, though something can be done without strength, requires vigor, which the enduring spirit produces in creatures that breathe. Among land creatures it is plain that all contained animals sleep. Of aquatic creatures, however, this is scanty; some, who are uncertain about the rest, do not think they sleep, but from the evidence of their eyes, since they have no eyelids, they are nonetheless observed to be as though drugged, in calm stillness, moving nothing but the tail, and startled at any disturbance. Of tuna it is more confidently affirmed that they sleep near banks or rocks; flatfish, however, in shallows, so much so that they are often lifted out by hand; for dolphins and whales are even heard snoring. Insects too are apparently silent in sleep, since they are not stirred even when a light is brought near. A newborn man is overcome by sleep for several months, and then his waking hours lengthen day by day.

Sleep, however, is not a disabling of the sensitive part in itself, but a passive condition arising from vaporization around the nourishment. This is according to Aristotle. For what has evaporated must necessarily be driven onward, then converted and transformed. Animal heat is naturally borne upward, and, once in the upper regions, it suddenly returns and is carried back down. And as it descends it drives the heat before it, weighs it down, and causes sleep. A sign of this is that all sleep-inducing substances produce heaviness in the head.

And sleep occurs mostly after meals, since much evaporation comes from food. Sleep also comes from exertion and from certain illnesses, namely those that come from an excess of hot, moist matter, like fever and lethargy. Moreover, the first age also induces sleep; for children sleep very deeply, since all their nourishment is carried upward, whence also their growth occurs. For this same reason epilepsy also occurs; for sleep is similar to epilepsy, and the onset of this ailment often happens to people while sleeping, since much spirit is carried upward; descending again, it swells the veins, by which it narrows the passage where breathing occurs. And so wine does not benefit children, nor nursing mothers, but they should drink watered-down drinks and little of them, for wine is flatulent, and mead even more so. In general, however, lovers of sleep are those who have hidden veins and empty, large heads; for their veins are narrow, so that the moisture that descends does not easily flow away. Those who have visible veins, on the contrary, are not sleepy, because of the easy flow through their pores. Nor are the melancholic, since their internal region is cold, and so there is not much evaporation from it. For black bile, being naturally cold, also makes the nutritive region cold. It is clear, then, that sleep is a gathering, that is, a certain assembly, a reciprocal internal movement of natural heat. Hence there is much movement in a sleeper. After a meal, this movement is strongest, since wine and other such things are heat-inducing and sleep-causing, and the cause of sleep is indeed heat.

Also, from the Gloss on the same book: Aristotle gives a fourfold cause of sleep: one which is the cause in itself, namely the evaporation of food; and three which are accidental causes, namely exertion, a certain illness, and the first age. Then he shows how the chilling and weighing-down of the senses is the cause of sleep. The stomach, when empty, is hotter, according to Aristotle; being full, however, cools it because of the motion involved. Just as the pores and regions in the head cool once the evaporation is removed — namely, when much food has been taken in, into which heat is drawn off, just as fire placed under logs cools and grows faint until it is consumed — sleep occurs for it, as has been said, while the corporeal element is carried upward by heat through the veins to the head, and is again driven back and flows downward. The region around the brain, however, is the coldest of all in the body; hence, as heat rises to the brain, the surplus that evaporates is turned into phlegm. The nutritive part, gathered below, is carried down, and what is hot is cooled. People wake, however, once digestion is complete and the thicker, purer blood has also been separated out. The thinnest and purest blood is in the head; the thickest and most turbid is in the upper parts of the body. Also from the Gloss: just as sleep is created from the chilling and immobility of the senses, so waking arises from the dissolution of that chilling, after the completion of digestion and after the separation of pure blood from impure. The upper parts of the body are nourished by the purer blood, the lower by the coarser and less pure; hence, since blood becomes most undivided right after the removal of nourishment, sleep occurs, and then the purest blood is gathered together, and the most turbid is gathered below. When this happens, people wake, once the heaviness of digestion is resolved.

Also the Author says: besides the four causes of sleep mentioned above, others are added, namely, the withdrawal of heat, and also intense concentration on some pursuit; of these more will be said below in the treatise on the soul. Avicenna also said: care or fear sometimes induce sleep too. Some also add languor. But this cause reduces to illness and exertion.

Since the first cause of sleep, according to Aristotle, is the evaporation of food, and sleep is common to all, it is clear that the same cause is shared by all living creatures. For some other causes of sleep too, like exertion, the first age, and illness, cause sleep only through the action of nourishment. For Philosophus says that exertion is a gatherer of nourishment through the multiplication of heat. This nourishment, namely, is raised somewhat to the brain. And the first age also induces sleep, because nourishment is raised to the upper parts and weighs down the head. Likewise, weakness and languor from fatigue, and this because the heat withdrawn from the outer members multiplies around the place of digestion and dissolves the nourishment found there and raises it to the head, and so induces sleep. So it is with the other causes too. Hence it is clear that all act through the action of nourishment, and this, as has been said, in all animals.

But someone might perhaps object that the beginning of sleep is from the heart, liver, and brain, or similar members, from which the evaporation of nourishment proceeds, and that no evaporation is the cause of sleep except that which is first heated by digested heat and then chilled by the coldness of the brain; but in some animals there is no head or brain, as in those that have only the sense of touch; hence in them there is no evaporation upward chilled in the head, and so the aforesaid cause is not universal to all sleepers.

We can answer that in every animal there is a brain or a member resembling a brain, as is expressly stated in the book On Animals. Nor is it necessary that it have all the operations of a brain; otherwise such animals would have common sense and memory and imagination, which is false. For, as is read at the beginning of the Metaphysics, animals are creatures naturally having sensation, and from sensation memory is present in some of them, in others not, as is plain in that some animals lack memory. And since, according to Philosophus, memory is a passive condition of common sense, this is also proven by the fact that they lack common sense.

And some grant this, adducing also the reasoning that common sense exists for two purposes, namely, to discern common sensible objects, which are not perceived by touch alone, and to compare objects proper to each sense. Hence, if in such animals there is only touch, common sense would be useless to them for both of these acts. We, however, say that, just as such animals are deficient in the number of their external senses, so too are they in the number of their internal ones, so that they have only a weak common sense and a slight imagination. We also say that common sense not only compares the sensible objects of different senses, but also the sensible objects of the same sense, like hot and cold, smooth and rough. Nor is it true that common sense does not perceive size through touch; otherwise it would not perceive heat in any given size either. Touch, in such animals, then, perceives its proper sensible object, which is size, though undetermined, and combines the objects of touch among themselves and with size.

There is also in them an imagination that discerns what is harmful and what is suitable, though weakly. Hence, if Philosophus says that creatures having only touch have no imagination, it should be understood that they do not have a complete imagination, since it is not moved except by the presence of a thing. For this movement, however, three things are required: imagination, determining what is harmful or suitable; and common sense, combining sensations with magnitude; and the proper sense, apprehending them.

But if it is objected that such animals are also immobile as regards place, it should be said that, although they do not move from place to place, they move with a motion of expansion and contraction; for they contract at the touch of something harmful and expand at the touch of something suitable. Without this motion, as Avicenna says, there is no animal, nor can it be recognized except through that motion.

bibl.author: Aristoteles, De somno et vigilia Aristotelis

cit.quote: Since, according to Aristotle, no animal is always awake or always asleep, the nutritive faculty, indeed, is always at work in the waking, and even more so in the sleeping. For so Aristotle says in the book On Sleep and Waking, that this faculty does its work more in sleeping than in waking; for the animal is more nourished and grows more then, as though the senses did nothing at that time. Hence certain animals, like dormice, sleep through the whole winter, as has been said above, and, remarkably, according to Isidore, fatten from that very sleep. As spring begins, when the sun sends out its warm rays, they return, in their natural way, to strength.

Aristotle also says, in the book On Animals, that certain animals and certain serpents can live long without food, and so sometimes hide in caves. Avicenna also says, in his book On Animals, that there are certain scaly creatures, like snakes and shellfish, that stay in their places for four months in winter and eat nothing. Likewise the bear and the wild goat sometimes hide themselves. The she-bear also sometimes hides for forty days, sometimes for many months, and gives birth at that time. Proof of this is that her giving birth is not well observed, since her young are found very thin when they are small.

When animals hide themselves or sleep, their nutritive function does not cease within them, except as regards taking in nourishment from outside; for there are certain animals that are cold and of weak heat, having little hunger. For the cause of hunger is the vigorous dissolution of nourishment; the cause of that dissolution, however, is the scantiness of matter and its fineness and the porousness of the skin, and strong natural heat, as well as the heat of the surrounding air aiding from outside, and likewise movement. And so, when one or more of these are lacking in certain gluttonous animals, through their appetite they accumulate many surpluses which their weak natural heat cannot dissolve, especially when not helped by outward heat except through movement. Such animals, then, because of the great cold surplus accumulated and their weak natural heat, become very sluggish in cold weather and desire rest and stillness of body; and so they hide themselves. And if in some of them there is some heat, those animals will grow thin and weakened; but if the heat is so weak that nature cannot cook the surplus, that undigested surplus is congealed by the coldness of the intestines into fat. And so animals become fatter during the time of their hiding. Further, since heat can do this more quickly or more slowly, according to this the time of their hiding is shorter or longer. This also frequently happens in certain human beings, and especially in women, if they are immobile as regards place; as in the city of Padua a certain woman abstained for forty days.

bibl.author: Aristoteles, De generatione et corruptione Aristotelis
Aristoteles, De somno et vigilia Aristotelis

cit.quote: It should also be known that certain powers of the soul move their organs by the proper motion of the soul itself, not of nature, like the motive power as regards place, and the sensitive power. And when such motion is not according to the nature of the organs according to their composition of elements, it therefore induces pain and toil in the organs. From this, then, arises the desire for rest and stillness, just as, in waking, the desire for sleep. Some powers, however, move their organs according to the nature of those organs themselves; and that movement is always weakening to the organs. So move all the powers of the vegetative faculty, and especially the nutritive one. Hence Philosophus says that the movement of generation is nutritive, following nature in its movement. So then, although the sensitive and motive power rest in sleep, for the desire of rest by the reason given above, the nutritive power, nonetheless, as has been said above, never ceases from its action. Hence Philosophus says in the book On Generation and Corruption that the body is indeed nourished until it dissolves and is corrupted, but it is not always growing. Not man alone dreams, moreover, but the horse and the dog and the bull and the he-goat and every animal that generates its like, according to Aristotle. This is plain from a dog's barking in its sleep. Also, in the book On Sleep and Waking, or the second: sensible objects, through each organ of sensation, produce sensation in us. And the passive condition that arises from them is present not only in the sensory organs while the senses are acting, but also, once they have withdrawn, it remains in what is imaginative. For imagination comes both from sense, according to the actual movement in the imaginative faculty, and is also a dream.

A dream, then, is an image received from the outer sense and set forth in the imagination; to the inner sense and the imagination in sleep, however, it is not true, since it is a deceptive object; for, once the external sensible thing has withdrawn, images of sensible things remain within. In this we are easily deceived, when we are under the influence of passions, as the fearful man in fear and the lover in love, so that the one seems, from a slight resemblance, to see enemies, and the other, his beloved. It is the same in anger and in every desire. And the more violently they suffer under these passions, the more they are deceived.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Dreams appear more by night than by day, since during the day, while the senses and the intellect are at work, dreams are pushed back and driven out, just as a small fire is overwhelmed near a great one, and small griefs and delights beside great ones. Immediately after taking nourishment, and in those who are still very young, like children, dreams do not occur; for there is much movement because of the heat that comes from the food. To some, however, confused or monstrous visions and worse dreams appear, as to the melancholic, the feverish, and the drunken. For all such conditions cause much movement and disturbance, namely around the brain. Pliny also, in the tenth book: an infant dreams right away, for it is roused by a vapor and changes its burping.

Sleep, moreover, is nothing other than a withdrawal into the middle of the body. Besides man, it is well known that horses, dogs, oxen, livestock, and goats dream; for this reason it is believed to occur in all live-bearing animals. Of those that lay eggs, however, it is uncertain, though it is certain that they sleep.

div.head: DE MORTE ET VITA, VIGESSIMUS QUINTUS TRACTATUS

cit.quote: Some animals are of longer life, according to Aristotle, some of shorter. Fire and water, and what is close to them, are the cause of generation and corruption; for whatever is composite shares in the nature of the opposing elements of which it is made. For corruption occurs only from an opposite; for it is impossible for matter capable of corruption not to contain within it an opposite.

...man and the elephant; and likewise, as is more often said, larger animals are of longer life than smaller ones. It should be understood that an animal is by nature hot and moist, and such is youth; old age, however, is cold and also dry and near to death. Hence the moisture must not be easily, that is, readily, dessicable, but rich. Nor, again, should the moisture be small in quantity, since a small amount of moisture is easily dried up. And so large animals and plants live longer; for it is reasonable that larger creatures have more moisture. There are, however, two causes of longer life, namely quality and quantity, that is, heat and moisture, and their amount. In some there is heat and richness together, which together makes it neither quickly dried nor quickly chilled. Such a creature is destroyed either by illness, or by nature, or even by diet, or by age. The heat and moisture, then, must not be excessive; for excess is a nature contrary and destructive to it. Hence creatures of excessive and abundant seed age quickly too. Further: whatever tires the male generative organs ages them more; for exertion dries. Old age, however, is naturally dry. But among men, males live longer than females, since the male is hotter than the female. And for the same reason, those who live in hot places live longer than those in cold ones. And since seed is a surplus, the mule, born of the horse and the ass, lives longer than either of them. And females live longer than males, if males approach them; while male sparrows are of shorter life than females. Creatures that take no nourishment, both plants and animals, are destroyed; for they consume themselves. For, just as a great flame consumes and destroys a small one when taking in or consuming its fuel, so too physical heat, that is, natural heat, is first digestive, and whatever it digests, it consumes the matter in which it resides.
