Aquatic animals are of shorter life than land-walking ones, since they are moist and watery, and such a nature is quickly corrupted, since it is cold and easily condensed. And likewise a bloodless animal, for the same reason, is quickly corrupted. Bees are of longer life than other, larger animals.

The same author, in the book On Animals: the elephant lives two hundred years, and perhaps three hundred. The horse, however, lives up to thirty or thirty-five years; the mare, however, up to forty. The male ox lives fifteen years; castrated, however, twenty. The camel lives thirty years and more. The dog up to fourteen. The pig up to fifteen. The sheep, properly in Ethiopia, lives fourteen. The goat, however, eleven. The dolphin, however, lives one hundred and thirty years or more, which is proven when one, caught, has its tail cut off and is released, and is afterward found again after a long time. The peacock lives twenty-five years. The dove and the turtledove, twelve. Man, however, lives longer than all animals, except the elephant.

Man's longevity, however, is due only to the fact that his complexion resembles the surrounding air. An infant born before seven months does not survive at all; one born before eight months may perhaps survive, but for the most part dies. In the bodies of the dead, the nature of the large veins does not appear, since they contract suddenly as the blood departs. Hair is harder after death. And the same happens with the nails.
Here ends the general treatise on animals.

div.head: <DE NATURIS ET PROPRIETATIBUS ANIMALIUM IN SPECIALI>

bibl.author: Iohannes Egidius Zamorensis, Historia naturalis Iohannis Egidii Zamorensis

cit.quote: ...on particular animals, that is, livestock, draught animals, and beasts, on creeping things and serpents and worms and on other small animals, arranged and ordered according to alphabetical order, which brother Juan Gil, doctor of the Friars Minor of Zamora, compiled. Amen. Having reached the end of the general treatise on the properties of animals in general, through him who is the end and completion of all things universally, there follows the particular treatise on particular animals, arranged according to alphabetical order. And first on animals beginning with the vowel A; second, on animals beginning with the letter B; third, on animals beginning with the letter C, and so on with the rest, until we reach Z, which is the last letter in alphabetical order. The names of all animals universally — that is, of livestock and draught animals, of great and small beasts, of creeping things and serpents, of snakes and asps and vipers and lizards and other ringed animals and worms — that begin with the vowel A are the following, which follow here: 'Afferatus,' a flying serpent. 'Affidius' and 'sabyn,' two serpents, according to Aristotle. 'Agnus' [lamb], so named as though 'pious.' 'Ahamet,' a beast; it has its gall in its ear. 'Alches' [elk], a beast resembling goats. 'Anabulla,' a beast of Ethiopia. 'Anffibena' [amphisbaena], a two-headed serpent. 'Anguis' [snake]. 'Aper' [boar], a wild pig. 'Apes' [bees], which are both animals and birds, and of which something has been said, and will be said, in the treatise on birds. 'Aptalo,' a beast. 'Aranea' [spider]. 'Aries' [ram]. 'Armenie serpens' [the Armenian serpent]. 'Asilus,' which is the same as the horsefly. 'Asinus' [ass]. 'Aspis' [asp]. Here end the titles. Here begins the treatise on all animals universally — livestock, draught animals, and beasts, and creeping things and worms — beginning with the vowel A, and first on the 'afferatus.' Amen.

div.head: <DE AFFERATO>

cit.quote: 'Afferatus' and 'alterati,' that is, leaping and flying serpents, are small, short, tiny serpents, which sometimes hide in trees, lying in wait so as to hurl themselves at passers-by, according to Avicenna. They are very hot and inclined to redness. From their bite, it is said, a violent pain arises and passes through the whole body, from which death also follows. Their treatment is the treatment for vipers.

div.head: DE AFFYDIO

cit.quote: 'Affidius' and 'sabin,' as the wise men have said, are two serpents having sandy-colored bodies, with white and black spots on their heads. And they are sometimes black and red and white. On their heads are cut white scales, and their movement has a rustling sound because of the dryness of the skin of their bellies. They are heavy in movement and have even teeth. Their bite ruptures the pores and natural passages, making blood flow from them, even from the corners of the eyes. And it is accompanied by bloody sputum and nosebleed and vomiting and stomach pain. And it is said that the place becomes an abscess and turns black, and a watery substance flows from it, and the bowels loosen, and the breath is constricted, and difficulty of urination occurs, the voice is lost, and the limbs go slack, and a state of forgetfulness overcomes the body, and spasm occurs, and the teeth fall out, and the patient dies. Their treatment, as regards its nearest part, is the treatment for vipers.

div.head: <DE AGNO>

cit.quote: Describing the properties of lambs according to the opinions of the philosophers, we shall first treat the properties of the ewe-lamb. Second, the properties of the ram-lamb. Third, their rearing. Fourth, their illness. Fifth, their powers and effects.

div.head: DE PROPRIETATIBUS AGNE, PRIMUM CAPITULUM

bibl.author: Isaac Iudeus, De dietis universalibus et particularibus Isaac Israeli

cit.quote: The ewe-lamb is the daughter of the ram, and is of smaller body and strength alike than the ram-lamb. And she is of less heat and greater moisture than the ram-lamb, by reason of her feminine complexion, as is said in the Diets. Her flesh, while she is suckling, is of greater stickiness, because of the surplus of moisture that dominates her body, both from her age and from her complexion. And so what is generated from her flesh is phlegmatic and sticky and is digested with difficulty, and, once digested, is scarcely dissolved from the members, by reason of the sticky, glutinous humor generated from it. It descends easily to the stomach, however, by reason of its slipperiness and moisture, as Isaac says. And its flesh is better roasted than boiled, since its surplus moisture is consumed by the force of the heat.

The ewe-lamb, however, is of greater simplicity and timidity than the ram-lamb, since the female has less natural heat than the male. And so she is less spirited. For this reason too she lacks horns, since they would be superfluous to her, as, because of her lack of boldness, she would not know how to use them, as Avicenna says.

Aristotle also says, in the third book On Animals, that an illness befalls lambs when they become too fat around the kidneys; for, if the kidneys become covered with suet, they die. And the suet multiplies from good pasture. And so they are kept from pasture, lest they become too fat.

div.head: DE PROPRIETATIBUS AGNI, SECUNDUM CAPITULUM

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis, Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: The ram-lamb, as Isidore says, is named as though 'pious,' from the word for recognizing. For among all the living creatures of the earth, it is found to be the most innocent and gentle. For it harms nothing with tooth, or horn, or claw. And whatever is found in it is entirely useful. For its flesh is for food, its hide for various uses, its wool for clothing, its dung for enriching the soil, its hoof and horn for medicine, and so on. Or, as the same Isidore says in the twelfth book: the Latins think 'agnus' is named from 'recognizing' ['agnoscendo'], since, more than other animals, it knows its own mother, so much so that, if it strays in a large flock, it immediately recognizes its parent's voice by her bleating.

According to Avicenna, or also Aristotle, some lambs are born in the spring season and some in the autumn. Spring lambs, however, are larger of body, stronger of strength, and fatter than autumn or winter lambs.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: In many regions, however, many prefer winter lambs to spring lambs, saying: this alone of all animals is usefully born amid the frost, as Pliny says, in the eighth book, forty-seventh chapter. And it is said in the same place that lambs conceived while the north wind blows are larger than those conceived while the south wind blows. For then the mothers are made pregnant. In lambs, the wool or fleece follows the color that the parents have in the veins of the tongue. For if the veins are white, the lambs too will be white; and if black, black; and if mottled, mottled, as the same author says. In the same place: the lamb, while suckling, bends its front knees. And, so that its mother gives it more milk, it presses her udder with its head. It seeks its mother by bleating. Once it finds her, wagging its tail to please its mother, head raised, it seeks her teats. And unless it first raises its head, it never suckles. It has fine, curly wool, folded many times over on itself. Cold harms lambs greatly, especially in rainy weather. It delights in the company of the flock. When it is alone, however, it grieves greatly and is afraid. It leaps ahead of the flock and plays as it leaps. When it sees a wolf it is violently afraid and suddenly takes flight. But afterward, stunned by fear, it suddenly plants its steps and, not daring to flee further, begs mercy for itself, not by bleating but rather by its simple expression. Also in the same place: a lamb captured by an enemy and bound by the butcher defends itself with neither horn nor tooth. And whether it is stripped of its fleece or its hide, like an innocent animal it falls silent. Whether it is led to pasture or brought to sacrifice, it does not groan, does not grumble, does not kick, but obeys. And, as Pliny says, it is dangerous to leave lambs alone; for, if thunder should happen to occur, they easily die. For a lamb naturally has a weak head. And so the remedy is to gather them together with others like them, so that, from mutual company, they are given heart, and comforted by the presence of many. Also in the same place: a lamb is a full ram-lamb at the age of one year. Within that year's span, it is the better the further removed it is from milk. For from milk its moisture of complexion increases.

bibl.author: Isaac Iudeus, De dietis universalibus et particularibus Isaac Israeli

cit.quote: But by separation from milk its heat is intensified and its surplus moisture is tempered, especially if it remains as yet uncastrated, as Isaac says quite plainly in the Diets.

bibl.author: Isaac Iudeus, De dietis universalibus et particularibus Isaac Israeli

cit.quote: Also, in the same place: a ram-lamb, whole in body and clean in flesh, is fit for sacrifice and for eating, even if it is spotted in its fleece.
For a spot in the fleece does not disqualify a lamb from sacrifice, unless there is foulness or corruption in the flesh or the skin, as the Gloss on the twelfth chapter of Exodus says.

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis, Commentarii Hieronymi in prophetas minores

cit.quote: And on Malachi, Jerome says, and also on Leviticus: the variety of a spotted fleece does not hinder the sacrifice, he says, if the body is whole and if there is no scab on the surface of the skin.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Also, in the same place: the ram-lamb, as Pliny says in the eighth book, forty-seventh chapter, was fit for the altars of the gods, and is necessary both in the use of its fleece and in the eating of its flesh for the uses of men. And so, just as, for the expense of men, the bodies of oxen are tended and cared for, so too must diligence be shown in the keeping of sheep and lambs.

div.head: DE AGNORUM EDUCACIONE, TERTIUM CAPITULUM

bibl.author: Palladius Rutilius Taurus Emilianus, Opus agriculture Palladii

cit.quote: The first breeding of lambs is in the month of November, according to Palladius, in the twelfth book. But a newborn lamb should immediately be brought by hand to its mother's udder. First, however, a small amount of the milk, in which the substance is thicker — which shepherds call colostrum — should be milked out; for this will harm the lambs unless it is removed. And for two days the lamb should be shut up with its mother, and then kept in enclosed, dark, and warm places. With the flock of young thus separated, the mothers may be sent out to pasture. It suffices, before they go out in the morning and when they return in the evening, to let the lambs drain the udders. Until they are weaned within the stall, they should be fed bran, or a little grass, or, if there is plenty, barley meal brought to them, until, having gained a little strength with age, they can share the common pasture with their mothers.

div.head: DE AGNORUM EGRITUDINE, QUARTUM CAPITULUM

cit.quote: An illness befalls lambs, according to Aristotle in the third book On Animals, from which many die, namely fatness of the kidneys. For, when they become too fat around the kidneys, if their kidneys become covered with suet, they die without fail. The suet multiplies in them from good pasture. And so they are kept from pasture, lest they become too fat.

div.head: DE AGNORUM COMPLEXIONIBUS<ET>VIRTUTIBUS, QUINTUM CAPITULUM

bibl.author: Isaac Iudeus, De dietis universalibus et particularibus Isaac Israeli

cit.quote: A suckling lamb, according to Isaac in the Diets, is close in stickiness to wild pigs, because of the closeness of the womb and the moisture of the milk on which it is fed. Accordingly its flesh is not unpraiseworthy, though indigestible, and by its slipperiness it descends from the stomach. It is indigestible especially for those eating it who have a moist and weak stomach.
Galen criticized suckling lambs.

bibl.author: Liber de natura rerum Thome Cantimpratensis

cit.quote: Yearling lambs, however, have a complexion midway between the moisture of the suckling and the dryness of the mature; and so they are better than the rest and easier to digest. For they generate better blood, and especially help the young who have a hot, dry complexion and inhabit a hot, dry region. Also, from the Book of the Nature of Things: lamb's flesh is very good for the strong and healthy, but bad for the sick; because, though it descends easily from the stomach, it is very hard to dissolve from the members. And so it generates a sticky humor.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Also Pliny, in the twenty-ninth book: a lamb's rennet is powerful against every harmful medicine, and is good against the bites or stings of sea creatures.
Also Avicenna: a lamb's blood cures epilepsy with wine. Its rennet heals from all poisons and bites.

Also, Dioscorides says that a lamb has black dung. If it is dissolved with vinegar and applied as a poultice, it clears black spots, removes corns from the body, cures erysipelas. Mixed with wax and oil it heals burns.

div.head: DE AHAME ET ALCHE ET ALOY, EX LIBRIS DE NATURA RERUM

cit.quote: The 'ahame,' according to Aristotle, is an animal the size of a stag, having, contrary to the custom of all animals, its gall in its ear, resembling human gall in color. And it is very bitter, biting, of violent anger and ferocity. So too Helinand, in the twenty-third book.

The elk is an animal of the Hercynian forest. These resemble goats in shape and in the variegation of their hides, but somewhat exceed them in size. They are without horns and have legs without joints or knots. They neither lie down for the sake of rest, nor, if they happen to fall by accident, can they raise or lift themselves up. For them, trees serve as beds; they lean against them and so, slightly reclined, take their rest. When hunters, from their tracks, learn where they usually retreat, they either uproot the trees there from their roots or cut them partway through, leaving only the appearance of them standing, or their stumps. When, by habit, the elks lean against these, the weakened trees give way under their weight and they fall down together with them.

...the elk is to be compared to a mule, so much inclined is its upper lip that it cannot graze on level ground. The island of Gangavia, opposite Germany, produces an animal like the elk, whose hocks, like the elephant's, cannot bend; and so it does not lie down to sleep, but leans against a tree only for drowsiness; hunters, threatening it near its fall, so that the beast crashes down while using its accustomed support, capture it this way. Otherwise it is difficult to take, since in that stiffness of its hocks it excels at incomparable flight. The Author: this same beast also appears to be the 'maclyn,' of which more will be said further below.

div.head: <DE ANABULLA>

cit.quote: The 'anabulla' is a beast of Ethiopia, having a neck like a horse, feet and legs like an ox, a head like a camel; it has white spots, with a very ruddy color marking each part of the body. And since the animal is so beautifully mottled, its hide, quite striking, sells for a high price to please the eye.

div.head: DE ANFFIBENA

cit.quote: Of serpents, the amphisbaena is so named because it has two heads: one in its proper place, the other on its tail, running from either head with the body's course circling. This alone of serpents exposes itself to cold, going out before all others. Of which Lucan says: 'and the amphisbaena, heavy, bending toward its double head, whose eyes shine like lamps.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Pliny also, in the eighth book: the amphisbaena has a double head, both at the head and at the tail, as though it were too little for venom to be poured from one mouth alone.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Jorath also, in the same place: the amphisbaena serpent exposes itself to cold, and, watchful and anxious over its eggs, broods upon them; for, while one part of it sleeps, the other nonetheless keeps watch. And when it moves along a path, it directs both heads, now the one, now the other, following behind. There is another kind that moves on its heel, so to speak, and upon its tail, in its mating. So also the Author.
Of serpents having two heads, more will be said below, according to Aristotle, among the monstrous serpents. So too Avicenna, as above.

div.head: DE ANGUIUM PROPRIETATIBUS ET NATURIS

cit.quote: Treating the natures and properties of snakes according to the opinions of the philosophers and the saints, we shall first discuss the difference or distinction of snakes as regards the naming of terms, among 'anguis,' 'coluber,' and 'serpens'; second, the difference of snakes as regards size, great and small; third, the difference of snakes as regards shape and disposition; fourth, the difference as regards color; fifth, the difference as regards location and habitat; sixth, the difference as regards variation of gait and movement, speed and slowness; seventh, the difference as regards cunning and cleverness; eighth, the difference as regards complexion and the vividness of certain senses; ninth, on the life or duration and renewal of snakes; tenth, on the origin of a certain serpent from human marrow; eleventh, on the disposition of snakes' internal organs; twelfth, on the egg-laying and generation of snakes; thirteenth, on the voracity of snakes; fourteenth, on the fear of snakes and their remedy through spittle and the like.

div.head: DE ANGUIUM DIFFERENCIA QUOAD NOMINUM IMPOSICIONEM, PRIMUM CAPITULUM

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis, Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: 'Anguis' [snake] is the name for every kind of serpent that can coil and uncoil. And from this 'anguis' is named, since it is angular ['angulosus'] and never moves in a straight line, as Isidore says, in the seventeenth book. And it is called a serpent ['serpens'] because it crawls ['serpit'] by hidden approaches; for it does not move by open steps, but crawls by the tiniest efforts or motions of its scales. And it is counted among creeping things, since it crawls on chest and belly, as Isidore says in the twelfth book. It is also called 'coluber,' either because it favors shade ['colit umbras'], or because the snake's neck ['collum'] glides into slippery, winding tracks while it is grasped.

div.head: DE ANGUIUM DIFFERENCIA QUOAD MAGNITUDINEM ET PARVITATEM SECUNDUM CAPITULUM

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis, Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX
Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: There are many kinds of snakes. And there are as many venoms as there are kinds, as many destructions as species, as many pains as colors, as Isidore says in the twelfth book. And just as snakes differ in size, so too in the malignancy of their venom. For some snakes are very large, as Pliny says, in the eighth book, fifteenth chapter: Megasthenes writes, he says, that Indian snakes grow to such a size that they devour whole stags and even bulls. Hence, too, in the Punic War, near the river Bagradas, a single snake, a hundred and twenty feet long, was killed by the commander Regulus with siege engines and catapults; its skin and jawbones were hung before a certain temple in Rome and lasted until the Numantine War. Under the emperor Claudius too, in Italy, a certain serpent was killed, in whose belly a whole boy was found. And such very large serpents harm now by bite, now by breath, now by the strike of their tail, now by constriction, now by sting, now by their very gaze.

Snakes are serpents, and there are others that are indeed serpents small of body, but of the greatest power to harm. For the 'dipsas,' as Isidore says, is of such smallness that, when trodden on, it can scarcely be seen. Its venom kills before it is felt, and brings no sadness to the one about to die.
Hence the Poet: 'the standard-bearer, a young man of Tyrrhenian blood, Aulus, his head twisted back — the trodden dipsas bit him. There was scarcely pain or feeling of the tooth,' and so on.
So Isidore says. Likewise the 'tyrus' is a tiny serpent. And yet a remedy for its bite is scarcely to be found, as Aristotle says, in the seventh book.

div.head: DE ANGUIUM DIFFERENCIA QUOAD FIGURAM ET DISPOSICIONEM, TERCIUM CAPITULUM

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Snakes likewise differ in shape and disposition. For some have two heads, like the amphisbaena, of which Isidore says: the amphisbaena is so named because it has two heads, one at the front and one on the tail, running from either head, with the body's course circling. This alone of snakes exposes itself to cold, going out before all others. Pliny also says the same, in the eighth book, twenty-fourth chapter: the amphisbaena, he says, has a double head, as though it were too little for venom to be poured from one mouth alone.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis, Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: There are other snakes having several heads, being doubled, tripled, or quadrupled, as Isidore says of the Hydra: the Hydra is a serpent of many heads, such as appeared in the province of Arcadia, in a marsh. And when one head was cut off, three grew back. But this is fabulous. For it is well established that the Hydra was a place spewing forth waters that laid waste to a neighboring city, in which, when one channel was closed, many others would burst forth. Seeing this, Hercules burned those very places and so closed the channels of water. And it is for this reason that Hercules is said to have killed the Hydra, a five-headed serpent, as Isidore says in the twelfth book.

div.head: <DE DIFFERENCIA QUOAD COLOREM, QUARTUM CAPITULUM>

cit.quote: Snakes likewise differ in the variety of their color. For some snakes are black and some reddish, like the 'tyrus.' And these are the worst. And some are spotted, like the 'scytale' serpent. For, as Isidore says, it gleams with such variety on its back that, by the grace of its markings, it draws onlookers into admiration of itself. And, since it is rather sluggish in crawling, it catches those it cannot otherwise overtake, astonished by its marvel. And the more variegated it is, the worse it is, since its venom is said to be the sharpest and hottest. For this same snake is of such heat that, even in wintertime, its cast-off skin, dropped in the snow, is still hot. Hence Lucan: 'and the scytale, which even now, amid scattered frosts alone, is about to shed its skin,' and so on, as Isidore says. Likewise the 'ephites' is a serpent marked with spots, having as many varied, distinct colors as it has markings. Hence Lucan: 'than the color of the Theban ephites, painted with scorched spots,' and so on.

div.head: <DE DIFFERENCIA QUOAD SITUM ET HABITACIONEM, QUINTUM CAPITULUM>

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis, Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Snakes differ in the diversity of place and location. For some hide in caverns of the earth and lick the dust and suck out its moisture, as Pliny says. Other snakes are aquatic, since they dwell in waters and on the banks of waters, like the 'enidris,' an aquatic serpent, by whose bite the struck swell up and develop dropsy. Many call it 'boa,' since it is treated with cattle dung, as Isidore says in the twelfth book. Likewise there is a serpent called the water-snake, which poisons water. For it corrupts with its venom every spring in which it dwells, as Lucan says: 'and the water-snake, defiler of the water,' and so on — Isidore, in the seventeenth book of the Etymologies.

Other snakes dwell in forests and shady caves, whose prey are birds and small creatures, from which they suck the moisture, as Aristotle says, in the eighteenth book. And such serpents lie in wait for sleeping creatures. And if they find the orifices of men or other animals, they enter them, seeking the warmth and moisture they find there alike. But against such snakes the 'saura' fights, a small creature, that is, a little lizard. For the 'saura,' sensing the snake's presence, leaps onto the sleeper's face and scratches with its feet, so as to warn or forewarn him against the snake, as Avicenna says.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis, Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: And the 'saura,' as Isidore says in the twelfth book, is a lizard whose eyes go blind when it grows old. And then it enters a hole in a wall and, opening its eyes toward the east, once the sun has risen, gazes at it and its sight is restored.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis, Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX
Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Certain kinds of snakes are also said to dwell in fire, as is plain in the salamander, which is named by Isidore and Pliny among venomous creatures. For the salamander, as Isidore says in the book of the Etymologies, is so named because it is strong and powerful against fires. Its power is the greatest of all venoms. For the other venomous creatures strike individuals, but this one kills many at once. For, if it crawls up a tree, it poisons all its fruit and infects and kills those who eat them. And if it falls into a well, the power of its venom kills those who drink from it. This creature, resisting fires, alone among the rest extinguishes fire. For it lives in the midst of flames without being consumed and without pain, and takes no burn from the fire; rather it calms or extinguishes the very blaze, as Isidore says in the same place. Others, however, say that nothing can live in fire. Pliny says the same, in every respect, in the tenth book, sixty-eighth chapter: the salamander, he says, is like a lizard in shape. It never appears except when it rains heavily. In clear weather it disappears. It has such icy stiffness that it puts out fire as ice does. It vomits a milky discharge from its mouth, and from its touch a man's body loses its hair, and whatever is touched by it turns to a most hideous color.

div.head: DE DIFFERENCIA QUOAD INCESSUUM ET MOTUUM VARIACIONEM, VELOCITATEM, ET TARDITATEM, SEXTUM CAPITULUM

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis, Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Snakes again differ in the quality of their gait. For some crawl always in a winding or twisting path, and some always straight. The 'cenchris,' he says, is a serpent that always makes a straight path, as Lucan says: 'and the cenchris, ever gliding on a straight track.' The 'chelydrus,' its path a smoking trail. This one always moves with its head held erect. For if it twists itself while moving, it immediately splits open, as Isidore says in the twelfth book. Snakes again differ in speed and slowness. For some are of very slow movement, like the 'scytale' mentioned above. And some are of such swift gait and light movement that they seem to fly, like the serpent called the 'iaculus,' which flies like a javelin. For it leaps up in trees. And, when some animal happens to pass beneath, it hurls itself upon it and kills it. Hence they are also called 'iaculi,' as Isidore says. Likewise in Arabia there are winged serpents, which many call sirens, which run faster than horses, and so are said to fly. Their venom is so potent that death follows the bite before the pain does, as the same author says.

Snakes, according to Aristotle in the eighth book, have this peculiar property: that they can move their head outward while the body remains still. And the reason for this is that the rings of the serpent's vertebrae are made of cartilage, and for this reason are capable of good bending. And this was necessary for looking backward, so that they could turn their head to look at their own long, narrow body. Otherwise they could not govern their body unless helped by raising their head to keep watch over the whole body.

Snakes, according to the same author in the same place, swim in water by the bending of their body, just as they crawl on land. For nature did not give serpents feet for walking or little fins for swimming. The reason is the excessive length of their body. For, if they had many feet, their movement would be poor, since they would be like points close together. Likewise, if they had many wings very close together, their movement would be heavy. And if they were spaced far apart, they would not suffice to support the rest of the long, flexible body. And so, what fish do by the contraction of their fins, and birds by the extension of their wings, snakes do by the bending of the body alone. Likewise certain fish, similar to snakes in length, which for the same reason have few or no fins, swim by the bending of the body alone, like morays and the fish called 'fastaror,' both called conger eels, which are sea eels, and the like. And so, since such fish are similar to snakes in their formation, they have only two wings or little fins in front, and use the flexibility of their body in place of fins and wings. And for this reason they crawl on land and live a long time even without water, just as snakes live without food.

div.head: DE DIFFERENCIA QUOAD SAGACITATEM ET INGENIACIONEM, SEPTIMUM CAPITULUM

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis, Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Snakes again differ in their malicious cunning, as is plain in the horned viper, a horned serpent, which hides itself under the sand and displays its horns, so as to lure, as though for bait, beasts or birds by their display. For it has horns like a ram's, which it leaves bare and exposed above the sand; and when a bird or another animal approaches these, it will find by experience that these are not a ram's horns, but a violent snake's. The boa snake, as Isidore says, of immense bulk, pursues herds of cattle and buffaloes in Italy, and, craftily entwining itself around their flowing udders and sucking, kills them. And from this, from its destruction of cattle ['boum'], it took the name 'boas,' as Isidore says. There are many other names and kinds of serpents, like asps, vipers, and dragons, of which more will be said later. But, as Isidore says in the twelfth book, there are as many kinds of death as there are names.

div.head: DE DIFFERENCIA QUOAD COMPLEXIONEM ET ALIORUM SENSUUM VIVACIONEM, OCTAVUM CAPITULUM

cit.quote: All snakes, generally, are for the most part of a cold nature and do not readily strike, except when they grow warm. For, when they are cold, they touch nothing. And so their venom harms more by day than by night; for they grow sluggish in the chill of night. And rightly so, since they are chilled by the night dew. In winter they curl themselves into knots and grow sluggish. In summer they unwind and thrive greatly in malice. Hence it is that whoever is struck by a serpent's venom first grows numb and then is quickly killed and destroyed. And so it is called venom ['venenum'], since it travels through the veins ['venas']. Its plague, spread through the body, strips the soul from the body and drives it out. Nor can it harm unless it touches the blood. Hence Lucan: 'the harm of serpents is a plague mixed with blood,' as Isidore says. And he adds: all venom is cold. And so the soul, which is fiery, flees cold venom.

Among the gifts of nature, however, which are common to men and brute beasts, the snake excels in a certain liveliness of sense. For it is read in Genesis: 'the serpent was more cunning than all the living creatures of the earth.' For Pliny says, as Isidore recounts in the same place, that a serpent's head, if it escapes between two fingers, lives on nonetheless. Hence it exposes its whole body to the striker to defend its head. Again the same Isidore: all snakes have dull sight and rarely look straight ahead. Nor is this a wonder, since they have their eyes not in the forehead but at the temples, so that they hear more quickly than they see.

No animal moves its tongue with such speed as the snake. For it moves it so quickly that it seems to have a threefold tongue, though it has only one. Also in the same place: the bodies of snakes are so moist that, wherever they go, they mark and stain the path with a certain viscous, muddy fluid. For a snake's tracks are such that, although they seem to lack feet, they nonetheless crawl by the effort of their ribs and scales, which they have arranged evenly from the top of the throat down to the belly. For they support themselves on their scales as though on claws, and on their ribs as though on legs. Hence, wherever it is wounded in the body, from belly to head, it becomes weaker in carrying out its course and the circuit of its movements, since, wherever that blow lands, it breaks the spine, through which the ribs' feet and the body's movement were carried out, as the same Isidore says.

div.head: DE ANGUIUM VITA SEU DURACIONE AC RENOVACIONE, NONUM CAPITULUM

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis, Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Serpents live long even without food, as Aristotle says. And they reach such a length of days that, having shed their old skin, they are said to lay aside old age and return to youth. Hence the skins of serpents are called their 'exuviae,' since, when they grow old, they strip them off. Once these are stripped off, they return to their former youth. And so their little skins, thus shed, are called 'exuviae' and 'induviae,' since they are stripped off ['exuuntur'] and, in their place, others are again put on ['induuntur'], as Isidore says in the twelfth book. The manner of the snake's own renewal, however, seems rather marvelous. For, as Pliny says, a snake, sensing itself burdened by sickness or old age, abstains from food and fasts for many days, so that its skin is more easily loosened from its flesh. Then, having tasted a certain bitter herb, it is driven by the herb's power to vomit, and so vomits out the poisonous or venomous humor that was the cause of its sickness and decline. At last, so as to soften and temper its stiff skin, it bathes and moistens itself in water, and so, seeking a narrow crack or hollow in some rock, it enters through the narrow crack and, passing through with some violence, entirely strips and sheds its old skin. And finally, exposed to the sun, it dries itself and recovers new skin on the surface of its flesh. Its strength recovered, it sees more clearly, moves and crawls more vigorously, and eats more eagerly than it did before shedding its skin.

Pliny describes this form of renewal, and Avicenna, who says, with Aristotle, that the 'tyrus' serpent sheds its old skin, first up to the eyes, then up to the neck, and so gradually strips itself entirely within a day, as he says in the fourteenth book.

Also, Dioscorides says that in wintertime snakes hide in darkness and caverns, where, from the daily darkness of the place, their sight grows dull. In springtime, then, when they begin to come out of their caves, they feel the dimness; but as a remedy they seek the herb fennel, or its root, by eating which they shake off their acquired blindness. Nor is the tortoise, fed on a snake's entrails, cheated of a remedy. For when it senses that a serpent's venom is creeping upon it, it seeks out wild marjoram, whose taste it finds as a medicine against the snake's venom.

div.head: DE CUIUSDAM SERPENTIS ORIGINACIONE EX MEDULLA HOMINIS, DECIMUM CAPITULUM

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis, Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX
Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Also Isidore, in the twelfth book, fourth chapter: Pythagoras, he says, asserted that from the marrow of a dead man's spine a serpent is generated. Ovid also touches on this, saying: 'there are those who believe that, when the spine has rotted in the sealed tomb, human marrow is changed into a serpent,' and so on. If this is believed, it rightly follows that, just as death comes to man through a serpent, so too, through the death of man, a serpent destined to die is engendered, as Isidore says. Pliny also says, in the tenth book, forty-sixth chapter: we have heard, he says, that a serpent is born from the marrow of a man's spine. For many things come about from hidden and obscure origins, even among quadrupeds, and so on.

div.head: <DE INTERIORUM ANGUIUM DISPOSICIONES, UNDECIMUM CAPITULUM>

cit.quote: The internal organs of snakes are similar to those of egg-laying quadrupeds; they do not, however, have testicles, but have passages, as fish do, and they have long, divided wombs. And their internal organs are long and narrow, matching the length of the body. And snakes' tongues are black, long, and thin, split in two and sometimes pointed. And for this reason they protrude a great deal and move easily. And a snake's belly is long and narrow, resembling a wide intestine. And that intestine resembles a dog's intestine. And after the belly it has a small intestine reaching to the exit of the waste. And it has its heart near the neck, resembling a kidney in appearance. And after its heart is its lung, in which there are sinewy, fine, coiled parts, hanging from the heart. And after the lung is the liver, long and extended. And above that is the gall bladder, as in larger fish; but in smaller ones the gall lies above the intestines. And the spleen in snakes is small and round. Likewise they have passages and intestines, from which the surplus sometimes exits; but they have no passage for the exit of urine, since they lack a bladder. Snakes' teeth are sharp, somewhat curved and joined together, though divided like a saw. And snakes have thirty ribs, matching the number of days in a month. And it is said that what happens to swallow chicks also happens to snakes, namely that if someone pierces and plucks out their eye, their sight returns again. And the tails of snakes, like those of lizards, grow back after being cut off.

div.head: <DE ANGUIUM OVACIONE AC GENERACIONE, DUODECIMUM CAPITULUM>

cit.quote: All snakes and serpents first lay their eggs internally, and then, not all at once but gradually, discharge the eggs from which animals are generated externally, except the 'tyrus,' that is, the viper. For the viper serpent, as Aristotle says in the third book, generates its young internally, but first lays eggs internally, and from those eggs the young are generated within. And so it is said in the same place that the womb of other snakes is long, matching the formation of their body. And their womb begins at the lower part and proceeds upward along either side of the spine. And it is divided into two parts, having, as it were, a wall between them. And so the eggs lie in the womb. And a snake does not lay all its eggs at once, but in succession. Snakes, according to Aristotle in the fifth book, at the time of mating join and coil around one another so closely that an observer would think they were a single body with two heads. Aristotle also, in the seventh book: a serpent, and especially the 'tyrus,' when it swallows a bird or something else, first raises itself up and then contracts itself, until what it has swallowed reaches inside. And this is because its stomach is small and narrow. And snakes can live long without food. This is plain from the snakes that dealers keep. Snakes, according to the same author in the same place, coil around one another when they come together for mating and love, since they have neither a penis nor testicles. For they lack a penis, since they have no legs, and they lack testicles because of the length of their body. And, if they had them, the seed would be chilled by the delay of its exit, and so would be less suited to generation. Also according to the same author, in the eighteenth book: error and monstrosity rarely occur in the generation of snakes. And this happens because of the shape of the womb, which is long and upright and narrow. Hence the eggs of snakes are arranged in a row, because of the length, within the womb.

These and many other natures of snakes Aristotle recounts, which would take long to pursue in order. But let what has been said in general now suffice. Of its common properties, and nearly all that are known, more will be said below, under the letter S, and further below under 'On the Asp.' And in the particular treatise on animals all these matters will be discussed. And likewise, in a similar way, in the treatise On Fish, further below.

div.head: DE ANGUIUM VORACIONE, DECIMUM TERCIUM CAPITULUM

cit.quote: A snake, when it is voracious, drinks little, according to Aristotle and Avicenna. It gladly eats flesh and sucks out its moisture, as a spider sucks flies. Likewise it swallows the eggs of birds and their living chicks. And when it swallows them, it brings them back to its hindquarters and expels them, not allowing them to remain in its belly.
Also, according to Aristotle in the eighth book: snakes greatly love wine and milk, and so can be drawn out of a man's belly by the smell of milk, as Dioscorides says.

div.head: DE ANGUIUM TIMORE ET EARUM REMEDIACIONE PER SPUTUM ET SIMILIA, DECIMUM QUARTUM CAPITULUM

cit.quote: A snake fears a naked man, according to Isidore, nor does it dare touch him, though it will leap at one who is clothed. Also, according to Aristotle in the eighth book: snakes fear the weasel, 'galiele,' and the weasel attacks snakes and protects itself against them by feeding on rue. It fights especially against snakes that eat mice, since it hunts mice itself. And the smell of rue puts snakes to flight. Those things that put snakes to flight are the following: the spittle of a fasting man, if swallowed by a serpent, harms it, according to Pliny. So too according to Avicenna, in the second treatise of the second book of the Canon.

div.head: <DE APRO>

cit.quote: Here begins the crafted treatise on the properties and natures of boars. Examining the natures and properties of boars according to the opinions of the philosophers and the saints, we shall first treat the reasonable and fitting derivation of its name; second, the boar's jealousy and passion for mating at that season; third, the bone of its right side, which serves as its shield and defense; fourth, the sharpening and cutting edge of its tusks; fifth, its skill in overcoming adversaries; sixth, its natural complexion; seventh, its effectiveness and power in the healing of the body's members.

div.head: DE NOMINIS APRI RACIONABILI ET CONGRUA IMPOSICIONE, PRIMUM CAPITULUM

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis, Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: The boar ['aper'] is named from ferocity ['feritate'], according to Isidore, the letter F removed and P put in its place. Hence among the Greeks it is called 'syagros,' that is, 'wild.' For everything that is fierce and untamed we loosely call 'agreste' [wild]. It is called by the Latins 'verres,' since it has great strength, according to Isidore, in the eleventh book. The boar, however, according to Pliny, is so savage and fierce that, once castrated, it scarcely shows itself tame, contrary to the nature of every other animal. It is so fierce, indeed, that, counting death as nothing, it flings itself fearlessly onto the hunter's blade. The pig is called 'porcus,' as though 'spurcius,' that is, filthy, or as though 'spurius,' since it is foul, base, and dirty, plunging itself into filth and dung. Females are called 'sues,' as though 'subingentes,' that is, seeking their food by rooting up the ground, according to Isidore in the twelfth book.

div.head: DE APRI ZELOPYPIA ET AMORE COYTUS TEMPORE, SECUNDUM CAPITULUM

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Great ferocity and cruelty is in boars when they are in mating season, according to Pliny, in the eighth book, fifty-fifth chapter. For then they fight fiercely for their mates, scrape the ground with their hooves, bristle their coats, brandish and shake their tusks, and show the fury of the herd most of all in a dreadful grunt; they eat little then, and run after the females then. Then they grow especially thin and lean. They seek their dwelling in dreadful, shadowy valleys and groves, where they guard their young. They live on roots and the fruits of wild trees. When they sense the onslaught of hunters or the attack of wolves, they go ahead of their young. And if there is no place for flight open to them, they expose themselves to danger for the defense of their young. The females of boars, after giving birth, are harsh and fierce and attack invaders of their young with a fierce bite. Likewise, male boars are of excessive roughness in mating, according to Pliny in the eighth book. Also, according to Pliny, male boars do not breed until they are a year old, and they are not found on the island of Crete, nor in Africa, nor is the wild pig.

div.head: DE OSSE LATERIS DEXTRI, QUOD HABET PRO SCUTO ET DEFENSIONE, TERCIUM CAPITULUM

cit.quote: The boar has, in its right side, a very hard, broad, thick bone, which it always turns to face the hunter's spear. For it uses that bone as a shield to protect itself, sensing that war or danger threatens it, according to Pliny and Avicenna, and charges the hunter with its body arched.

div.head: DE CULMORUM ACUICIONE ET INCISIONE, QUARTUM CAPITULUM

cit.quote: The boar has hard, hooked, that is, curved, tusks in its mouth, strong and sharp, with which it savagely and harshly strikes anything that resists it. For it uses its tusks like a sword to attack its adversary. For when it senses war coming, it rubs its tusks against trees, to test whether its tusks have become blunt. And if it finds them blunt, it seeks out wild marjoram and chews it, so that by its power it may sharpen and strengthen its tusks, as Avicenna says.

The boar strikes upward, and so it can do little harm to one lying prostrate or fallen. The female, however, does little harm even to one standing. While it is enraged and fighting, it foams at the mouth. Likewise while it mates with its female, according to Pliny.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: The same Pliny also says, in the fifth book, that the wild pig loves roots greatly and splits the ground and the root with its tusks, and fattens when it rests for six days, and especially when it drinks little. Also, boars in India have paired, cubit-long curved teeth projecting from the snout, and as many again projecting from the forehead, like a calf's horns, according to Pliny in the eighth book. Also, according to the same author in the eleventh book, males have more teeth than females. Their tails, however, are like a bear's. Also in the same place: a boar's blood does not thicken.
The Physiologus also says: a boar's tusk retains its cutting edge while it lives; once dead, however, the extracted tusk loses its cutting power.

div.head: DE APRORUM INDUSTRIA IN ADVERSARIORUM IMPUGNACIONE, QUINTUM CAPITULUM

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: The boar hates the wolf, as Pliny says, since the wolf by nature hates it; for the wolf lies in wait for its young and often carries them off. And so, as the same author says in the fourteenth book, nature gave the boar tusks to defend its females and young, since the females are weaker in themselves and of poorer complexion. Hence the males are bolder and have stronger strength than the females. The female, however, when enraged, rages fiercely and attacks by digging and biting and tearing with its teeth. When they begin to sense the onslaught of hunters or the attack of wolves, they go ahead of their young, as has been said. And if there is no place for flight open to them, the female exposes herself to many dangers for the defense of her young.

Nonetheless, when it must or is expedient to fight, it hardens its own sides by rubbing against trees, according to Aristotle, and rolls itself in a mud-wallow; then it dries its muddy sides in the sun and cakes the mud together and thickens it among its bristles, so as to withstand the blows of its adversaries more strongly in battle. It turns the bone of its right side toward its adversaries like a shield and arches itself so as to take the blow upon it. It strikes, however, from an angle and indirectly, in a remarkable way, so that its tusk seems to cleave into its adversary more like a sword than a tooth.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: The same Pliny also says, in the fifth book, that the wild pig loves roots greatly: it cuts and digs the ground with its tusks and splits the root with its tusk, and fattens when it rests for sixteen days, and especially when it drinks little, just as was also said above.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii maioris

cit.quote: Boars, after giving birth, are harsh and cruel, and tear apart invaders of their young with a fierce bite, according to Pliny in the book of Natural History. Boars sometimes fight so fiercely that one or both die. The bear too fights with wild boars. The boar is exceedingly irascible and foolish, and takes no instruction in good conduct, according to Aristotle, even if castrated.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii maioris

cit.quote: The female boar too is castrated, so that it does not need mating, so that it may fatten quickly; but food is first withheld from it for two days. Pliny also, in the eleventh book: boars heal themselves with ivy when wounded, and by eating crabs cast up by the sea. The same author also, in the tenth book: boars and stags are hard to tame, unless perhaps reared from infancy.

bibl.author: Liber de natura rerum Thome Cantimpratensis

cit.quote: Also, as is found in the Book of the Nature of Things: if, in the morning, before the boar is attacked by hunters, it is easily tired; but if it has urinated before or during the chase, it yields to capture only with difficulty; yet even tired, it does not yield, but stands its ground on its hindquarters and, with rigid ferocity, hides its weariness, offering combat to the hunter. It does not, however, presume to strike or attack a man unless it has first received a blow from him. But let a man take care, for, unless he delivers with the first thrust of his spear-point a deadly wound between the shoulder and the side ribs, he may risk his life, unless perhaps he finds nearby a tree to climb for refuge, or presses his whole body flat to the ground in some lower place; for the beast's teeth, turned back and curved, cannot reach anyone unless he is raised up and upright. He will, however, endure being trampled by its feet until, lying thus, he is rescued by someone nearby.

The boar surpasses all beasts in hearing. On its right side it has a bone shaped like a shield, which it turns against spears and blades. And, as the Physiologus says, a boar, once roused, when forced to flee, does not turn back to strike again.

div.head: DE NATURALI EIUS COMPLEXIONE, SEXTUM CAPITULUM

cit.quote: Boar's flesh, according to Isaac, is drier and less cold than that of the domestic pig. This is because of the continuity of its movement, the dryness of its diet, and the heat of the air to which it is exposed. For this reason too its fat is tougher and its flesh more delicate to eat. For this reason too domestic boars are vigorously chased and even beaten before they are killed, so that their flesh becomes more tender and tastier from the violence of the movement.

div.head: DE APRI EFFICACIA ET VIRTUTE IN EGRITUDINUM CURACIONE, SEPTIMUM CAPITULUM

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: The boar's urine, as Pliny says, in the twenty-eighth book, tenth chapter, heals ailments of the ears, if mixed with rose oil. Likewise its gall. Also, its brain, according to the same author, is praised against snakes when mixed with blood. Its liver too, aged with rue, taken as a drink in wine. Its fat too, with honey and resin. In the same way, aged liver and brain drunk in wine. Also, a boar's brain, or the blood of its genitals, heals carbuncles or boils. Likewise it rouses the lethargic.

In the liver of a female boar small stones are found, which, crushed and drunk in wine, expel gravel. A boar's lung, roasted and eaten that same day while fasting, wards off drunkenness. Boar's gall dissolves scrofula. Drunk, it also calms the spleen. The same, with fat, is applied to the lung and heals chilblains. Boar's gall, with resin and white lead, also heals spreading ulcers. The ash of a boar's jawbones heals spreading ulcers. Likewise its boiled and bound-on bacon heals fractures, mending them with remarkable speed. Boar's urine, and even its bladder, taken as food, heals torments of the bladder and stones, if both are first softened in smoke. Likewise, if a boar's bladder is roasted and eaten, it checks incontinence of urine. Boar's urine, or even the bladder, given gradually in a drink, helps the dropsical, more effectively when dried together with its bladder. Also, boar's urine with vinegar benefits epilepsy. ...having drunk boar's testicles in mare's milk or water. Boar's urine, too, kept in a glass vessel, heals earache and ear ailments. Finally, so strong is boar's urine that it cannot escape unless it is discharged and, overcome, as it were, suppressed; hence it is reported that boars burn from it.

bibl.author: Liber de natura rerum Thome Cantimpratensis

cit.quote: The ash of burnt boar dung, sprinkled into a drink of warm wine, heals the dysenteric. The same dung, and fresh boar foam with vinegar, is good for dislocations. The dung of a sow that has not given birth is more effective in use; among boars too it is much more excellent. The use of its lard is good, rubbed into the members, for softening, warming, dispersing, and cleansing the weariness of travel. Also, from the Book of the Nature of Things: fresh, warm boar dung is a chief remedy against nosebleed.
Dioscorides also says of the boar that its dried dung, drunk with water, is a singular remedy for those spitting up blood. It cures pains of the side with vinegar, and heals and mends broken bones.

div.head: <DE APIBUS>

cit.quote: Bees ['apes'] can also be called land-animals, since they move on many feet. For they are many-footed creatures, that is, of many feet, and of a ringed body. They can also be called birds, since they fly through the air, as is plain. The smallness of their body, however, is offset by the greatness of their cunning. They can therefore be classed both among land animals and among birds, and have a place in both categories. Treating, then, the natures and properties of the bee according to the opinions of the wise, not confusedly but distinctly, not by chance but rather methodically, we shall first treat the reasonable naming of bees and the natural disposition of their members and their delicate complexion; second, their excellence in the sharing of life in common and the fineness of their works; third, their skill in the building of their works and their foresight of the seasons and the like; fourth, the generation of bees and the marvelous propagation of the kings of bees, and the breeding of wasps, frogs, and gnats; fifth, the multiplication and cunning formation of the young of bees; sixth, the distinction or discernment of male and female bees and of the younger and older; seventh, the manifold condition of the kings of bees and the reverent submission of their subjects; eighth, the manifold kinds of bees and the choosing of the best; ninth, the prolonging of their life and the restoration and revival and buzzing or humming of the dead; tenth, their food and drink and sleep; eleventh, their dwellings, and the marvelous distinction of dwellings for kings and commoners; twelfth, the seeking out or pursuit of bees; thirteenth, the choosing, placing, and rearing of bees and the planting of flowers or pastures for them; fourteenth, the going forth and flight of bees, the signs of their flight, their warfare, its pacification, and vigilant guarding; fifteenth, the restoration of bees; sixteenth, the process of bees toward work; seventeenth, the distinction of their various offices; eighteenth, the fighting and mutual attack of bees and the remedy for their stings; nineteenth, the diligent work of bees; twentieth, the arrangement of the honeycomb and the fitting reason for its name; twenty-first, the production of wax and its fitting to various uses; twenty-second, the quality of wax and its application in medicines; twenty-third, the flow of honey; twenty-fourth, the threefold kind of honey; twenty-fifth, the choosing and testing of honey; twenty-sixth, the quality or condition, power, and diversification of honey; twenty-seventh, on hydromel and mead and oxymel and claret and the making and variety of other drinks from honey; twenty-eighth, on poisonous honey and its contamination and cure; twenty-ninth, on the building and cleaning of beehives; thirtieth, on the proper culling of beehives; thirty-first, on the usefulness of beehives in medicine; thirty-second, on what is hostile and harmful to bees; thirty-third, on the illnesses or diseases of bees; thirty-fourth, on the comparison of Saint Cecilia to bees as a builder; thirty-fifth, on the fitting likening of Saint Ambrose to bees.

div.head: DE APUM RACIONABILI NOMINACIONE AC NATURALI MEMBRORUM DISPOSICIONE ET DELICATA EARUM COMPLEXIONE, PRIMUM CAPITULUM

cit.quote: Bees are named either because they bind themselves to one another by their feet, according to Isidore, or because they are born without feet; for afterward they receive both feet and wings.

The bee is an animal of ringed body, having a member or appendage projecting from its mouth, by which it tastes and draws in and receives food. It lacks blood. It has teeth unlike those of other animals. It flies in company and is light of body and has four wings. It has two feet on the right and two on the left, and has no more than four, so as not to hinder its flight. This animal does not take in air, that is, does not breathe. Animals that eat many different foods are, for the most part, of varied body and color. And so the color of bees is uniform, but the color of wasps is varied. They eat honey, especially in time of need; hence, when they begin to fall ill, a diminishing of the honey appears, since they eat from it and do not replenish it. They love pleasant scents and delight in running water.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Pliny also, in the eleventh book: nature gave bees a sting, kept within the belly, for a single strike. Once this is delivered, some think they die at once, others think not. They delight in applause and the ringing of bronze, and are called together by it. The same author, in the thirtieth book: bees dead in honey soften the hard edges of ulcers.

Also: bees love cleanliness, according to Aristotle and Pliny; they hate cold, foul smells, and smoke. They fly in swarms. They are diligent about their work and cast out idlers. Rough on the outside, they have sweetness within. They are easily hurt, and hurt easily in turn. Having lost their sting, they are useless.

div.head: DE IPSARUM EXCELLENCIA IN VITE COMMUNIONE ET OPERUM EXQUISICIONE, SECUNDUM CAPITULUM

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Among all insects, the highest rank belongs to bees, according to Pliny in the eleventh book, the only creature of that kind born for the sake of man. They gather honey and the sweetest, finest, and most wholesome juice, they build honeycombs and wax, they endure labor comparable to what life requires, they carry out their tasks and always hold councils, and have leaders and chiefs in their swarms. And, most remarkably, they have moral character and know nothing that is not shared in common.

Also Aristotle: the bee, more scrupulously clean than other animals, discharges its own dung while flying, since it has a strong smell; for a foul smell burdens bees, while a good one delights them. Also Ambrose: bees seem to manage, as it were, a kind of republic. They alone, among every kind of living creature, have offspring shared by all, dwell in a single home, share labor in common, common food, and the begetting of a common fruit.

bibl.author: Liber de natura rerum Thome Cantimpratensis

cit.quote: Also, from the Book of the Nature of Things: bees excel other animals in dignity and usefulness, and thrive in nobility and agility, vigor, spirit, and subtlety of intellect and of labor; all of them have virginal wholeness of body, and yet they suddenly send forth a vast swarm of offspring. They alone have common offspring, common roofs like a city, and live under great laws, being mindful of one fixed home or homeland and its fixed dwelling-places, and, mindful of the coming winter, undergo labor in summer and store in the common store what they have gathered. Seeking their living, they keep vigilant watch, and are trained in the covenant of peace in the fields. Some, among the enclosures of their homes, gather the tear of the narcissus and the sticky gum from bark. The first lay the foundations of the combs, then hang the clinging wax; others, in hope of their kind, rear the grown young, pack in the purest honey and stretch the cells with liquid nectar. There are those to whom the guarding of the gates has fallen by their strength, and they take turns watching the waters and the clouds of the sky, or take up the burdens of those arriving, or, forming ranks, drive the lazy drone herd from the hives. All share one rest, all share one labor in their tasks.

div.head: DE IPSARUM SOLERCIA IN OPERUM SUORUM HEDIFICACIONE ET TEMPORUM PREVISIONE ET HUIUSMODI, TERCIUM CAPITULUM

cit.quote: The bee, though weak in body, is strong in vigor of wisdom and virtue, according to Ambrose in the Hexaemeron. For what architect taught bees, out of a discerning mind, to hang their thin waxen cells with equal sides between the walls of their homes, to pack in honey, and to stretch, with a kind of nectar, storehouses woven through with flowers?

Also Aristotle: bees perceive from a distance, which they can do only from a fine sense of perception. Some go out to work at the start of the day, others rest; then they fly out and go forth likewise to work; and when they return, they buzz loudly at first, then gradually their noise quiets, then one of them remains, flying and circling, as though to signal that it is now time to sleep; then they all rest together.

They have the greatest subtlety of intelligence, which is recognized in winter, since then they do not go out from the hives as they wish, but roam about within; and thus the watchers among them recognize coming rain. And when they hang from one another within the hive, it signifies that they wish to descend from the hive. All of them, however, discharge their dung while flying, or in their own small chamber apart.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Pliny also, in the eleventh book: let us, then, estimate how great is the cunning present in creatures so very small. They shelter themselves in winter, for from this they draw strength to endure frost and snow and the blasts of the north wind. They shelter themselves, however, on the third day before the Ides of October, in the evening, that is, from the setting of the Pleiades, and stay hidden past their rising. Before the beans flower they go out to their tasks and labors, and no day is lost in idleness whenever the sky permits.

First they build the combs, they shape the wax, that is, they make their homes and cells, then their offspring, and afterward the honey. They make wax from flowers, and propolis from the tears of trees that produce a gluey resin. They watch for favorable winds; and, if a storm arises, having seized little stones, they steady their small weight. Near the ground, once the brambles are cleared, they fly. There are marvelous observances of order in their work; they note the idleness of those who slack off, as in a military camp, and punish it with death. There is also a marvelous cleanliness in their work: everything is removed from the middle, since it would lie there most filthily among their tasks. Indeed, they gather even the waste of their own workers inside, so that they need not go far, collecting it together in one place, on stormy days and during a lull in work. And as evening falls, they buzz less and less within the hive, until one flies around with the same murmur by which she roused them, as though ordering rest, in the manner of a military camp, and then all suddenly fall silent. And, remarkably, they have moral character and know nothing except what is common.

div.head: DE APUM GENERACIONE ET REGUM APUM MIRABILI PROPAGACIONE ET DE VESPARUM ET RANARUM ET CULICUM PROCREACIONE, QUARTUM CAPITULUM

cit.quote: Some say that the words of Aristotle seem to contradict those of Ambrose regarding the young of bees.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Pliny, in the same place: how bees produce their offspring has been a great source of disagreement among the learned; for their mating has never been observed. Most have thought it must be gathered from a mixture of flowers, and some, from the mating of a single individual, called the king in each swarm, who alone, they say, is the male, distinguished above all by his size, so that he does not weaken, that is, fail. There occurs, however, in certain combs, what is called a 'nail,' a bitter hardness of wax, when they have not brought forth young from it, through disease or laziness or natural infertility: this is the miscarriage of bees.

Also Aristotle: we say that bees are generated from bees when they mate with one another, and kings are generated from kings, or from the 'kanke' and those called the females of bees. Bees resemble kings in their sting and their vigor; the 'kikenes,' however, resemble kings in size — and if they had a sting, they would be kings. It is necessary, however, that kings come from something; and since they do not come from ordinary bees, nor from the 'kikenes,' it is necessary that ordinary bees come from kings.

From the mating of little bees a worm resembling an egg is produced, and no other animal is generated from them, but it remains so. And so the offspring of bees neither resembles their own kind, nor differs entirely from it, since worms come forth from them. In the first stage of formation of bees and similar creatures, the lower part is small, the upper large. Nor does deformity occur in the bee or the wasp, since each of their young is in its own cell separately. Since, then, kings are created for the sake of generation, they always remain within the hive and do no work and have a large body for the sake of generation. Otherwise, if the generation of bees did not come from them, they would not be left within the hive doing nothing. The 'kakines,' however, are the idle males of bees, since they lack the member suited to fighting, because of the heaviness of their body. Bees, however, are of a size midway between these two, and in this way are suited to the creation of young. And just as it happens to the lioness that she bears five cubs, then fewer, until she reaches one, so it happens to the kings of bees that they generate many at first, then few, since the surpluses in their body diminish. That the generation of bees comes from mating, namely between kings and ordinary bees, is shown by the fact that they are found in the cells of the hive.

bibl.author: Liber de natura rerum Thome Cantimpratensis

cit.quote: Bees, as has been said above, are so named in one way because they are born without feet; for, once born, they receive both feet and wings. Many, however, have found by experience that they are born from the carcasses of oxen; for, to breed them, the flesh of slaughtered calves is beaten, so that from the rotting blood worms are created, which afterward become bees. Also, from the Book of the Nature of Things: bees are born from bull's hide buried in the ground; wasps, however, from donkey's hide; mint-flies from the dung of flies; and frogs from saltwort, and gnats from tainted air, that is, from breath.

div.head: DE PULLORUM APUM MULTIPLICACIONE ET INGENIACIONE, QUINTUM CAPITULUM

cit.quote: Bees gather pollen from leaves and grasses with their mouths, and suddenly send forth a very great swarm of offspring. And whereas other birds scarcely lay a single brood in a year, bees produce twin broods and outweigh others by a double fecundity, according to Ambrose in the Hexaemeron. Also Aristotle: in rainy years the young of bees multiply greatly, since, because of the moisture, the surpluses in the bodies of the kings multiply. In years of temperate complexion there is a decrease in the young. It is reported, however, that when a young bee is lost somewhere, its guardian immediately seeks it until he finds it, since he recognizes it by its own scent. The 'kikin' and the 'coz,' among bees, do nothing, but corrupt the work of others. And so the good bees overcome them and kill their leaders, since these draw out the young of bees.

Bees, indeed, once they make the wax, begin to breed young. And when they are breeding, nothing prevents both the young and the honey and the 'kikines,' that is, the male bees, from being gathered together in the same wax. The king of bees does not leave the hive except with a great escort of bees, and he himself is in the middle. He goes out, however, three days before the young emerge; then a few bees go out and fly around the hive. And when the young are gathered together, they will fly and separate among themselves, and one group will go with each king. The same Pliny, as above: at the edges of the comb, larger bees are sometimes born, which drive off the rest. When the membranes are broken that enclose each bee's young, the whole company emerges in the manner of eggs; the brood, moreover, is completed within forty-five days. Once hatched, however, they at once work with their mothers under a certain discipline, and an equal crowd escorts the young king. Several kings begin at once, so that offspring may not later be lacking from these, once it has begun to mature. By unanimous agreement they kill the worst, lest they scatter the swarms.

div.head: DE MARIUM ET FEMINARUM APUM ET IUNIORUM AC SENIORUM DISTINCCIONE SEU DISCRECIONE, SEXTUM CAPITULUM

cit.quote: In the kind of bees, as in other ringed creatures, the male is smaller and the female larger, according to Aristotle. The female of the leader, however, is double the size of the better ordinary bee. Males lack stings and sometimes want, as it were, to sting, but cannot. Bees, however, kill the males when the space in which they are becomes crowded; for a multitude of males in the hive does not make them more industrious. The bodies of young bees are soft, those of old bees hard. The kind of bee that is strong makes hard honey. And it is said that there are young bees because they are not yet practiced in the craft. Moreover, the young never fight as strongly as the old.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: The same Pliny, in the same place: some think that offspring are produced from the mating of one individual, called the king in each swarm, and that he alone is the male, distinguished above all by his size, so that he does not weaken, that is, fail, and that without him no brood is produced, and that the rest of the bees attend him as females attend a male, not as a leader.

bibl.author: Liber de natura rerum Thome Cantimpratensis

cit.quote: Also, from the Book of the Nature of Things: it is said that, if the leader of the bees is alive, the males will be inside with the females. Finally, males, when solitary, occupy more homes than the homes of bees, and males sometimes build many homes for themselves. It goes better for bees when few males are with them, since males do not make them more industrious.

The bodies of young bees are soft, and those of old bees hard. Young bees, too, never fight as strongly as old ones. Old bees, however, make sweeter honey than younger ones, since they have experience.

div.head: DE REGUM APUM MULTIPLICI CONDICIONE AC SUBIECTARUM REVERENTI CONDESCENSIONE, SEPTIMUM CAPITULUM

cit.quote: Bees, according to Ambrose in the Hexaemeron, appoint a king for themselves, not by chance but by judgment. And, although placed under a king, they are nonetheless free, since they retain the privilege of judgment and the devotion of loyal affection, and love their king as though appointed by themselves. This king, however, is formed with clear marks of distinction by nature, so that he excels both in size of body, and — what is most important in a king — in gentleness of character. For, though he has a sting, he does not use it for vengeance. For the laws of nature are not written in letters but impressed in character, so that they may be gentler in punishing, since they possess the greatest power. But bees that do not obey the king's laws punish themselves with the condemnation of repentance, so that they die of the wound of their own sting. Finally, they defend their own king with the greatest protection and think it a fine thing to die for him.

While the king is unharmed, they cannot change their judgment or waver in their resolve; but once he is lost, they abandon their loyalty to duty and plunder their own honey, since he who held the principle of their office has been destroyed. Some peoples of the Sarmatians, however, observe such reverent devotion toward bees that none dare leave their homes or go to any pasture, unless the king has gone out and claimed the leadership of the flight for himself.

Also Aristotle: bees, like cranes, have watchful kings over them, whom they obey. There are two kinds of leaders of bees: the better one is reddish, the other black. The female of the leader is double the size of the ordinary bee that is superior. If the king falls from the hive, the bees at once raise him up and place support beneath him. The homes in which kings live are only at the edge, and their number is not great. Ordinary bees come from kings, and kings are generated by themselves. Since kings, as has been said above, are created for the sake of generation, they always remain within the hive and do no work, and have a large body for the sake of generation.

These strike and drag off the males of bees like fathers; for it is good that fathers punish idle sons. There are few kings, however, and few bees are generated from them, since the first time they generate many, and the second time few, because the surpluses in their body diminish. Kings of bees do not leave the hive except with all the bees. And if a young bee is lost, its leader seeks it until he finds it. If the leader fails, they die. If the leader of the bees grows weary in flight, the bees around him especially die too. If there are many leaders, they sometimes abandon their own king and desert to the king who governs more of them. And the first king pursues them and kills them.

bibl.author: Seneca Lucius Anneus, De clementia Senece

cit.quote: Also Seneca, in the book On Clemency: bees are most irascible and, for the size of their body, most combative, according to Seneca in the book On Clemency, and they leave their stings in the wound. The king himself is without a sting; nature took the weapon from him and left his anger unarmed. This example is all the more valid for kings: let them be ashamed not to draw their character from such small creatures, since the mind of men ought to be the more restrained the more powerfully it can do harm.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Also Pliny, in the eleventh book: when the king is destroyed by disease, the common bees grieve with sluggish sorrow: they do not gather food, do not go forth, but gather with a sad murmur around his body and, unless helped, die of hunger. The brood of bees, once hatched, works at once with their mothers under a certain discipline, and an equal crowd escorts the young king. He has shorter wings, straight legs, a darker mark on the forehead, as though a whiter diadem.

Kings also differ much from the common bees in their sheen. It is not agreed among authorities whether the king alone has no sting at all, armed only with majesty, or whether nature did give him one but denied him its use. This, however, is agreed: that the ruler does not use his sting, and there is a remarkable obedience of the common bees around him. When he goes forth, the whole swarm is united and gathers around him: it surrounds and protects him and does not allow him to be seen. At other times, when the people are at labor, he himself goes about the work within, like one exhorting, alone exempt. Around him are certain attendants and constant lictor-like guards. He goes forth outside only on the authority that the swarm is about to migrate. And this is known some days in advance, either by a murmur buzzing within, a sign of the preparation of those choosing the timely day. If his wing is clipped, the swarm will not flee. When he has gone where he wishes, those nearest him rejoice to be seen at his service. They lift the weary on their shoulders; the more exhausted, they carry entirely. If any bee grows tired and fails or strays, he pursues it by scent. And there, wherever he has settled, is the whole camp of them all. The whole company is always held together by its leader going before. Once he is lost, the company scatters, migrating to others; for they cannot exist at all without a king. Reluctantly, however, when there are several, they kill them; rather they tear apart the homes of those being born.
