div.head: DE APUM MULTIPLICI SPECIE ET MELIORUM ELECCIONE, OCTAVUM CAPITULUM

cit.quote: Some bees are rustic and wild, according to Pliny, of rough appearance, more irascible, but more outstanding in work and labor. There are also urban ones, of two kinds: the best are short, variegated, and compact and rounded; the worse are long, resembling wasps. The worst of these are hairy. In Pontus there are certain white bees that make honey twice a month. Around the river Thermodon there are two kinds: some make honey in trees, others underground. With a triple arrangement of combs, they yield the richest harvests.

There are several kinds of bees. The good bee is small and round, dense and compact in itself; there is a bee like the 'tribus,' long; and there is the 'koka,' broad-bellied, large. The 'kikam' are larger and heavy, having no stings.

...bees that make fine honey. The strong kind of bee makes hard honey. Small-bodied bees are better, build more diligently, are more patient of labor, and produce more honey; they have fewer males and make honey from mountain flowers, producing fine honey. They have delicate wings, and their color is black, as though scorched. There are, however, solitary, idle bees, which, flying through the air as though busying themselves along with the industrious bees, enter the hives and eat the honey; but the industrious bees fight with the idle ones and kill them. The kings of bees especially do this and drive them out of the hives; for it is better that fathers punish idle sons. Ornamented bees are counted among those that produce nothing of honey. Bees that come from those that feed on mountain flowers are smaller, stronger, and more patient of labor; bees, however, born from those that feed on garden flowers, are the opposite in every respect.

div.head: DE VITE IPSARUM PROLONGACIONE ET MORTUARUM RESTAURACIONE ET HANELACIONE ET SONITU SEU CLAMORE, NONUM CAPITULUM

bibl.author: Aristoteles, De morte et vita Aristotelis

cit.quote: Bees are of longer life, according to Aristotle in the book On Death and Life, than other, larger animals. Also, in the book On Animals: the buzzing of bees comes from within the body and is not through breath expelled, since they do not breathe; for their hissing sound arises through a membrane beneath a wall-like part, at the place where the body is divided in two, and they make no sound except while flying, that is, by extending and contracting the wings falling through the air between themselves and the body. They do not, however, buzz at night.

Bees, too, have a sweetness in the hoarse murmur of their voice, though they are shown to have neither a lung nor the use of breathing, but instead an airy vesicle for breath. Finally, if someone accidentally pours oil on them, they are nearly killed, since, their pores blocked, they cannot draw in that airy breath; and immediately, if someone then pours vinegar over them, they revive at once, since it is said that the moisture of vinegar opens those blocked pores.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Also Pliny, in the same place: they think that insects have not a voice but a sound, produced in the passing of breath, both in insects and where the sound is enclosed and resonating. Some, however, produce a murmur, like bees; for it is accepted that flies and bees, having two reed-like passages beneath the chest, sound through them internally, a mobile membrane striking against them from the friction.

And so, after the day's labor, as evening falls, as has been said, they buzz less and less in the hive, until one flies around, as though ordering rest to be taken, with the same hum by which she roused them. They delight in applause and the ringing of bronze, and are called together by it. By which it is clear that they too have a sense of hearing.

There are those who think dead bees revive, if kept under a roof in winter and then warmed by the spring sun. If entirely lost, however, they think they can be restored from the fresh entrails of oxen buried with dung. Virgil, however, says: from the lifeless body of draught animals, nature changes some things into others.

div.head: DE IPSARUM CIBO ET POTU ET DORMICIONE, DECIMUM CAPITULUM

cit.quote: The life and nourishment of bees is above ground, and their proper taste is honey, according to Aristotle. They love sweet things and do not settle on foul or bad-smelling, bad-tasting things; for a foul smell burdens them, and a sweet smell delights them. And so, since it smells, they discharge their dung while flying. They also love clear, running water. They do not, however, hunt at all, but work and store food. They also have another food, called 'kokizon,' as sweet as figs; they bring this on their legs, as they do wax.

When honey is taken from the hive, however, enough should be left to suffice for the bees' food in winter; otherwise the hive will be ruined; for the bees' food in winter and spring comes from honey. They also sometimes prepare food from a hard substance resembling wax. Moreover, the keepers of hives, because of the small amount of remaining honey, sometimes feed bees with figs and other sweet things. They should leave honey in proportion to the number of bees, since, if they leave much, they will afterward work less, and if it is scant, they will grow old before finishing their work. They drink from a river, if they have one, and not elsewhere; otherwise they will drink in another place. Nor do they drink until they have set down the weight they carry.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Also Pliny, in the eleventh book: Aristomachus reports that bees never touch the flower of the cytisus shrub for food. The same author, in the twenty-first book: for the sake of bees one should plant thyme, rose, violets, lily, bean, poppy, and the like; for they are most eager for these flowers, and mustard too. It is a wonder that they do not touch the flower of the olive. Moreover, if bees lack food, it is useful to place dried raisins or spread-out figs near their hives, or wool dyed with horehound, or plenty of water-soaked things, and even the bare flesh of hens. The same author: food should be provided in a dry summer, when the flowers fail.

Also Aristotle: it is plain that ringed animals sleep, from the fact that bees rest and do not buzz at night; for, if someone brings a candle to them at night, he will see them at rest. Some, then, go out to work at the start of the day, others wait until they wake, others rest, then fly out and go out to work together, and, returning, buzz loudly; then their noise gradually quiets, until one of them remains, flying and circling, since it signals that it is time to sleep; then they all rest together.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Also Pliny, in the twenty-first book: bees are sustained from the rise of Arcturus at the winter solstice by sleep for sixty days, without any food, and from the rise of Arcturus to the spring equinox, as the weather warms, they are already awake; but even then they keep to the hive and seek the food stored up for that time.

div.head: <DE MANSIONIBUS ET MANSIONUM PRO REGIBUS ET PLEBEIS MIRABILI DISTINCCIONE, UNDECIMUM CAPITULUM>

cit.quote: The bee is among the animals having dwellings, like the ant, the mouse, and the mole. Bees remain in their caverns during the days of great cold and eat nothing of the food they have stored. A sign of this is that, when one of them leaves its opening, it appears as though small, and there is nothing within it. And it remains after the setting of the Pleiades until spring. They abandon their homes, however, if honey is scarce. And what is found in the homes of bees is either young, or honey, or 'kikines.'

So then, they first begin to make the homes of ordinary bees from wax, then, once wax is abundant, the homes of kings, then the homes of the 'kikiccio,' when honey is plentiful. And they begin to build under the walls of the hive above, not ceasing to descend gradually until they reach the bottom of the hive. And one home has two doors, one on the outside and another inside, and it has a place inside the entrance. The wax homes, those covered with wax, are for the most part full of wax. The homes, however, in which the kings live, are only at the edge.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Also Pliny, in the same place: bees build homes first for the commoners, then for the kings. If a longer yield is expected, however, extra chambers are added even for the drones: these are the smallest of the cells. Bees build royal chambers for their future rulers on one side of the hive, spacious and magnificent, set apart, with a raised inner chamber. If these are pressed too hard, however, no offspring is produced; all the cells are six-sided, made by the work of each individual's feet. At the solstice, when the thyme begins to flower, the wax is at its finest for cell-building.

div.head: <DE APUM INVESTIGACIONE SEU QUESICIONE, DUODECIMUM CAPITULUM>

cit.quote: Bees should be sought in suitable places: Palladius, in the fifth book. Places good for honey are shown if bees graze very frequently around springs; for, if they appear rarer in such places, honey cannot usefully be made there; but if they often come to drink where their swarms are, we can find them this way, and first explore whether they are far off or nearby. Let us carry liquid red ochre poured into a small vessel, and watch the springs or nearby waters; then let us touch the backs of drinking bees with a stick dipped in that liquid, and wait there: if those we have marked return quickly, we shall know their dwelling is near; if slowly, we judge it more distant, by the length of the delay.

If one bee has tasted the food, going on to gather more it will attract others; and, noting the growing number of returning bees, following the marked ones all the way to their doorstep. But if the swarm has hidden itself in a cave, it will be driven out by smoke, and, once it emerges, frightened by the sound of bronze, it will settle in a bush or in some part of the forest, and so, a small vessel brought up, it will be gathered in. But if it is on the branch of a hollow tree, that same branch, cut above and below with a very sharp saw and wrapped in a clean cloth, can be carried away and placed among the hives. They should be tracked, however, so as to have a whole day sufficient for following; for in the evening, once work is done, they generally do not return to water. The vessels in which they are gathered should be rubbed with beeswax or pleasant herbs and sprinkled with a light shower of honey. This should be done with smoke, and hives so scented placed around springs: in places where bees are frequent, they will draw a swarm to themselves of their own accord. They cannot, however, be kept safe from thieves.

div.head: <DE APUM ELECCIONE ET COLLOCACIONE ET EDUCACIONE ET FLORUM SEU PASTUUM EARUM PLANTANCIONE, DECIMUM TERCIUM CAPITULUM>

bibl.author: Liber de natura rerum Thome Cantimpratensis

cit.quote: Bees, as is found in the Book of the Nature of Things, are better when small, round, dense and compact in themselves, producing fine honey. Also Palladius, in the first book: if bees are to be acquired, let us see to it that they are acquired in full. Whether the swarm is full is shown by inspection, or by the volume of its murmur, or by the frequency of bees going out and returning, preferably from a nearby rather than a distant region, so that they are not troubled by unfamiliar air. But if they must be carried from farther off, they should be transported by night. We should neither place nor open the hives except as evening approaches. Let us then watch after three days, lest the whole swarm go out its door; for this is a sign that they mean to take flight. They are believed, however, not to flee if we smear the rims of the hive-vessels with the dung of a firstborn calf.

We should locate the bee-stand not far from the master's house, or in a secluded and sunny part of the garden, away from the winds and in a warmer spot; laid out in a square, it should keep off thieves and the approach of men and livestock. Let it abound with flowers, which our diligence should provide in grasses, in shrubs, or in trees. Let it nourish, among the grasses, marjoram, thyme, wild violets, asphodel, sweet marjoram, hyacinth, narcissus, saffron, and other most fragrant grasses and flowers. Among the shrubs, let there be roses, lilies, yellow violets, rosemary, and ivy. Among the trees, almond, peach, pear, and fruit-bearing trees, whose flowers carry no bitterness of sap; and wild ones too: acorn-bearing oaks, terebinth, mastic, cedar, lime, small holm-oak, and thyme; but yews should be kept away, as their enemy. Let the trees be arranged on the north side, and let the shrubs and saplings follow their own rows below in the layout; then let us plant grasses in the open ground behind the shrubs. A spring or stream should suit this place, gentle enough to form shallow pools as it passes, which sparse, crosswise twigs should cover, offering safe resting-places for the bees when they need them.

Also Aristotle: in winter a warm place is fitting, and in summer a cool one. The hive's openings, too, should be closed against strong wind, so it does not enter. It is also fitting to plant myrtle, mountain pine, peas, beans, poppy, and almonds near the hive.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Also Pliny, in the twenty-first book: bees do not touch the flower of the olive, and so it should be kept far from them. Some things, however, are suited to be planted nearby, which invite swarms of flying bees and do not let them go far off. One should also beware of the cornel tree, since bees die from tasting its flower. A remedy for this is crushed sorb-apple with honey, or human or cattle urine, or pomegranate seeds sprinkled with Aminean wine. Broom, however, is very welcome to plant near hives.

div.head: <DE APUM EGRESSU ET FUGA ET SIGNIS FUGE ET GUERRA EARUM ET PACIFICACIONE ET SAGACI CUSTODICIONE, DECIMUM QUARTUM CAPITULUM>

cit.quote: New swarms go forth at the very end of June, according to Palladius in the second book. And so the keeper must be attentive, since new bees, their minds wandering, will easily escape unless watched. Those going out will die at their entrance within a day or two unless they are caught and put into new hives at once. The attentive keeper, however, will watch until the eighth or ninth hour; for after this time they do not usually take flight or migrate, although some do not hesitate to go out and depart immediately.

These are the signs of flight: for two or three days beforehand, the mass is disturbed and murmurs; unless the watchful observer notices this frequently beforehand, he should be more anxious about it. They are accustomed to make this same sign when they are about to fight; and their fights are checked by dust or a shower of honeyed water sprinkled on them. The leader's authority is present among them to restore the harmony of their kind. But when the pacified swarm settles this way on a branch or in any place, if they hang suspended from a single cluster, you will know that either there is one king for all of them, or that, all reconciled, harmony remains; but if they hang suspended in two or more clusters, the people is divided and discordant, and you will recognize as many kings as you see clusters. Where you see the clusters of bees more frequent, search there, hand anointed with honey syrup or celery. There are, moreover, bees somewhat larger and more elongated than the rest, with straighter legs and not large wings, of beautiful, shining color, light, without hair, unless perhaps, when fuller, they seem to carry hair on the belly, which, however, they do not use for a sting. There are others, dark and shaggy, which should be destroyed and left to their punishment; and this kind is often kept, along with swarms taken from others; for, while it remains, none will leave. But if no swarms are born, we can combine the contents of two or three vessels into one, but we shall keep the bees, sprinkled with a sweet liquid, still enclosed for three days, honey food set before them, leaving only a small breathing-hole in the cell.

Also Aristotle: bees delight in noise and are gathered by it. Nothing occurs except for delight or out of fear. And when they hang from one another within the hive, it signifies that they wish to descend from the hive. When the keepers sense this, let them sprinkle sweet wine inside the hive.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Also Pliny, in the twenty-first book: bees do not flee if the hives are rubbed all over with balm-mint, and they delight in no flower more, and their swarms are most easily kept by its sprigs. The same is also most effective against their stings.

div.head: <DE APUM REPARACIONE, DECIMUM QUINTUM CAPITULUM>

cit.quote: If, according to Palladius, the number of a beehive has been reduced by some plague, and you wish to restore it, you should look, among other thriving hives, at the wax of the combs and the edges that hold the young, and, where you find the sign of a future king, cut it out along with its brood and place it in another hive. This is the sign of a future king: among the other cells that hold young, one appears larger and longer, like a teat. They should be transferred, however, only when, the cell-covers already thin, they strain to push out their heads for hatching; for if you transfer them too immature, they will die. But if the swarm suddenly rises, let it be frightened with the noise of bronze or pottery: then it will return to the hive, or hang on a nearby branch, and be gathered by hand or scoop into a new vessel sprinkled with the usual herbs and honey. Once it has settled in that spot, let it be placed among the others in the evening.

div.head: <DE PROCESSU APUM AD OPERACIONEM, DECIMUM SEXTUM CAPITULUM>

cit.quote: Bees gather as flocks do, according to Aristotle, and some go out to work at the start of the day, some wait until they wake, others rest, then, flying, likewise go out to work. The idle ones, however, draw more than they labor when hunger comes upon them and at the start of spring. Their kings, who are created for the sake of generation, always remain within the hive and do no work; but the 'kikines,' who are the males of bees, are idle for the reason given above.

Also Ambrose: no bees dare leave their homes or go out to any pasture unless their king has gone out first and claimed the leadership of the flight for himself. Their advance, however, is through fragrant countryside, where there are gardens rich in flowers and grasses; from these flowers and sweet herbs they lay the first foundations of their camp.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Also Pliny, in the sixty-first book: the idleness of bees is roused to work by frequent smoke. They rest until morning, until one rouses them all with a double or triple hum or trumpet-call of some kind. Then, if the coming day is to be mild, they all fly forth together; for they foreknow winds and rains. But then bees stay in their shelter. Before the beans flower they go out to their tasks and labors, and no day is lost in idleness when the sky permits. They go by two entrances around each passage, so that some enter by one and others exit by the other. And as evening falls, they buzz less and less in the hive, until one flies around, as though ordering rest to be taken, with the same hum by which she roused them, and this in the manner of a military camp. Then they all suddenly fall silent. Moreover, once their work is done, they take a formal exercise, ranging in the open, and, rising in circling flights, only then return to their food.

div.head: <DE DIVERSORUM OFFICIORUM DISTINCCIONE, DECIMUM SEPTIMUM CAPITULUM>

cit.quote: Bees are assigned to different tasks, according to Aristotle; for some bring in flowers, some make honeycomb wax, and others bring water. Their tasks have no fixed time; but, once conditions are right, they hasten suddenly and work steadily in fair weather. Also Ambrose: you may see them all vying over their task: some keeping watch, seeking provisions; some anxiously mounting guard over the camp; others foretelling coming rains and watching the gathering of clouds from a height; others shaping the finished wax; others gathering with their mouths the dew poured on the flowers; yet none lies in wait for another's labors or seeks a living by plunder. And would that they need not fear the ambush of robbers! They have, nonetheless, their own stings, and pour venom amid the honey, if provoked, and lay down their lives in the wound.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Also Pliny, in the same place: so then, when the company goes out to work, some gather flowers with their feet, others water with their mouths and in droplets on the down of their whole body. The young go out to work and carry in what has been described above; the older ones work inside. Those that bring in flowers are loaded on their front legs, and for this reason their front legs are naturally rough near the beak, and they return entirely laden with their burden. Others receive these loads, three or four unloading at once.

For there are also different tasks inside. Some build, some polish, some bring supplies, others prepare food from what has been brought in; for they do not eat separately, lest an inequality of work, food, and time arise.

div.head: <DE APUM PUGNA ET MUTUA INVASIONE ET PUNCCIONUM EARUM REMEDIACIONE, DECIMUM OCTAVUM CAPITULUM>

cit.quote: Bees, as has been said and according to Ambrose, have their own stings, with which they pour venom amid the honey, if provoked, and lay down their lives in the wound out of the ardor of vengeance. Also Isidore: bees have an army and kings, and wage battles. Also Aristotle: bees do not flee any animal, but some of them flee certain ones and fight among themselves. And if someone approaches them, they will kill him, if they can. They die, however, when they sting, since the sting cannot come out unless it presses the spot and draws the sting from itself. For even large animals are killed by a bee's sting, as was once seen with a certain horse.

Moreover, the leaders of bees never sting, but the others, once such a leader is lost, if he is pursued, they kill and drive him from the hives. Indeed, the 'kikin' and the 'torth,' among bees, do nothing, but corrupt the work of others; and so the good bees overcome them and kill many of their leaders, since they draw out their young, and then all of them depart. Bees also fight against those who wish to take honey from them. Also, shorter bees fight fiercely against longer ones and work at driving them from the hives. Finally, if something not of the hive enters it, it will be killed by them. Some, then, sitting apart one by one, keep watch lest anything foreign enters. But if, through their negligence, something enters, it will scarcely escape.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Also, the same Pliny: bees, if food runs short in the hive, sometimes make an attack on their neighbors with the intent of plunder, and the others draw up their line against them. If a keeper is present, whichever side senses him favoring it does not attack him. They also fight for other reasons, and two generals draw up their opposing lines. The greatest quarrel is over the gathering of flowers, each side calling its own. This fighting, indeed, is entirely broken up by throwing dust or by smoke; it is reconciled, however, with milk or honeyed water.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: The same author, in the twentieth book: they say that a man anointed with crushed asparagus in oil is not stung by bees. Against their stings, the juice of rue is drunk with wine, and its crushed leaves are applied or eaten. Those anointed with its juice, too, are said not to be stung by them. The same author, in the twenty-first book: nature gave bees venomous stings, against which it is beneficial to anoint oneself with the juice of mallow or ivy leaves, or to have those struck anointed with it. The same author, in the twenty-third book: wine is a remedy against bees, but a decoction taken from bay leaves also resists their venom. The same author, in the twenty-fourth book: poplar sap, mixed with water, is also an effective remedy; for bees produce their poplar sap from the leaves, with water. The same author, in the twenty-eighth book: those stung by a scorpion are never afterward stung by bees.
Also Avicenna, in the second book of the Canon: a decoction of marshmallow mixed with oil, or with wine, helps a bee's sting when applied. Bay oil also helps it.
Also Avicenna, in the fourth book of the Canon: the bee has conditions very close to the wasp's, except that it leaves its sting in the wound. And its treatment is very close to that for a wasp.

div.head: <DE APUM SOLERTI OPERACIONE, DECIMUM NONUM CAPITULUM>

cit.quote: Bees are skilled in the task of producing honey, according to Isidore, and build their homes with indescribable art. Also Aristotle: bees do not hunt, but work, and bring into their hives what they need for preparation from various kinds of flowers, namely of the oak and the willow and others, in which there is a certain stickiness, and with this they coat the surface of the hive against harmful creatures and narrow the entrance of the hive if it is too wide; then they build the homes of the kings; finally, those of the rest.

And they begin building beneath the walls of the hive above, and do not stop descending gradually until they reach its bottom. Each home has two doors, one inside and one outside. And when a bee flies, it does not aim at various flowers, but gathers from one what it needs and returns to the hive.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Also Pliny, in the eleventh book: bees first build the combs, that is, make cells out of wax, then their offspring, and afterward the honey; wax from flowers, propolis from the tears of trees that produce a gluey resin, like the willow, the elm, and the like. With these they first coat the whole inside of the hive with a kind of plaster, and, with other more bitter juices, guard against the greed of animals, as though aware that what they are about to make could be coveted by them.

div.head: <DE FAVORUM ORDINACIONE ET NOMINIS EIUSDEM CONGRUA RACIONE, FAVORUM ORDINACIONE ET NOMINIS EIUSDEM CONGRUA RACIONE, VIGESSIMUM CAPITULUM>

cit.quote: Bees, then, build the honeycomb from various flowers and, weaving the wax, fill their camp with countless offspring, according to Isidore. Also Ambrose: bees arrange their combs like a military camp, in which the small, round cells support one another by their joined curves. A sweet work, made from flowers and sweet herbs. What architect taught them to build the hexagonal cells with a seamless equality of sides, and to hang the thin waxen cells between the walls of their homes, to pack in honey, and to stretch, with a kind of nectar, storehouses woven through with flowers?

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Also Pliny, in the same place: the combs, fixed at the top, gradually cling to the sides too, and hang free at the bottom, touching the hive, now slanting, now round, according to how the hive demands. Sometimes there are also two kinds, when two swarms of harmonious peoples have had different builds. Falling combs, the swarm props up, so that there is access for repair. The first rows are usually built empty, so that nothing readily invites a thief. The last, however, are filled with honey, and so combs are built facing the entrance of the hive. All cells are six-sided, made by the work of each individual's feet.

bibl.author: Liber de natura rerum Thome Cantimpratensis

cit.quote: Also, from the Book of the Nature of Things: the comb ['favus'], according to Isidore, is so called because it is eaten ['comeditur'] rather than drunk; for 'fage' in Greek means 'to eat.' The comb, however, is sweet and flavorful, since it holds honey within the wax.

div.head: <DE CERE PRODUCCIONE ET EIUSDEM AD VARIOS USUS ACCOMODACIONE, VIGESSIMUM PRIMUM CAPITULUM>

bibl.author: Liber de natura rerum Thome Cantimpratensis

cit.quote: Bees take wax from flowers and, with their front feet, according to Aristotle, gather it, then pass it to their middle feet, then to the thighs of their hind feet, then fly with it, and then its weight becomes apparent. Also, from the Book of the Nature of Things: wax lies hidden in the comb, pure and fragrant, fuel for light and material for writing. It is soft, tenacious, and brittle; hardened, it softens again at the fire, and takes and holds whatever shape is pressed into it.

Also Isidore, in the eleventh book: wax tablets are the material of letters, nurses of little children; they give children their first understanding and the beginnings of sense. The Greeks are proven to have first handed down their study.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Also Pliny, in the same place: bees make their wax from the flowers of all trees and crops, except sorrel and dog's-mercury. I think olives are wrongly excluded, since it is certain that a great deal is produced from the olive crop. They harm no fruits at all.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: The same author, in the twenty-first book: wax is made by pressing the combs, but first purified with water and dried for three days in the dark, then melted on the fourth day. It is cooked in a new fire in the same pot with the same water, and taken up in another, cold vessel smeared with honey. The wax called Punic, the next closest to it in quality, is tawny, of a honey-like smell, purely native, Pontic; then there is Cretan, which has the most propolis in it; after these, Corsican, since it is made from bee-bread and has great medicinal power. But Punic wax is most useful in medicines. Wax blackens when fig-ash is added, just as it reddens when mixed with alkanet, and is drawn into various colors by pigments for making likenesses.

div.head: <DE CERE QUALITATE ET EIUSDEM IN MEDICINIS APPOSICIONE, VIGESSIMUM SECUNDUM CAPITULUM>

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: All wax softens, according to Pliny in the twenty-second book, and warms and fills out the body. Fresh wax is better for sucking, and is given to the dysenteric, as is the comb itself.

Also, honey's wax is useful, both the reddish, fatty, and fragrant kind, having the smell of honey, and the pure kind, like the Pontic and Cretan. White, fatty wax has a secondary power. All wax has a warming and filling power. It is mixed into juices and gruels prepared for the dysenteric, some honey being added so that the decoction becomes palatable. Taken in the amount of a pea, it loosens curdled milk from the hand. All wax has the power of relaxing, and softens hardnesses; for it is midway between hot and cold, dry and moist; hence it is the base material for other medicines, since poultices and other preparations are bound together from it.

Propolis wax is useful, both the reddish, fragrant kind, like storax, and the not very soft kind, which you may shape by hand if you wish, like storax. Its power is hot and 'pispatic,' that is, helpful, and restorative and softening. It expels splinters lodged in the body. Its fumigation, with the mouth open, cures old coughs and corrects hernias. This is found in the vessel of the bees, where the bees seal their bodies away. It has the powers of wax, but more effective; for it heats excessively. It has an expelling and thinning substance. Also Avicenna, in the second treatise of the second book of the Canon, in the final chapter: it soothes abscesses and sinews and the chest, and fills unclean ulcers.

div.head: <DE MELLIS EMANACIONE, VIGESSIMUM TERCIUM CAPITULUM>

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis, Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: 'Mel' [honey] is proven to take its name from the Greek, from bee ['apis']; for a bee, in Greek, calls itself 'melle,' according to Isidore, in the twentieth book. At first, however, honeys came from the dew and were found on the leaves of reeds. Hence Virgil: 'hitherto, the heavenly gift of honey from the sky.'

Indeed, up to now in India and Arabia it is found congealed, clinging to branches, resembling salt. All honey, however, is sweet. Sardinian honey, however, is bitter, because of the wormwood, on whose abundance the bees of that region are nourished.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Also Pliny, in the sixth book: honey is at first thin as water, and in the first days ferments like must and purifies itself; on the twentieth day it thickens, and soon a thin membrane forms over it, congealed from the very froth of its fermentation. This the bees gather on clear days. And it comes from the air, and especially from the rising of the stars, and shines most brightly at the rise of Sirius itself, and not at all before the rising of the Pleiades, in the pre-dawn hours. And so at first dawn the leaves of trees are found dewy with honey. And if anyone is under the open sky early in the morning, his clothes and hair become tinged and matted with the liquid. Whether this is a sweat of the sky or of the waters, it is pure, liquid, and of its own nature. But how does it fall from such a height, growing dirtied for so long as it comes, and tainted by the earth's exhalation below? The same author, in the twelfth book: honey flows in the morning hours.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: The same author, in the twenty-first book on bees: beekeepers hope for a good yield of honey when thyme flowers abundantly, as it does around the solstice. When the bees gather it, Attic honey has the highest praise in the whole world. Wine and thyme were transplanted to Mount Ida in Crete. Flies are not found there. Native honey they never touch. And this is proven as a singular test for medicines.

Also Ambrose: bees, in the midst of their camp's valleys, pour in the moisture of dew, which, gradually gathered into honey over time, and combined with the fragrance of wax and flowers, begins to give off its sweetness. This fruit of the bees is indeed not discerned by the difference of persons, but grows sweet with equal delight for kings and commoners alike. And it is not only for pleasure, but also for health; it sweetens the throat, heals wounds, and even pours its remedy into the internal organs.

Also Aristotle: honey is properly the taste of bees, and is their food in winter and spring. When keepers extract honey from the hives, out of the devotion they have for it, they eat that same honey beyond their usual amount. And when flowers appear, they then make honey, and so the keeper should extract the finished honey then, since in its place they will suddenly make more. The herbs from which they take it are king's crown, myrtle, cinquefoil, and many others. The strong kind of bee makes hard honey. And they say young bees do this, since they are not yet practiced in the craft. There is, however, a small worm, found in the depths of the hive, which, as it grows, makes a spider-like web and dominates the whole hive; and so the honey putrefies.

div.head: <DE TRIPLICI MELLIS GENERE, VIGESSIMUM QUARTUM CAPITULUM>

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: There are three kinds of honey in any given region or province, according to Pliny in the eleventh book. The spring kind is drawn from combs built from flowers, and so is called 'anthinum.' Some forbid touching this, so that a strong brood may emerge from abundant food; others leave nothing less for the bees, since great abundance follows the rising of the greater stars; but those who are more careful leave a fifteenth part of this crop for the bees. The fixed day for starting the harvest is set at thirty days after the swarm is hatched, that is, around the month of May.

The second kind of honey is the summer kind, called 'horeon' from its particular seasonableness, shining forth about thirty days after the solstice, when Sirius itself shines. Likewise, from the rising of any star, if the sky is very cloudy, or a rainbow appears, if no rains follow, if the sun does not warm with its rays, medicinal remedies are produced, not honeys — heavenly gifts for the eyes and ulcers and internal organs. Summer honey is reddish and best suited, we judge, for the drier sort of illness. Cassius Dionysius favors leaving a tenth part of the summer harvest for the bees, if the hives are full; if less, in due proportion; or, if empty, not touched at all. This harvest the Athenians began with the wild fig; others, however, with the day sacred to Vulcan. There is a least esteemed kind of honey, the wild kind, called 'heath honey.' It is gathered after the first autumn rains, when, in Africa alone, the tamarisk flowers in the woods. This harvest, then, closes around the setting of the Pleiades, near the Ides of November. Reason persuades that two parts of it be left for the bees.

The same author, in the twelfth book: Arabia produces sugarcane, but it is more praised in India. It is, however, honey gathered from reeds. There are also trees called 'ochi,' resembling fig trees, in the valleys of Hyrcania, from which honey drips for two morning hours. Also the Gloss on the third book of Maccabees: wild honey in the desert was Job's food, namely what he took from tree trunks or plants.

div.head: <DE MELLIS ELECCIONE AC PROBACIONE, VIGESSIMUM QUINTUM CAPITULUM>

cit.quote: The best honey, according to Avicenna in the second book of the Canon, is that of true sweetness, of good smell, inclining toward sharpness and redness, not thin and sticky. The best is the spring kind, then the summer, but the winter kind is bad. There is also a sharp, poisonous kind of honey.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Also Pliny, in the eleventh book: the best honey is found where it is stored in vessels made from the finest flowers, namely, in the region of the Athenians. The best is drawn from oak leaves and reeds, least tainted by foliage.

The highest quality of a particular region, however, is judged in several ways. In some places, indeed, the combs are notable for their wax, as in Sicily; elsewhere for abundance of honey, as in Crete and Cyprus and Africa; elsewhere for size, as in the north; in Germany indeed a comb eight feet long has been seen. Honey is gathered fat at the full moon of spring, on a clear day. In all honey, that which has flowed of its own accord, like unburnt oil, is most praiseworthy. All summer honey is reddish, best suited, as we judge, for drier conditions, outstanding, of golden color, most pleasant taste; while stored in jars it is, as a rule, thick and fat above all. What becomes sharp is praised most. Thyme-flavored honey does not clump and, touched, sends out drawn-out threads, which is the first proof of its quality; but droplets that break off and spring back at once are held to be a sign of inferiority. The next test is that it be golden and, from something sweet, sticky, translucent.

Also Aristotle: good honey resembles gold; white honey too is better than black. It is good for ailments of the eyes and for sores. In fertile years honey multiplies. And the time for making honey is when the flowers appear, when it can also be drawn from the hives; then a great deal of new honey is suddenly made. Spring honey is cleaner and sweeter and altogether better than autumn honey. And new wax too is better; for old wax turns red and spoils, like wine in old skins. Likewise honey from the lower part of the comb is cleaner.

div.head: <DE MELLIS QUALITATE SEU CONDICIONE, VIRTUTE ET DIVERSIFICACIONE, VIGESSIMUM SEXTUM CAPITULUM>

cit.quote: Honey is hot and dry in the first degree, according to Avicenna in the second treatise of the second book of the Canon. Honey called 'tabarzed' and 'decamus,' however, is hot in the first degree, but not dry — rather perhaps moist in the first degree. The power of honey is cleansing, opening the orifices and veins, and dissolving moisture. It expels moisture from deep within the body and prevents putrefaction and corruption of the flesh. An ointment made from it prevents lice and nits, and kills both. Likewise it cleanses filthy, deep ulcers and clears the darkness of sight and strengthens hearing. Cooked until it thickens, it makes fresh wounds close. Cooked with dill, it heals impetigo. A gargle made from it heals suffocation. Honey-water strengthens the stomach and stirs the appetite for food.

Cane honey soothes the bowels; the honey called 'tabarzed,' however, does not. And honey whose froth has not been removed bloats and loosens the bowels; but if its froth is taken off, it holds back, and, cooked, does not move the bowels, but sometimes constringes the phlegmatic, and is very nourishing. Cooked with water it provokes abundant urine. Honey warmed with rose oil and drunk helps the bite of venomous worms and one who has drunk opium. Swallowing it is also a cure for a rabid dog's bite. The practical wisdom on honey more clearly holds that honey is hot in the first degree, but dry in the second. Honey is skillfully composed by the bees.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Also Pliny, in the twenty-second book: honey, of pleasant taste, is most useful for every desire of the mouth, for tongues parched with fever. A decoction of it should be given to those with pleurisy, and for wounds from a serpent's bite, and against poisons. It bloats the stomach and creates distaste, and by itself is useless for the eyes.

bibl.author: Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris, Plinius maior

cit.quote: The same author, in the thirtieth book: honey in which bees have died especially heals bruises. It also helps the dysenteric, and cures gripes with it.

bibl.author: Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris, Plinius maior

cit.quote: The same author, in the thirty-second book: the nature of honey is such that it does not let bodies putrefy. Dropped into the ears with rose oil, it kills lice and the foul creatures of the head. Its use, once skimmed, is always suitable; but it does bloat the stomach.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: ...where dead bees remain, it is good against poisoned honey. It is also most useful for the eyes. Drunk in wine, it is a remedy for the ills that arise from fish as food.

Also Constantine, in the fifth book of the Pantegni: honey is hot and dry in the second degree, and of cold complexion, and suited to the phlegmatic and the elderly. It generates good blood and strengthens the natural complexion. It harms the bilious and the young, since it generates red bile and hot, acute illnesses, especially in summer. It is cleansing, and thereby laxative. It is also sharp, and so causes thirst.

Also, according to Avicenna in the second treatise of the second book of the Canon: some bees gather honey that is a hidden dew falling on flowers and the like; for a vapor rises up and thickens, and is transformed and ripened in the air, and thickens at night, and the honey so made falls. It varies at night according to what it falls on, whether tree or stone. And men gather what appears of it; the hidden part, however, the bees gather, so as to feed on it and store it. I think, however, that the bees' own labor sometimes leaves its mark on it too.

Also Isaac: bee's honey is hot and dry in the second degree; it has a certain sharpness, which it acquired from the nature of bees; and so it cuts and cleanses corrupted humors and casts out an abundance of harmful humors from the body's interior through the pores of the skin. It cleanses the impurities of the veins excellently. And so it suits the cold and moist well, and especially the elderly; for it quickly generates blood in them. It is unsuited to the hot, however, and especially if their complexion is dry, since it gives their bodies an inflammatory sharpness and is converted into bilious humors; and even if it is converted into blood, it does not make it praiseworthy, but rather it is hotter, and gives no nourishment at all to their bodies. Warmed, however, if mixed with rose oil, it eases coughing, resolves difficulty of urination, and moistens the bowels. Cooked, applied to impetiginous places, it cleanses them. Tempered with beans, it cleanses freckles.

Honey from bees fed on calamint and other such plants is hot and dry; and so it suits epileptics and paralytics, and dissolves putrid humors and cleanses festering wounds. Again: bees feeding on wormwood and the like make honey more cleansing and opening than the rest, especially for blockage of the stomach, liver, and spleen; and so it helps fish poisoning, drunk with camel's milk or goat's whey. And if drunk skimmed, it is good against a rabid dog's bite. Moreover, the effect of honey varies according to the different ways of taking it; for some take it raw, some cooked, and in various ways of cooking. Raw honey, eaten, generates bloating and flatulence and roughness of the chest through its sharpness, and increases vomiting and produces loose stools. Honey cooked with much water is thin and moist; hence no sharpness at all is found in it; correspondingly, its pleasant sweetness is diminished, and it moistens the bowels, but bloats and does not provoke vomiting, but quickly permeates the bodies of those who eat it and nourishes swiftly. It eases roughness of the chest and brings on urine. Cooked without water and skimmed, however, it has less sharpness than the rest, and yet its effect is close to the previous kind; nonetheless, it does not resolve difficulty of urination.

div.head: <DE AQUE MULSE ET MEDI EX OXIMELLIS ET CLARETTI ET CETERORUM POCULORUM EX MELLE CONFECCIONE AC VARIACIONE, VIGESSIMUM SEPTIMUM CAPITULUM>

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: There are two kinds of honey-water, namely fresh and aged. This is good in the food of the sick, for restoring strength. Soothing to mouth and stomach and cooling burning fevers, it softens the bowels. It eases the breath or passage of the spirit and calms every disturbance of the mind through food. It is useful for those coughing, and induces vomiting. Against poison it is poured into the ears. With long age it turns into wine. Most useless for the stomach, though not exactly harmful. Mead made from old wine is most useful; it restores the appetite for food, softens the belly. Drunk cold, it checks the bodies of many; drunk hot, it increases a long old age for many; for the vigor of mind and body is preserved within by mead, without by oil. The same author, in the thirty-second book: honey-water is a wholesome remedy against poison from nettles, with oil added; against henbane poisoning too, with ass's milk.

Also Isidore, in the twentieth book: mead ['mulsum'], as though mixed from honey, is a drink of water and honey, which the Greeks call 'melicratum.' Further, 'nivemellum' is must mixed with honey and vigorously stirred and agitated. Oxymel is so called because it is made from a mixture of vinegar and honey; hence it retains both sweetness and sharpness. Rose-honey is so called because rose syrup is mixed with honey. It is also called 'medus,' since it is made from honey, as though 'better' ['melius']. Also Rhazes, in the Almansor: a drink made from honey is intensely hot and productive of red bile; it helps, however, those suffering from cold ailments. Mead. Medo. Claret. Spiced wine. Oxymel.

div.head: <DE MELLE VENENOSO ET EIUS INFECCIONE AC CURACIONE, VIGESSIMUM OCTAVUM CAPITULUM>

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: There are also certain poisonous honeys in Spain, according to Pliny in the twenty-second book. In Heraclea in Pontus, in certain years, honeys made by bees prove most deadly. There is indeed a white herb, called 'goat's-bane' for its deadliness, especially to goats. Its flowers take up a harmful poison of a watery, withering nature. And so it happens that this harm is felt in some years.

bibl.author: Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris, Plinius maior

cit.quote: The signs of poisoned honey are that it does not thicken at all, that its color is more reddish, its smell foreign, at once causing sneezing, and that those who have eaten it throw themselves to the ground under its harmful weight, seeking to cool themselves, for they also break out in sweat. And against such things the remedies are old mead made from the best honey and rue, and salted foods, frequently taken. It is certain, moreover, that this harm reaches even dogs through excrement, and afflicts them likewise. It is established, however, that much of it, once aged, is harmless, and that women's skin is improved by nothing better than by honey sealed with costus and aloe. There is also another kind of honey in the same Pontus, drawn from the rhododendron flower, with which the woods teem, from which madness is generated; and that people, when they sent wax as tribute to the Romans, never sent honey, since it was deadly. In Persia too, and in Mauretania, poisoned combs are produced. Nature also gave the bees themselves, as has been said above, venomous stings. Against these, a wholesome remedy is to anoint oneself with mallow or ivy-leaf juice, or rather to drink it. The same author, in the thirty-ninth book: against poisoned honey, honey in which bees have died is effective.

Also Avicenna, in the second book of the Canon: the smell of poisonous, sharp honey causes thirst and takes away reason; but eating it also causes a sudden loss of reason and cold sweat. Its cure is eating salted fish and drinking honey-water and vomiting with it. The same author, in the fourth book: the honey brought mostly from the region of Arcadia is bad and poisonous; it is sharp, causing one who smells it to sneeze, and causes fainting and chills the sweat and produces bad symptoms. The cure, however, is like the cure for black henbane: that one eat rue and salted fish and drink a syrup of honey-water, and not cease eating or vomiting as much as possible.

div.head: <DE ALVEARIUM APUM FABRICACIONE AC PURGACIONE VIGESSIMUM NONUM CAPITULUM>

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: The best hives, according to Pliny in the twenty-third book, are of bark, the second best of fennel-stalk, the third of wickerwork. It is most useful if the hives are coated with cattle dung. A cover at the back is also needed, and a walkway, so that the interior may be inspected if the hive is large or the work sparse, and so the bees do not abandon their labor in despair; this is gradually brought back as the failing growth of their work deceives them. It is also useful to cover the hives with straw in winter and to fumigate them often, especially with cattle dung. It is also fitting for the hives to face the equinoctial east; but the north wind, and no less the west wind, should be avoided.

bibl.author: Palladius Rutilius Taurus Emilianus, Opus agriculture Palladii

cit.quote: Also Palladius, in the first book: hives are better when made from the bark of the cork-oak, since they do not let through the force of cold or heat. They can, however, also be made from fennel-stalk; but, if these are lacking, they should be made from willow and wicker, or from a hollowed tree, or from boards like barrels; earthenware hives are the worst, freezing in winter and overheating in summer. But stands three feet high should be built, against the harm of lizards and other creatures, which are apt to creep in, and above these stands the hives should be placed, so that rain cannot penetrate them, spaced apart from one another with small gaps left between.

A narrow entrance, however, should admit the swarms, against the harm of cold and heat. Indeed, a high wall should hold back the colder winds, and be able to warm the place with sheltered positions. All entrances should face the winter sun, and there should be two or three on a single piece of bark, of a size that cannot admit anything larger than a bee; for thus harmful creatures will be kept out by the narrowness. Or, if bees wish to besiege the entrance, since another is not lacking, they will go out and use the other exit.

bibl.author: Palladius Rutilius Taurus Emilianus, Opus agriculture Palladii

cit.quote: The same author, in the fourth book: in the month of March, around the Kalends of April, the hives should be tended, so that all refuse is removed, and the filth that the winter season has gathered, and small worms and moths and spiders, by which the use of the combs is spoiled, and butterflies, which cause worms to be born from their own dung. Then smoke of dried cattle dung, burnt, should be applied, which is beneficial to the bees' health. This cleaning should be repeated often, up to the autumn season. You should do all this, and everything else, chastely and soberly, and apart from baths or sharp foods and unclean smells and all salted foods. The same author, in the fifth book: in the month of April too the hives should be cleaned of filth and of the butterflies, which are most abundant then, since other things are flowering, as will be said where butterflies are treated.

div.head: <DE ALVEARIUM APUM DEBITA CASTRACIONE, TRIGESSIMUM CAPITULUM>

bibl.author: Palladius Rutilius Taurus Emilianus, Opus agriculture Palladii

cit.quote: Hives are culled in the month of June, according to Palladius in the eighth book. That they are ripe for the extraction of honey is shown by several signs. First, if they are full, we hear the fine murmur of the bees, for empty rows of combs, like hollow buildings, amplify the sounds they receive; so, when the sound of the murmur is loud and hoarse, we recognize that the honeycomb frames are not yet ready for harvesting. Also, when they drive the drones from their seats — the larger bees, meant for breeding — this attests to the honey being ripe.

bibl.author: Palladius Rutilius Taurus Emilianus, Opus agriculture Palladii

cit.quote: Hives should be culled in the morning hours, however, when the bees are sluggish, and, so that they are not roused by the heat, smoke of galbanum and dry buffalo dung should be applied while they are sluggish, which it is fitting to kindle in a small pot, coals having been made. That vessel should be shaped so that it can release smoke through a narrow opening, and so, as the bees fall, the honey is gathered back for the swarm's food. At this time, a fifth part of the combs should be left. Rotten and defective combs should of course be removed from the hives. Then we make the honey by gathering the combs onto the cleanest cloth and diligently pressing them; but before we press, we shall cut away the corrupted parts of the combs, or those holding young; for these spoil the honey with a bad taste. Fresh honey should be kept for a few days in open vessels and skimmed on top, until, cooling, it ferments with the heat of new must. The finest honey will be that which flows out on its own before the second pressing, as it were. In this month we also make the wax, which, in a bronze vessel full of boiling water, will be softened along with the finely chopped remains of the combs, and then, dissolved in other vessels without water, poured into molds. The same author, in the eleventh book: in the month of October too, hives should be culled in the manner described. And if there is abundance, take some; if only a moderate amount, leave the middle portion because of winter scarcity; but if barrenness appears in the cells, take nothing at all.

Also Aristotle: when flowers appear, the bees then make honey, as has been said; and so the keeper should then extract the honey from the hives, since they will then suddenly make more in its place. In extracting honey, enough should be left for the bees' food in winter; otherwise the hive is ruined. The keeper, however, should leave them honey in proportion to their number; for, if he leaves them much, they will afterward make less honey, and if it is scant, they will grow old before finishing their work. Sometimes, however, because of the scarcity of remaining honey, keepers feed the bees on sweet things, like figs and the like.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Also Pliny, in the eleventh book: care is needed in extracting the combs, since the bees despair, or die, or scatter from lack of food. On the other hand, abundance breeds idleness. When honey is extracted, it is most useful to drive off the bees with smoke, lest they grow angry or greedily devour the honey themselves. It is prescribed that the honey be extracted by clean, washed hands. Bees also hate theft and women's periods, that is, menstruation. The same author, in the twenty-first book: when honey is extracted, the exits should be encircled with broom or white bryony, so that the bees do not flee the hive. Vessels for honey and combs, they advise, should be washed with water, and, once boiled, make a most wholesome vinegar.

div.head: <DE ALVEARIUM UTILITATE IN MEDICAMINE, TRIGESSIMUM PRIMUM CAPITULUM>

cit.quote: Beehives are also useful in medicine, according to Avicenna in the second treatise of the second book of the Canon. For their debris is warming toward the end of the second degree. The green kind is better: it greatly cleanses impetigo and draws out splinters and thorns. This is sometimes used in place of ammoniacum. The same author, on 'medum.'

'Puri' is the wall of bees' homes, in which they lay their eggs and young, and honey collects in it. 'Muri,' however, is black, the filth of the windows. The nature of 'muri' is an even, soothing substance; it fills unclean ulcers and moistens by accident, since it seals together and blocks the pores, and is the base of all plasters. In it there is a slight ripening effect and some dissolving power, from the great dissolving power of honey. And in black 'muri' there is a strong drawing power; for it draws splinters and thorns lodged deep in the flesh, and in it there is little fineness or cleansing, but the greatest soothing. It soothes sinews and hardness of abscesses. It also helps roughness of the chest, applied, and especially swallowed. It is also good for ulcers of the intestines. It is also said to draw out poisons, and is applied to wounds from poisoned arrows. Black 'muri,' by the strength of its smell, causes sneezing.
Also Aristotle: bees enclose, at the far edge around the hive, what is called 'micoz': it is very black, like dregs, coming from the earth; its smell is very sharp and it is good for burns.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Also Pliny, in the eleventh book: propolis, the third layer in the crust, is of great use for medicines: it has a strong smell, for which many use it in place of galbanum.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: The same author, in the twenty-second book: propolis draws out stings and everything lodged in the body, disperses swellings, cooks hard ones, greatly eases pains of the sinews, and closes into a scar ulcers that are already dispersing.

div.head: <DE HIIS QUE APIBUS SUNT CONTRARIA ET NOCIVA, TRIGESIMUM SECUNDUM CAPITULUM>

bibl.author: Palladius Rutilius Taurus Emilianus, Opus agriculture Palladii

cit.quote: Their own good fortune often harms bees, according to Palladius, in the fourth book. For if the year is too abundant in flowers, while they occupy themselves solely with the care of making honey, they think nothing of their offspring. Neglecting to replenish this, the same people, worn down by labor, is destroyed by the ruin of their whole race. And so, when you see excessive honey flowing from a large, continuous harvest of flowers, after three days, closing the opening, do not let them go out, and so they will be turned to breeding offspring.
Also Isidore: bees are put to flight by smoke, and roused to anger by disturbance.

bibl.author: Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris, Plinius maior

cit.quote: The same Pliny, in the eleventh book on bees: they hate smoke and women's periods, that is, menstruation; and so, when the honey is extracted, they are driven off with smoke. They also hate foul smells and even perfumes. And so scented ointments trouble them.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: ...wasps and hornets, and of the gnat family, those called mule-flies, swallows and certain other birds. Frogs lie in wait for them coming to drink, especially when they are breeding. Toads too come uninvited, and frogs are said not to feel the sting of bees. Sheep are also their enemy, their wool difficult to free itself from once entangled. They are also killed by the smell of crabs, if any are cooked nearby. They are also harmed by an echo resounding, which strikes them with fear by its shifting position. Mist too is their enemy. Spiders are also hostile, when they prevail enough to weave over the hives, and do harm. The lazy butterfly too, fluttering about, is destructive when lamps are lit. It feeds on the wax itself and leaves excrement from which wood-worms are born. A spider, too, wherever it goes with its thread, especially envelops their wing-down. Wood-worms are also born in the wood itself, and especially seek out the wax. The greed for pasture also troubles them, an excessive abundance of flowers, especially in springtime, quickly filling their bellies. The same author, in the twenty-eighth book: it is certain that bees flee hives touched by menstrual blood.

Also Ambrose: if someone accidentally pours oil on bees, they are nearly killed, since, their pores blocked, they cannot draw in that airy breath, as has been said above. Also Aristotle: bees are weakened in their work by what they suffer from small creatures; these indeed harm bees, but the bees kill and remove them. The creature that flies around a candle knocks the combs to the ground when it breathes in, and bees do not sting it, but it flees when fumigated. Wasps too, and swallows, and frogs, harm bees, catching them when they come to drink. Bees, however, flee no animal; but some of them flee others, since they fight among themselves. The swan watches the entrance of the bees and strikes forcefully there so that they come out; and if one flies out, it seizes and eats it. Nor is it harmed by the bees; but it is perhaps killed by the keeper of the hive.

Moreover, it harms bees to come near wasps and sheep. A multitude of males also hinders the bees' business. Rainy weather also harms bees. In the hives is found a worm that makes a web like a spider's and dominates the whole hive and rots the honey. There are also certain solitary, idle bees, which, flying through the air as though busying themselves with the industrious bees, enter the hives and eat the honey; but the industrious bees fight with the idle ones and kill them and drive them from the hives, and especially their kings do this.

div.head: <DE APUM INFIRMITATIBUS SIVE MORBIS, TRIGESSIMUM TERCIUM CAPITULUM>

bibl.author: Liber de natura rerum Thome Cantimpratensis

cit.quote: Illnesses befall bees for the most part in fertile hives, as is found in the Book of the Nature of Things. And illness comes upon them from their own idleness and from the filth of the hives. When they fall ill, they eat more than they used to before, out of the devotion they hold for honey. They die, however, from many causes, especially if there are many leaders and each one governs a single faction. And if any part of the hive dies, the rest remove it. Bees indeed have small creatures born among them; and if the bees are strong, they kill and remove them. Other bees, however, are weakened in their work by what they suffer from these small creatures.

bibl.author: Palladius Rutilius Taurus Emilianus, Opus agriculture Palladii

cit.quote: Also Palladius, in the fourth book: in the month of March, illness is especially apt to befall bees; for, after the winter fast, greedily seeking out the bitter flowers of spurge and elm, which flower first, they suffer looseness of the bowels and perish unless you are quick with a remedy. You shall then offer crushed pomegranate seeds with Aminean wine, or raisins with Syrian resin and dry wine, or all these together, ground and cooked in harsh wine, which should then be cooled and set in wooden troughs. Also, rosemary decocted in honey-water congeals, and its juice is applied in a small dish.

But if they appear listless and shrunken, sluggish in their silence, and their dead bodies are frequently found, you should pour into troughs made of reed honey cooked with oak-gall powder and dried rose gall. Above all, it will help to always trim away, with the finest, sharpest tools, the rotten parts of the combs or the empty cells, which a swarm reduced by some mishap will not be able to fill, lest, one part of the combs disturbed, it forces the bees to abandon their shaken dwelling.

Also Aristotle: bees fall ill especially when flowers dry up from dry air, since that season is dry. They die, however, if their heads are anointed with oil and placed against the sun. A bee that loses a limb does not die, but dies once it stings. Bees also die if they have too many leaders. Illnesses also often arise from the barrenness of the hives, and sometimes from their idleness, and also from the foul smell of the hives.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Also Pliny, in the eleventh book: the health of bees is judged by their cheerfulness and sheen; for they sense their own dead by nature, the sign of which is a sluggish sadness. They also attend funerals in the manner of mourners. When their king is destroyed by disease, the common people grieve with sluggish sorrow, neither gathering food nor going forth, but gathering with a sad murmur around his body and, unless helped then, dying of hunger. They are killed by oil, however, especially if their heads are anointed and they are placed in the sun. Sometimes they even bring death upon themselves, when they sense the honey being taken and greedily devour it.

div.head: <DE BEATE CECILIE AD APES HEDIFICATORIA COMPARACIONE, TRIGESSIMUM QUARTUM CAPITULUM>

cit.quote: Cecilia, in her own legend, is compared to the bee because of her manifold virtue, and so that verse written in the ninth chapter of Ecclesiasticus is fittingly applied to her: 'the bee is small among flying things, and her fruit has the beginning of sweetness.' Among bees, according to blessed Ambrose, the art of building their homes is shared, the labor of making honey is shared, the purity of conceiving their young is shared. For, according to him, they have virginal wholeness, since they mate with no coupling, are undone by no lust, nor shaken by the pains of childbirth, and yet establish a swarm of many offspring; for, while other birds lay but a single brood a year, bees produce twin broods. So too blessed Cecilia, from the beginning of her infancy, took up the art of catholic belief, the labor of bodily austerity, the purity of virginal wholeness. And of these three things it is said in her legend: Cecilia, instructed in the faith of Christ from her very cradle, as to the first; clothed in a hairshirt against the flesh, as to the second; she carefully preserved her virginity, as to the third. By the first she avoided the heretical falsehood of the devil, by the second she condemned the corrupting vanity of the world, by the third she rooted out the slippery pleasure of the flesh. And so the counsel of the Wise Man is to be held and taken up, who, after saying that the bee is small among flying things, in commendation of blessed Cecilia, then instructs us to imitate her, saying: do not glory in your clothing, and be not exalted in the day of your honor. And it continues: before you hear, answer not a word, and do not stand among sinners. Do not glory in your clothing, nor be exalted with pride, but rather, understand, be humbled by the austerity and mortification of blessed Cecilia's example. Do not stand among sinners, but rather, understand, be purified by the wholeness and incorruption of blessed Cecilia's example. Before you hear — that is, what must be done, through instruction in the faith — answer not a word, that is, understand, do not, after blessed Cecilia's example, rush into action through indiscreet activity — just as bees, in flying, extend their wings and, once extended, draw them in. In extending and drawing them in they make a sound. So blessed Cecilia made a sound in prayer through her sighing, extended her wings in contemplation toward the Lord, and drew them in again in preaching to her neighbor. And this is the right order of preachers: that through prayer they may deserve to receive remission of sins, through contemplation the illumination of hidden things, through preaching the accumulation of merits. And of these three things it is said in her legend: she did not cease from prayer, day or night, as to the first; nor did she cease from holy conversations, as to the second; she called Tiburtius and Valerian to their crowns, as to the third. And so, following her example, the Wise Man instructs preachers, adding in the authority quoted above: before you question, do not blame anyone, and, when you have questioned, reprove justly. Before you question — that is, in prayer — do not blame anyone — that is, in preaching — but rather, after blessed Cecilia's example, first question — that is, seek divine counsel in prayer; and afterward reprove — that is, vice, in preaching — and this justly, that is, with due discretion and care, which is fully worked out in contemplation. It should also be noted that bees help one another mutually in working, spur on the sluggish to make honey, and give their lives for the defense of their homes. So blessed Cecilia helped the poor through the giving of alms, roused unbelievers to the faith through the working of miracles, and laid down her life for the home of her homeland through martyrdom and suffering. She began her suffering first, since for this she was brought before the judge; she adorned it second, since through this she was judged innocent; she completed it third, when her soul was separated from her body. The first showed her charity and love, the second her sincerity and innocence, the third her steadfastness and patience. Of these three things it is said in her legend: Cecilia herself was in the end investigated over the wealth of Valerian, which she had already given to the poor — behold the first; that Almachius, after a long dispute, when he could not overcome her, ordered her to be burned in a boiling bath, once she had been brought before him — behold the third; but, while the attendants continually stoked the fire, she remained a whole day and night as though in the coldest place; whom the executioner struck three times and could not sever her head, but left her half-alive, and she, surviving three more days, strengthened those present in the faith — behold the second. And so the Wise Man adds, in the authority quoted above: there is a man needy and rich in his poverty, and the eye of God looked upon him and raised him from his lowliness and exalted his head, and many marveled at him and honored God. Surely blessed Cecilia was needy through her constant act of giving aid, but rich through the feeling of her honey-sweet love; she is looked upon by God through the grace of his acceptance, raised from the lowliness, that is, of her sex, through the constancy of her suffering, her head is exalted through the abundance of her reward, many marvel at her through the effectiveness of the working of miracles, and honor God through the offering of thanksgiving.

div.head: <DE BEATI AMBROSII AD APES CONGRUA ASSIMILACIONE, TRIGESSIMUM QUINTUM CAPITULUM>

cit.quote: Blessed Ambrose can likewise be compared to the bee, and so that verse written in the fourteenth chapter of Judges can most fittingly be applied to him: 'a swarm of bees was in the lion's mouth, and a honeycomb.' For while he was still a small child, a swarm entered his mouth, as is commonly recorded in his legend. The swarm of bees is the gathering of virtues, the honeycomb is sweet instruction, the lion's severity is due correction. Or, in the lion's mouth is noted his true preaching, in the swarm of bees his holy way of life, in the honeycomb his useful fruitfulness. And these three things suit him, since he was a teacher, a saint, and a bishop and prelate. His way of life is rightly signified by the swarm of bees for a fourfold reason. For the bee has purity in its feeding, since it chooses the best flowers; diligence in its action, since it is never idle; cunning in its perception, since it builds its home and makes honey with wondrous skill; fecundity in its bearing, since it produces twin broods every year. So blessed Ambrose had purity of incorruption against the pleasure of the flesh, constancy of good action against faintheartedness of heart, cunning of vigilance against presumption, fecundity of devotion against despair. And these are the four virtues that exclude the four temptations. And so of him can be explained that which is said: the bee is small among flying things, and her fruit has the beginning of sweetness. Surely blessed Ambrose was a bee in the diligence of his good work, small in the humility of his own regard for himself, flying in the lightness of his incorruption, honey-flowing in the sweetness of his devotion and prayer. It should also be noted that Ambrose's teaching is rightly signified by honey. For honey has a fourfold power, namely a cutting one, and so it is put in syrups; an inflaming one, and so it harms the bilious; a loosening one, and so it helps the internal organs; a healing one, and so it benefits wounds. So the teaching of preaching and theological instruction cuts through the threat of punishments, aims through the remembrance of blessings, purges through the rebuke of sins, heals and saves through the promise of rewards. By the first it instills fear, by the second love, by the third grief, by the fourth hope and sweetness. And these are the four affections of the mind. And so it is said in Revelation, chapter ten: I took the little book from the angel's hand, and it was in my mouth as sweet as honey, and, when I had eaten it, my belly was made bitter. Surely the teaching of theological instruction is called a book that strikes us with fear of the condemnation of the wicked, an angelic book that rouses us to love through the bestowal of blessings, sweet since it offers sweetness in the expectation of rewards, but bitter, instilling grief from contrition for sins.

div.head: <DE APTALO>

bibl.author: Liber de natura rerum Thome Cantimpratensis

cit.quote: The 'aptalo,' as is found in the Book of the Nature of Things, is a most fierce animal, so much so that a hunter cannot approach it. It has long horns, shaped like a saw, so that it can even cut down large, tall trees and bring them to the ground. And when it is thirsty it comes to the river Euphrates and drinks. There is a shrub, called in Greek 'beretice,' having thin, long shoots, with which, as it plays with its horns, it entangles them in its branches, and so, crying out for a long time, it is heard and killed by the hunter.

div.head: <DE ARANEA>

cit.quote: Describing the natures and properties of the spider according to the opinions of the philosophers, we shall first treat the naming of the spider and the fitting derivation of that name, the disposition of its body, and the fragile condition of its work; second, the distinction of the sexes and their generation; third, the manifold kind or diversity of spiders; fourth, the marvelous weaving of the spider's webs; fifth, the hunting or preying of spiders; sixth, the active hunting of spiders and the remedy for their venom; seventh, the effectiveness and power of the spider and its web in the healing of illnesses.

div.head: <DE ARANEE NOTIFICACIONE ET NOMINIS EIUSDEM CONGRUA IMPOSICIONE ET CORPORIS DISPOSICIONE ET SUI OPERIS FRAGILIS CONDICIONE, PRIMUM CAPITULUM>

cit.quote: The spider, according to Avicenna, is a small, creeping, many-footed animal, having six or eight feet, which are always in pairs and never odd in number. And this was necessary so that its gait might always be even, as would its own burden. And this is general in creatures having two or more feet. It has some feet shorter and some longer, because of the different tasks it performs; for with some it thins the threads and draws them out lengthwise, with some it weaves the threads together, with some it crawls along the threads. And, when it wishes, it hangs itself motionless on the surface of its web.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis, Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: The spider, however, according to Isidore in the twelfth book, is a worm of the air, named from its nourishment by the air. Though small in body, it draws out long threads, and, always intent on its web, scarcely ceases from its labor. It endures, however, a perpetual loss in its labor or work, since often, from a slight gust of wind or a drop of rain, its web is torn and it loses its work, since its labor passes away swiftly, at the cost of its work.

div.head: <DE SEXUUM DISCRECIONE AC GENERACIONE, SECUNDUM CAPITULUM>

cit.quote: Spiders have a distinction of sex, according to Aristotle in the fifth book. The female is of larger body than the male, and has longer, more flexible feet, better suited to movement and also to weaving. And, as he says in the same fifth book, at the time of love and mating the female draws the male in by the threads, and afterward the male draws the female, and this drawing will not cease until they are joined. And the male is placed above the female's belly. And this manner of coming together is necessary for them because of the roundness of the belly. And this joining occurs especially at the end of spring and the beginning of summer, and sometimes in autumn and the beginning of winter. And then they are most harmful, and their stings most venomous.

div.head: <DE ARANEARUM MULTIPLICI MANERIE SEU DIVERSIFICACIONE, TERCIUM CAPITULUM>

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: There are many kinds of spiders. There is a certain kind, according to Pliny in the tenth book, fourth chapter, called the 'spalanen,' which is similar to an ant but of far larger body, having a red head, while the rest of its body is black in color, sprinkled with white spots. And its sting is more frequent than a wasp's. It lives especially near ovens and mills. The remedy against its sting is to show it an animal of the same kind, similarly struck, and for this purpose they are kept once found dead. Their crushed and drunk shells heal a weasel's bite.

There is also another, woolly kind, with a large head, and the pain of its sting is like a scorpion's, and its bite causes the knees to give way and brings on dimness of sight and vomiting.
