There is also another kind of spider, named 'myrmicoleon' or 'myriceon,' otherwise called 'formicaleon' [antlion], resembling an ant, with a white head, having a black body marked with white spots, whose bite torments with the pain of a wasp. And it is called 'formicaleon,' since it hunts ants as a lion does and sucks out their moisture. But it is devoured by sparrows and other birds, as the ant is.

Aristotle also says, in the eighth book On Animals, that some spiders are small and of varied color and are of sharp, quick movement; others are larger and black in color, and their front legs are longer, and they are of slower movement, except when stirred by mating. And the black ones usually weave near the ground, among crevices, and stay in their web until some small creature, like a fly, falls in and they catch it. And if they are hungry, they suck out its moisture, and then carry it to their own place, where they store and keep it until they are hungry again. And when they have drunk all the moisture, they cast away the rest and return to hunting again.

And they do not hunt until they have repaired what was torn in the web. And if someone tears the web, the spider will begin to repair it around sunset or around sunrise. And it works hardest then, since more small creatures fall into the web at that time. And the female hunts as well, and the male helps her. The spider hides itself beneath the web or the weaving, so as not to be seen by small creatures, and especially when it is large, since because of its size it cannot easily be hidden. The female lays eggs, from which small spiders are afterward formed. And, as soon as they are born, she places them in the web, and at once they move and set themselves to weaving, as though they had been trained in the mother's womb, and to hunting too; hence they immediately fit their nets to suit their prey.

There is a certain species of spider that hunts a small lizard. For it first begins to weave over the lizard until it binds its opening with a strong binding, and then leaps upon it and stings it until it dies. Also, in the same place, he says that certain spiders are often found in beehives, and these corrupt the honey and suck out its liquid, and weave against the combs and corrupt them. Avicenna says the same.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: And Pliny, on the generation of spiders, in the eleventh book, twenty-fifth chapter, says thus: the nature of spiders is especially worthy of wonder. There are several kinds of it. Among these is one called the 'spalongio,' whose body is not small, varied, pointed, quick to leap, and has a harmful bite. Another species is of larger body and black color and longer leg, weaving itself burrows near the ground. A third species is one that weaves conspicuous webs with skillful construction.

div.head: <DE TELARUM ARANEE MIRABILI CONEXIONE, QUARTUM CAPITULUM>

cit.quote: It is a marvel, however, how such fine, wool-like material can suffice for so great a work, drawn out, as is believed, gradually from the spider's own body for the weaving of so great a web. And yet its body is scarcely ever found empty of such material. Nor does what Democritus says seem to be true, that there would be such decay of the spider's belly that so great a fertility of wool-material would be generated from its own waste. Hence Aristotle refutes Democritus in the eighth book, saying that he did not speak the truth on this matter. The reason for this seems to be that spiders and other such ringed creatures need little nourishment and little food, because of their scant blood and heat. Hence, since a spider does not take in so much food that it could incomparably emit more, continually, for the preparation of its web, the emission of surplus would be greater than the intake of food, and the surplus waste greater than the necessary digestion for the animal's proper preservation, as the same author says.

Also Pliny, in the same place: with a moderate claw it draws out a round, smooth thread, and with marvelous skill leads the warp threads from bottom to top, and again draws a crosswise thread from point to point.
